ACL Tear

Knee & Sports · 1 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidencecommon · ~400,000 ACL reconstructions / yr · 100,000–200,000 ruptures / yr in US (OB) · half of all knee injuries

Most injured knee ligament (TO)MCL > ACL · ACL = most commonly operated knee ligament (MCL mostly nonop)
✗ Wrong options: LCL · ALL

Female : male4.5 : 1 (Orthobullets, OB) · 2–9× (OB) · ~8× (TO) · "twice as likely" (OB) — read the options · gap not seen until puberty

Femalesinjured younger, on the supporting leg (males → kicking leg) · ACL = 24.5% of ligamentous knee injuries in high-school athletes

Risk factorsfemale soccer, male basketball · valgus moment at knee + adduction moment at hip on landing · previous concussion (neuromuscular alteration)
✗ Wrong options: varus alignment · LLD · prior meniscal tear · ↑ hamstring strength (protective)

Associated injurieslateral meniscus tear 54% in acute tears (most common intra-articular injury) · medial meniscus in chronic · PCL, LCL / PLC (high energy, knee dislocation) · chronic ACL-deficient knee → chondral injury, complex unrepairable + bucket-handle MM tears

Anatomy – AM/PL bundles, footprints (resident's & bifurcate ridges), blood supply & ALL

Anteromedial (AM) Posterolateral (PL)
Named for Tibial insertion Tibial insertion
Tight in Flexion (TO: taut in flexion + extension) Extension; loose in flexion + mid-flexion
Isometry More isometric Greatest length change
Main job Anterior tibial translation (esp. in flexion) Rotation near extension; resists tibial IR + pivot shift
Exam Lachman / anterior drawer Pivot shift
Size (TO) Longer + bulkier (~38 mm) Shorter (~18 mm) (✗ Wrong options: "PL bulkier + longer")
Femoral footprint Proximal to bifurcate ridge; high + deep; 10:30 Distal to bifurcate ridge; low + shallow; 9:30
Tibial footprint Anterior Posterior

Both bundlesentire femoral insertion lies posterior to the lateral intercondylar ridge (medial wall of LFC) · femoral insertion nearly vertical in extension (AM proximal to PL), nearly horizontal at 90° · parallel + taut in extension (TO) · no fibre truly isometric · no histological separation of bundles (TO)

Footprint areas (TO)AM femoral 47 ± 13 mm², tibial 56 ± 21 mm² · PL femoral 49 ± 13 mm², tibial 53 ± 21 mm²

Femoral ridgeslateral intercondylar ridge = resident's ridge → anterior edge of ACL, runs proximo-distal · bifurcate ridge → separates AM / PL, runs antero-posterior (⟂ LIR) (Orthobullets, OB) · TO: "resident's ridge separates AM + PL" — read the options

Medial intercondylar ridge + bifurcate prominenceon lateral wall of MFC → PCL footprint
✗ Wrong options: ACL

Ideal femoral tunnel (OB)6.1 mm posterior to resident's ridge + 1.7 mm proximal to bifurcate ridge
✗ Wrong options: distal to BR + anterior to resident's ridge

Tibial insertion (OB)11 mm anterior to anterior border of PCL · ~6 mm anterior to median / medial tibial eminence · ~9 mm posterior to intermeniscal ligament · medial + anterior to posterior border of anterior horn LM · meniscal roots variable (unreliable alone)
✗ Wrong options: 15 mm anterior to PCL · 16 mm / 11 mm anterior to eminence · 17 mm behind IML

Dimensions32 mm long (22–41 mm) × 7–12 mm wide · 31–38 mm (TO) · narrowest at mid-substance; insertions > 3.5× larger (TO)

Tibial insertion (TO)broader than femoral (~120%), fibres fan out · fibres pass under transverse intermeniscal ligament, blend with anterior horn LM · stronger than femoral → avulsion on tibial side, substance tear femoral side

Course (TO)intra-articular but extrasynovial (intracapsular) · origin posteromedial LFC (medial wall of LFC) → runs inferomedially → tibia between spines

Composition90% type I + 10% type III collagen
✗ Wrong options: type II (articular cartilage, nucleus pulposus) · type III (Dupuytren) · type IV (basement membrane)

Blood supplymiddle genicular artery + synovium · MGA arises directly from popliteal, pierces oblique popliteal ligament / posterior capsule, runs along dorsal ACL · inferior medial + lateral genicular → distal ACL (minor) · no significant supply from bony attachments (Scapinelli) · proximal ACL better supplied
✗ Wrong options: superior genicular · inferior medial genicular as main supply

Avascular zone (TO)5–10 mm proximal to tibial attachment (anterior fibrocartilage) → poor healing

MGA also suppliesPCL (+ fat pad) · ACL tear haemarthrosis = MGA branches · menisci → inferior / superior medial + lateral genicular (LM = inferior lateral, MM = inferior medial)

Innervationposterior articular nerve (branch of tibial nerve)

Function85% of restraint to anterior tibial translation · secondary restraint to tibial IR + varus / valgus (TO: resists varus at full extension) · strength 2200 N

ACL reflex (TO)mechanoreceptors (Ruffini, Pacini, Golgi-like) → proprioception via fusimotor system · not a protective mechanism · loss / inhibition → quadriceps weakness
✗ Wrong options: explains female tears · explains poor healing

Notch (TO)narrower in women · notch width index (epicondylar : notch width) small → ↑ ACL tear · notch roof = Blumensaat's line; notch roof angle 37° (23–60°)

PCL contrast (TO)bundles named for femoral footprint · AL 55%, bulkier, tight in flexion · PM 45%, tight in extension · 38 mm long, 10–11 mm diameter · tibial insertion wider than femoral
✗ Wrong options: "ACL named for femoral, PCL for tibial"

ALLorigin proximal + posterior to lateral epicondyle / LCL · insertion anterolateral tibia halfway between Gerdy's tubercle + fibular head · anterolateral rotatory stabiliser · Segond = ALL avulsion · LET recreates it

Lateral knee distractorstibial tubercle = patellar tendon · anterior fibular head = LCL (femur just posterior to lateral epicondyle) · posterior fibular head = biceps long head · lateral gastrocnemius → femur posterior + proximal to LCL · popliteus → femur anterior + distal to LCL · lateral epicondyle = ALL origin

Genes & lab markers

COL5A1 genotype↓ risk of ACL rupture in women
✗ Wrong options: GH dislocation · cuff tear · patellar dislocation · discoid meniscus

CollagenACL 90% type I / 10% type III

Post-ACLR septic arthritisESR 105 + CRP 44 at 4 wk (TO) · CRP 100 mg/L, ESR 40, aspirate 52,000 WBC/mm³ at 3 wk (OB) → infection

ACL-deficient kinematics & gait

Gaitabsent normal femoral IR in terminal swing · ↓ anterior tibial translation in late swing (adaptive: ↓ quads / ↑ hamstrings)
✗ Wrong options: absent femoral ER · ↑ posterior femoral translation · ↑ midstance flexion · ↑ hip adduction

Normal gaitheel strike near full extension, femur IR on tibia → midstance flexion + femoral ER · late swing: anterior tibial translation (quads)

Kinematics↑ paradoxical anterior femoral translation with flexion · larger AP translation of MFC · LFC more posterior in full extension · axial rotation same in first 30°, differs beyond
✗ Wrong options: no change

Medial tibial translationat higher flexion in ACL-deficient knee → ↑ contact of tibial spine with inner MFC → degeneration

Dynamic imaginganterior shift + IR of tibia at low flexion = ACL · posterior shift = PCL · ↑ IR + posterior translation = PCL + MCL · ↑ valgus + slight IR = MCL · ↑ ER = PLC (LCL, popliteus, arcuate)

Consequenceabnormal loading → post-traumatic OA, meniscal + osteochondral injury

2Mechanism

Pathoanatomy

Non-contact pivottibia translates anteriorly with knee in slight flexion + valgus · or blow to lateral knee · soccer, basketball, skiing, football

Bone bruise mechanismvalgus–ER of femur on fixed tibia → LFC impacts posterior lip of lateral tibial plateau (= pivot-shift event)

Segond mechanism (TO)IR + varus in flexion · capsular avulsion (mid-lateral capsule / ALL; meniscotibial ligament — OB)

Hyperextensionkissing contusions of anterior tibia + femur (PCL-type)
✗ Wrong options: ACL pattern

Female predispositionlanding biomechanics + quadriceps-dominant neuromuscular activation (biggest role)

Mechanism – PCL injury on flexed knee (TO)

Lands on flexed knee, foot plantarflexed (TO)dashboard-type posterior force on tibia → PCL
✗ Wrong options: ACL · PLC · LCL

Female athletes – risk factors & neuromuscular prevention

Female risk factor (TO) Detail
Quadriceps dominance More quad than hamstring activation; slower to peak hamstring torque · males decelerate with hamstrings
Erect landing Insufficient knee + hip flexion; ↑ hip IR + adduction on landing
Pelvis / alignment Wider pelvis, ↑ Q angle, knee valgus
Notch / ligament Small intercondylar notch, smaller ACL
Laxity Greater ligament laxity
Hormones Oestrogen, relaxin — indirect, via neuromuscular system
NOT a risk factor (TO) ↑ external rotation at landing · hamstring dominance

Other risk factors (TO)hard field surface, inappropriate footwear, ↑ BMI, high tibial slope, foot pronation, female sex

Greatest contributorneuromuscular factors · notch far less important
✗ Wrong options: notch width · BMI · laxity · limb alignment

Highest-risk cohortwomen with knee valgus moment on landing
✗ Wrong options: hip adduction moment · men

Landing pattern (OB)↓ hip + knee flexion, ↑ knee ER, dynamic valgus · TO says ↑ ER at landing is NOT a risk factor — read the options

Hamstringsrelative hamstring weakness / ↑ quad : hamstring ratio, electromechanical delay · after menarche quad strength ↑ more than hamstrings → hamstring-focused programmes

Menstrual cycleno consensus
✗ Wrong options: ovulatory · post-ovulatory phase

Preventionneuromuscular training / plyometrics (jump training) — core, abductor + hamstring synchrony, avoid dynamic valgus; land with more knee flexion, less valgus (Griffin; FIFA 11+) · skiers → teach how to fall

Bracingno proven prevention except ACL-deficient skiers
✗ Wrong options: brace to cut re-injury risk

3Presentation

History"pop", pain deep in knee, immediate swelling (70%) / haemarthrosis, instability, can't return to sport, hard to weight-bear

Non-contact + acute haemarthrosisACL tear > 60% (literature > 70%; Maffulli 71 / 106) · acute effusion → ACL; slow effusion → meniscus
✗ Wrong options: MCL · MM tear · patellar dislocation · contusion

Inspectioneffusion · quadriceps avoidance gait · varus → ↑ re-rupture risk

Motionlacks extension → meniscal block (locked bucket handle) or arthrofibrosis · check McMurray, dial, varus / valgus

Lateral joint line tendernesslikeliest extra finding with + pivot shift (LM tear)
✗ Wrong options: MJL tenderness · dial · varus at 30° · posterior drawer

Neurovascularperoneal function after high-energy / multiligament pattern

Diagnosis – Lachman grading, pivot shift mechanism, hemarthrosis

Lachman grade Orthobullets OB
1 3–5 mm 0–5 mm
2 5–10 mm 6–10 mm
3 > 10 mm > 10 mm
A / B A = firm endpoint · B = no endpoint B = soft / no endpoint

Lachman20–30° flexion, stabilise femur, translate tibia · compare sides (physiological laxity) · 2B = 9 mm, soft endpoint at 30° · 4 mm firm = 1A · 12 mm firm = 3A · at 90° = anterior drawer

PCL tear"false" Lachman (posterior subluxation)

Test Sensitivity Specificity Note
Lachman 87% 93% Most sensitive; mainly AM bundle
Pivot shift 61% 97% Most specific; PL bundle / rotation; easier under anaesthesia
Anterior drawer (90°) 48% — Lower sensitivity
KT-1000 — — Quantifies anterior laxity; slight flexion, ER 10–30°

Pivot shift — mechanismextension + tibial IR + valgus → lateral tibial plateau subluxed anteriorly (impinges LFC) → flex → ITB becomes a reducing force → LTP reduces with a clunk
✗ Wrong options: medial plateau · ER · reduced in extension

Reduction angle20–30° (Orthobullets) · 30–40° (OB) · 15–20° (Delhi active test, TO) — read the options

Pivot shiftmimics the giving-way event · patient fully relaxed · better gauge of functional outcome · stays abnormal with vertical graft
✗ Wrong options: anterior femoral tunnel

Pivot shift grade Finding
0 Normal
I Glide (may be physiological)
II Clunk
III Clunk with locking (gross / explosive)

Delhi active test (TO)standing, active test for complete ACL tear · limb abducted, foot on table (tibial IR) · flex → at 15–20° subluxed LTP relocates (shift / clunk) · extend → anterolateral subluxation (jerk)
✗ Wrong options: supine · PCL

Positive test Points to
Pivot shift / Lachman ACL
Quadriceps active test, reverse pivot shift, posterior drawer (12 mm at 90°) PCL
Dial ↑ ER > 10° (~15°) at 30° only PLC
Dial at 30° + 90° PLC + PCL
Varus laxity at 30° LCL / PLC (at 0° + 30° if ACL torn too)
McMurray, extending with IR + varus Lateral meniscus
McMurray, extending with ER + valgus Medial meniscus
Patellar apprehension Patellar instability / MPFL

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings — MRI & bone bruises, Segond fracture

Study Finding / use
X-ray — AP, lateral, sunrise / Merchant Often normal; Segond; deep sulcus sign; tibial spine avulsion
Segond fracture Avulsion of proximal lateral tibia by ALL (AP or notch view) · pathognomonic · ACL tear in 75–100% · present in 9% of ACL tears
Deep sulcus (terminalis) / lateral femoral notch sign Lateral X-ray: LFC depression at terminal sulcus (junction of tibial + patellar articular surfaces) · > 2 mm deep = diagnostic (uncommon, specific) · PD-FSE MRI: sulcus terminalis impaction + oedema
Post-ACLR X-ray Tunnel position (vertical = both tunnels steep) · tunnel osteolysis / widening around screws · fluoroscopy: tibial centre at 40% along Amis–Jakob line
MRI — confirm + concomitant injury Sens 97% / spec 100% (Orthobullets) · accuracy 90–95% (TO)
MRI direct signs Discontinuity on T2 (often proximal), ACL too flat vs Blumensaat, non-visualisation (subacute: only small distal stump), tibial spine avulsion
Femoral bony avulsion (adolescent) AP X-ray fragment at femoral condyle · MRI: lax fibres + attached bony fragment → repair
MRI coronal Fibres fail to reach femur · empty notch / lateral wall sign (fluid at femoral attachment → proximal avulsion)
Bone bruise Middle ⅓ LFC (sulcus terminalis) + posterior ⅓ lateral tibial plateau · > ½ of acute tears (~50%) · ↑ T2 (fat-sat), ↓ T1 = trabecular haemorrhage
Other indirect (TO) Anterior tibial translation, PCL buckling (non-specific), haemarthrosis (non-specific)
CT Revision — most sensitive + specific for bone loss / tunnel widening

Bruise "not ACL" (TO)medial tibial plateau bruise · anterior proximal tibia oedema (hyperextension) (✓ posterolateral tibia + LFC)

Chronic ACL on MRIfibres scar to PCL → acute (flat) angle

Bone bruise significancedelayed recovery of ROM after ACLR · subchondral change persists years → long-term chondral damage · when present, pathognomonic
✗ Wrong options: re-rupture · laxity · infection

Double PCL signdisplaced bucket-handle MM tear (vs LM)

Avulsion / pattern Means
Segond (anterolateral proximal tibia) ACL (ALL avulsion)
Arcuate sign (fibular head tip — LCL / biceps) PLC
Intercondylar eminence fragment ACL bony avulsion
Pellegrini–Stieda (medial femoral condyle ossification) Chronic MCL
Medial patellar facet + LFC bruise Lateral patellar dislocation
Widened lateral joint, squared condyle, cupped LTP Discoid meniscus
Large lateral plateau fracture through weight-bearing surface Plateau fracture (✗ Wrong options: Segond)

Diagnostic criteria (MRI signs, TO)

Sign Threshold
ACL–Blumensaat angle Normal ≤ 15° · > 15° (apex anterior) → torn, collapsed ACL
Deep lateral femoral notch > 2 mm
Anterior tibial translation ≥ 5 mm indicative · > 7 mm diagnostic
PCL index (B ÷ A: PCL chord ÷ max perpendicular to PCL) < 3 (buckled PCL) → ACL tear
PCL buckling after ACLR Graft laxity

Tibial eminence avulsion – meniscal block (TO)

Meyers–McKeever OB (3 types) Modified (TO, 4 types)
I Non- / minimally displaced anterior margin Little or no displacement
II Anterior aspect elevated, posterior hinge intact Elevated anteriorly + proximally, posterior cartilaginous hinge
III Completely displaced Completely displaced, intact fragment
IV — Comminuted

Epidemiology (TO)2–5% of knee injuries with effusion, age 8–14 · unossified eminence (< 14 yr) fails through cancellous bone · ACL attaches to medial spine · same mechanism as ACL tear

ImagingX-ray → CT + MRI · subtle in adults → MRI (OB)

Block to closed reduction (TO)anterior horn MM > intermeniscal ligament > anterior horn LM · entrapment 26% type II (6/23), 65% type III (37/57) (Kocher) (TO stem says "tibial tubercle" — means eminence)

Tibial eminence fracture
  • Type I or type II reduced in extension→aspirate, cast in slight flexion 6 wk
    • then→controlled-motion brace, full ROM by 10–12 wk
  • Type II–III not reducible, type IV→arthroscopic / open reduction + suture or screw
Fixation (TO) Pros Cons
Screw Less demanding, earlier mobilisation Needs large fragment, irritation, not for comminuted, impingement, iatrogenic comminution, physeal damage, removal if malpositioned
Suture Minimal physeal damage, comminuted OK (through ACL base) Technically demanding, cinch loops constrict vascularity

Concomitant injurymeniscal most common

Complications (TO)persistent ACL laxity ~40% (types III–IV) · malunion (commoner; delayed diagnosis → extension block → debride fragment / notchplasty) · nonunion (more with nonop) · loss of extension · arthrofibrosis 36% if ROM after 4 wk vs 0% early ROM (Patel)

Posterior knee (ACL mucoid degeneration / ganglion) (TO)

Mucoid degeneration (TO)glycosaminoglycan infiltration of ACL · posterior knee pain (impinges PCL + posterior capsule, bone erosion), pain in flexion (AM tightening) or terminal extension, heaviness on stairs

Treatment (TO)arthroscopic debulking / debridement
✗ Wrong options: ACL reconstruction · CKC → OKC rehab · PCL reconstruction

5Management

Acute ACL tear
  • Low demand, low laxity, no cutting / pivoting→3 months supervised PT, lifestyle change
  • Stiff, effusion, can't SLR→pre-hab: PT for ROM + quads first
    (not acute ACLR, immobilisation, rest 4 wk)
  • Young / active / pivoting sport / instability→ACL reconstruction
    • Locked bucket-handle meniscus→ACLR + meniscal repair, urgently

Operative criteria

Decision Indication / threshold
ACLR — patient Young + active (↓ meniscal / chondral damage), children (activity limitation unrealistic), older active (> 40 not a CI), partial tear with instability, prior failure
ACLR — knee Full ROM restored first (unless meniscal block)
Nonop Low demand, ↓ laxity, recreational without cutting / pivoting · non-op ↑ meniscal / cartilage damage (buckling episodes, level I–II sport)
ACL repair Femoral / tibial avulsion without mid-substance rupture, paediatric · (✗ Wrong options: mid-substance tear)
LET (OB) Age 14–25 with ≥ 2: return to contact pivoting sport, pivot ≥ grade 2, Beighton > 4 · also Segond, chronic ACL, lateral femoral notch sign, lateral laxity, recurvatum > 10°
ALL reconstruction (TO) Grade 3 / explosive pivot, pivoting athlete, Segond, revision ACLR, subjective rotational laxity, chronic ACL, high-level sport, LFC depression, Telos > 10 mm (✗ Wrong options: high-grade tear in young man alone)
Two-stage revision Tunnel > 15 mm, malpositioned tunnels / hardware blocking, infection
Staged revision (TO) Motion problem: lacks 5° extension or 20° flexion (stability fine)
Osteotomy with ACLR Varus (> 3° between mechanical axes or WBA medial to medial tibial spine tip) · slope > 12°
HTO contraindications Inflammatory arthritis, BMI > 35, flexion contracture > 15°, flexion < 90°, > 20° correction, varus thrust, PF arthritis, (lateral meniscectomy)
HTO indications < 50 yr, active, non-obese, one compartment, good vascular status, compliant
Acute MCL repair Grade III distal avulsion (pes entrapment) · grade III with valgus instability
Graft size ≥ 8 mm (< 8 mm → failure)

Timing – restoring motion before surgery; arthrofibrosis & cyclops lesion

Pre-habregain full ROM + quad strength before ACLR; wait for swelling / inflammatory phase to settle · acute ACLR in stiff, weak knee → arthrofibrosis + weakness

Stiff acute kneee.g. ROM 5–70°, can't SLR → PT for ROM · Segond + ROM 10–75° + dial 5° → ACL; PT to optimise ROM (dial < 10–15° asymmetry = no PLC)

Adolescent with deep sulcus signPT, then early reconstruction (delay → instability, secondary meniscal damage, degeneration)
✗ Wrong options: immediate ACLR · ORIF · PT + RTS

Predictors of post-op motion lossfemale, acute surgery, limited preop ROM, classic bone bruise

Preventionpre-hab, wait out inflammation, correct tunnel position, aggressive cryotherapy

Shelbourne arthrofibrosis (TO) Extension loss Flexion loss Patella
1 < 10° Normal Normal
2 > 10° Normal Normal
3 > 10° > 25° ↓ mobility (tight)
4 > 10° > 30° ↓ mobility + patella infera

TO key> 10° extension + > 25° flexion loss, patella normal → Type 2 (patellar mobility is the discriminator) — read the options · prevalence 4–38% · Rx arthroscopic debridement

Loss of motion after ACLR (most common complication)
  • < 12 weeks→aggressive PT + serial splinting
  • > 12 weeks→lysis of adhesions / MUA

Cyclops lesionfibroproliferative nodule blocks extension, "click" at terminal extension · anterior tibial tunnel → cyclops (TO) · not graft-related (OB)

Infrapatellar contracture syndromeuncommon · ↓ patellar mobility, patella infera (baja) — poor prognostic sign · loss of extension + active AND passive flexion
✗ Wrong options: "active but not passive"

Reconstruction technique — tunnel targets, tensioning & fixation

Goalanatomic restoration of AP + rotational stability · arthroscopic · clear remnant to see bony landmarks (remnant kept vs removed — no difference)

Single vs double bundleno patient-reported difference · single most common · double may restore kinematics, ↓ laxity · no definitive clinical benefit

Horizontal graft (TO)prevents pivoting · femoral tunnel obliquity sets rotational stability · isometric (vertical) graft → translation only · 10 o'clock also avoids PCL impingement in flexion
✗ Wrong options: vertical · roof-top · 11 o'clock

Femoral tunnel — coronallateral wall 10 o'clock right / 2 o'clock left (Orthobullets, OB) · 10:30 right / 1:30 left (OB) · 9:30–10 o'clock right (TO) — read the options

Femoral tunnel — sagittal1–2 mm rim to posterior cortex (Orthobullets) · ~2 mm, knee at 90° (TO) · centre on bifurcate ridge, posterior to resident's ridge · OB: posterior to LIR, just proximal to BR, ~1 cm anterior to posterior articular margin of LFC · drill in > 70° (70–90°) flexion → no posterior wall blowout

Pinczewski (radiographic)femoral tunnel 86% along Blumensaat's line (0% anterior → 100% posterior) · tibial tunnel 48% AP and 46% medial → lateral across plateau · graft coronal inclination 19°

Tibial tunnel — sagittalcentre 10–11 mm anterior to PCL (Orthobullets, OB) · 7 mm anterior to PCL = best guide (TO) — read the options · 6 mm anterior to median eminence · 9 mm behind intermeniscal ligament · 15 mm behind anterior tibial edge (TO) · in line with posterior edge of anterior horn LM (most used landmark) · posterior + parallel to Blumensaat's line in full extension · native insertion starts 10–14 mm behind anterior tibia (TO)

Tibial tunnel — coronal< 75° from horizontal (Orthobullets) · 60–75°, well-placed ~75° (OB) · start halfway between tubercle and posteromedial tibial edge · lateral fluoroscopy: tibial centre at 40% of Amis–Jakob line

Tensioningpre-conditioning ↓ stress relaxation up to 50% · 20 N vs 40 N → no difference · fix in 20–30° flexion · initial tension falls soon after fixation

Fixationaperture (interference screw) vs suspensory (cortical button, screw + washer post, staple) · alone or combined

No effect on outcomegraft type, one vs two incisions (OB) · tunnel position does (anterior to LIR = definitive adverse effect)

Femoral tunnel drilling – anteromedial portal vs transtibial

Transtibial Transportal (AM portal)
Femoral tunnel drilled Through the tibial tunnel Through the AM portal (AL portal = scope)
Clock position ≥ 11 o'clock / roof-top 12 o'clock Anatomic 10 o'clock
Graft Vertical Oblique / horizontal — more anatomic
Drawbacks Poor access to lateral wall Shorter femoral tunnel, posterior wall breach, risk to posterior LFC cartilage + subchondral bone; hyperflexion
Outcome No clinical difference (Orthobullets) · not itself a re-rupture risk

Too-anterior tibial tunnel + transtibialvertical (12:00) graft
✗ Wrong options: oblique 10:30 / 1:30

Transtibial guide reaching 11:30drill femur via AM portal (hyperflexed) or two-incision · lower notch start point
✗ Wrong options: revise tibial tunnel (bone loss) · transtibial double bundle · hyperflex + same guide

Graft choice – BTB vs hamstring vs allograft, biomechanics & graft size

BPTB autograft Quadrupled hamstring Quadriceps tendon Allograft
Load to failure 2600 N (Orthobullets) · 3000 N (TO) ~4000 N — highest; ~1.5× BPTB 2185 N —
Healing Bone-to-bone → fastest incorporation Slower (TO: delayed) ± bone block Longest; more immune reaction
Fixation Rigid screws at joint line Suspensory → windshield-wiper, tunnel widening As hamstring —
Pros Gold standard; low laxity, durable, ↑ RTS, low revision (TO) Small incision, ↓ peri-op pain, ↓ anterior knee pain, kneeling pain, extension loss No kneeling-zone scar, spares physis, often free in revision No donor morbidity; revisions
Cons Anterior knee pain 10–30%, kneeling pain, extension loss, patella fracture, patellar tendon rupture Flexor torque deficit (↓ flexion strength at 3 yr), numbness (saphenous), ↑ mid-term failure, female hamstring weakness As hamstring (suspensory) ↑ re-rupture in young, cost, disease transmission
Re-rupture risk Age < 20, graft < 8 mm Graft < 8 mm, age < 20 — 4.3× odds age 10–19; revision > 2×

Native ACL tensile strength~2200 N · 1725 N (Orthobullets graft section) — read the options · all grafts stronger than native ACL

Skeletal ageonset of menarche = best predictor in girls · maturity ~2 yr after menarche (OB) · most growth in 18 months after menarche (OB) · ~9 mm distal femur + 6 mm proximal tibia growth / yr · Tanner good; menarche delayed in elite athletes
✗ Wrong options: shoe size · doubled height at 2 · patellar ossification

Open physis< 14 yr · 60% of adolescent tears partial

Nonop (peds)compliant, low demand, no other pathology, partial tear with near-normal Lachman + pivot · otherwise poor: instability, secondary meniscal + chondral damage, ↓ return to sport

Maturity Technique
Pre-adolescent (M ≤ 12, F ≤ 11) Combined intra- + extra-articular ITB (physeal-sparing)
Approaching maturity, open physes (12F premenarchal, Risser I) All-epiphyseal or partial transphyseal, soft-tissue (hamstring) autograft, tunnel < 8 mm
Near / at maturity (M ≥ 16, F ≥ 14), Tanner IV, post-menarche Adult-type transphyseal — BPTB, quad or hamstring autograft
Femoral-sided avulsion, near maturity Arthroscopic repair + transphyseal fixation (femoral tunnels + cortical button)
Stiff knee (ROM 20–70°) PT for ROM first, then decide

Tunnel size> 12 mm most important; 8 mm < 3% vs 12 mm > 7–9% of physis (Orthobullets) · > 8 mm ↑ injury; 7–9% of physis enough for disturbance (OB) · < 8 mm keeps < 5% (OB) — read the options

Malposition Graft behaviour Clinical picture
Femoral too anterior (anterior to resident's ridge) Tight in flexion, lax in extension (cam effect → stretch) Loss of flexion ("captured knee"), graft elongation · e.g. ROM 0–75°, negative pivot
Femoral too posterior / over-the-top Lax in flexion, tight in extension Limited extension, ↑ translation in flexion · TO: "positive error", only blowout risk
Femoral vertical (12 or 11 o'clock) Controls AP translation only + Pivot, − Lachman / drawer, cutting instability, PL bundle not restored, ↓ Lysholm · TO: PCL impingement, extension block
Femoral anterior + vertical (TO) — + Pivot + ROM 0–70°
Tibial too anterior Tight in flexion + roof impingement in extension Loss of extension ("nutcracker knee"), cyclops (✗ Wrong options: flexion deficit (TO))
Tibial too posterior Impinges PCL Loss of flexion, graft tear (TO) · gross + Lachman / pivot (OB)
Tibial too medial / lateral Impinges MFC / LFC —
Lax in flexion AND extension Under-tensioned graft (not tunnel) —
No knee cycling before tibial fixation Residual laxity in flexion + extension —

Incidence< 1% · most superficial · CoNS (S. epidermidis) commonest, S. aureus 2nd · presents 2–14 days post-op (Orthobullets) · first 10–14 days (OB) · TO case at 4 wk

Riskgraft contamination, dropped graft · vancomycin soak may ↓ risk · sequential antibiotic washes → no ↑ infection in dropped grafts

  • Gächter 1–2→arthroscopic I&D, retain graft, ≥ 6 wk IV antibiotics (culture-based)

1 Blurred effusion, hyperaemic synovium

Adductor Strain

Knee & Sports · 2 / 61

1Basics

Incidence10–30% of soccer and hockey players

Adductor complexadductor longus (most commonly injured), adductor magnus, adductor brevis, gracilis, obturator externus, pectineus · all obturator nerve (Orthobullets)

2Mechanism

"Pulled groin"forceful hip extension + external rotation of an abducted leg → strong eccentric contraction of adductors

Avulsionmuscle fails in tension as the leg is abducted

Repetitive hip extension + abduction (hockey, soccer) → athletic pubalgia — adductor longus torn and retracted from the common aponeurosis with rectus abdominis (detail in Athletic Pubalgia & Adductor strain chapter)

3Presentation

Painimmediate, severe groin pain

Tendernesssubcutaneous border of the (inferior) pubic ramus · medial pubic ramus

Strengthpain ± weakness on resisted adduction vs other leg

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
X-ray: AP pelvis + lateral hip Fleck of bone if avulsion
MRI Avulsion from pubic ramus, muscle oedema + haemorrhage · T2 ↑ fluid signal at tendon origin

Adductor strain classification

Degree Findings
1st Pain, minimal loss of strength + motion
2nd Compromised strength
3rd Complete disruption, loss of muscle function

5Management

Groin injuries — adductor strain / avulsion management

Mainstay (incl. avulsion)rest, ice, protected WB as needed → gentle stretching → resistance → core strengthening → gradual return to sport

Avoid immobilisationpromotes muscle tightness + scarring / contracture

Rugby player, MRI adductor avulsionimmediate rehabilitation with increasing passive + active motion
✗ Wrong options: strict immobilisation in flexion + adduction · tendon repair · tenodesis · repair + allograft

Open repairno data / no high-level evidence it beats nonoperative care

Hockey groin syndromeexternal oblique aponeurosis tear + ilioinguinal nerve entrapment → ilioinguinal nerve ablation + external oblique reinforcement

Adductor insertion avulsion syndrome ("thigh splints")

Whatpainful proximal-to-mid femur at adductor insertions · insidious thigh pain + limp, no trauma

Exam / labspain on resisted adduction only · afebrile, normal WBC, ESR, CRP

ImagingX-rays normal · MRI (TSE inversion recovery) → linear high signal along medial (posteromedial) periosteum of proximal–mid femoral shaft, 4–9 cm long

Treatmentactivity modification + NSAIDs, observe · resolves in 1–2 months
✗ Wrong options: antibiotics · I&D · prophylactic fixation (not a stress fracture) · biopsy

Differentialosteomyelitis, neoplasm · biopsy only if pain persists or increases

X vs Y

Adductor strain Thigh splints
Onset Acute, severe Insidious
Site Pubic ramus (origin) Femoral shaft (insertion)
MRI Avulsion / oedema at pubis Periosteal high signal, posteromedial femur
Treatment Rest, ice, protected WB, early motion Activity modification, NSAIDs

Why adolescentsapophysis weaker than the musculotendinous unit during forceful contraction

Site Muscle Frequency (Rossi, 203)
Ischial tuberosity Hamstrings (BF long head, SM, ST) + adductor magnus ~50% — most common
AIIS Rectus femoris (direct head) 25%
ASIS Sartorius + TFL 20%

Iliac crest Abdominals 1% — least common
Lesser trochanter Iliopsoas —
Greater trochanter Gluteus medius + minimus —

Most common siteischial tuberosity ~50% (Rossi, OB) · AIIS most common (Schuett, 228 avulsions, OB — see ASIS chapter) — read the options

Sportssoccer + gymnastics most common

Rectus femoris origin avulsion — mechanism, innervation & nonoperative care

Mechanismeccentric contraction of rectus femoris as hip extends + knee flexes → avulses origin · kicking (missed ball, foot strikes ground) · hurdler's trailing limb striking hurdle

MRI labelrectus femoris = anterior central thigh muscle
✗ Wrong options: vastus lateralis · vastus intermedius · vastus medialis · sartorius

Nervefemoral
✗ Wrong options: genitofemoral (cremaster) · pudendal (levator ani, bulbo- / ischiocavernosus) · obturator (obturator externus, adductor longus / brevis, gracilis) · superior gluteal (gluteus medius / minimus, TFL)

Distractor insertionssartorius → pes anserinus · TFL → Gerdy's tubercle via ITB · iliopsoas → lesser trochanter · gluteus medius / minimus → greater trochanter

Historysudden "pop" in the pelvis

Examantalgic gait · anterior hip pain + hip flexion weakness · pain on resisted hip flexion, local tenderness

DifferentialSCFE, Perthes, congenital hip subluxation, malignancy, infection

Key radiology findings

RadiographsAP pelvis / AP + frog lateral hip show the AIIS avulsion · X-rays sufficient to diagnose + decide
✗ Wrong options: MRI before treatment

5Management

AIIS avulsion
  • Minimally displaced (almost all)→REST, ACTIVITY MODIFICATION, PT
  • Selected cases→SURGERY
    • Displaced > 2 cm / painful nonunion→ORIF
    • Symptomatic heterotopic ossification→ARTHROSCOPIC EXCISION

Nonoperativealmost all succeed · bed rest, ice, activity modification, NSAIDs, supervised PT · hip flexed 2 wk (↓ stretch on muscle + apophysis) → guarded WB 4 wk

Pelvic avulsions (OB)protected WB 2–4 wk → stretching + strengthening → normal activity ~2 months

16-yr soccer, minimally displaced AIISrest, activity modification + physical therapy
✗ Wrong options: corticosteroid injection (impairs healing) · early aggressive strengthening (displacement / delayed union) · MRI · ORIF

Operative criteria

Surgery for Detail
Significant displacement Commonly > 2 cm
Painful nonunion ORIF
Symptomatic heterotopic ossification Excision (arthroscopic)
High-level athlete Persistent limitation despite adequate nonop

Skeletally mature elite athletescomplete / retracted proximal rectus femoris avulsion → surgery gives faster RTP + lower recurrence · individualise

Post-traumatic rectus femoris HOarthroscopic excision → better pain, ROM, function at 2 yr

Complicationsloss of reduction · delayed union

Knee & Sports · 4 / 61

1Basics

Whoadolescents 14–17 yr approaching skeletal maturity, males > females · sprinting, running, baseball, soccer, hockey

Avulsion physiologysudden violent contraction or excess stretch across an open apophysis · often no external trauma · low-energy → no associated life-threatening injuries

Anatomy

Muscle from ASIS Nerve Insertion
Sartorius Femoral Pes anserinus → source of pes anserine bursitis
Tensor fascia lata Superior gluteal Gerdy's tubercle via ITB

Insertion distractorsfibular head = biceps femoris · femoral insertion anterior + distal to LCL = popliteus · ACL autograft = gracilis (inferior pubic ramus) + semitendinosus (ischial tuberosity), both at pes · extends hip + flexes knee = hamstrings

2Mechanism

Sartorius origin avulsion — mechanism, innervation & protected weight bearing

Mechanismindirect · sudden forceful (eccentric) contraction of sartorius ± TFL · hip extended (+ knee flexed) → sprinting (out of blocks, 400 m) or swinging a baseball bat
✗ Wrong options: external oblique · rectus femoris · iliopsoas · gluteus medius

Avulsed muscle nervesartorius → femoral
✗ Wrong options: sciatic · obturator · pudendal · inferior gluteal

History"pop" or snap · may be misdiagnosed as a muscle strain

Examtender over ASIS (superior to hip joint), groin ecchymosis · pain with straight-leg raise · weak hip flexion + knee extension · limp if severe

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP pelvis Displaced fractures visible · small fragment easily missed
CT / MRI Confirm nondisplaced fractures
CT (relative) Rarely needed — measure displacement, or tell ASIS vs AIIS origin (✗ Wrong options: urgent CT · extensive work-up)

Diagnostic criteria

Criterion ASIS avulsion
History Sudden contraction of sartorius + TFL
Exam ASIS tenderness, pain on SLR
Age Adolescent / young adult
Radiographs Fracture on standard pelvis views

White Muscle Activity Fragment
Type 1 Sartorius Sprinting Small, displaced anteriorly + inferiorly
Type 2 TFL Twisting trunk / start of bat swing Larger, displaced laterally

5Management

ASIS avulsion
  • Displacement < 3 cm (most)→PROTECTED WB, CRUTCHES, EARLY ROM
  • Displacement > 3 cm or painful nonunion→ORIF

Nonoperativerest, ice, NSAIDs, protected / progressive WB as tolerated with crutches, early ROM + stretching, PT · position limb to ↓ stretch on muscle · return when pain-free motion · outcomes equivalent to surgery

14-yr sprinter, pop, ASIS fragmentprogressive weightbearing, return when pain-free
✗ Wrong options: fix femoral neck stress fracture · iliopsoas recession (internal snapping hip has normal X-rays + can bear weight) · fix sartorius origin · fix rectus femoris direct head (that is AIIS)

1 wk after injury, improving, still on crutchesWBAT + crutches for 3 weeks total
✗ Wrong options: NWB 6 wk · closed reduction + pinning (operative choice is ORIF) · aspiration · urgent CT

12-yr bat swing, 2 cm displacedrest + protected WB with crutches
✗ Wrong options: ORIF with rectus femoris / sartorius / iliopsoas · excision

Operative criteria

ORIFdisplacement > 3 cm (Orthobullets, most OB) · > 2 cm in elite athletes or failed nonop (OB) — read the options · painful nonunion

High-energy paediatric acetabular fractureORIF if > 2 mm intra-articular or triradiate displacement (contrast with low-energy avulsions)

Iliac crest apophysis avulsion — abdominal wall innervation

Mechanismrapid lateral trunk flexion / twisting → contraction of external + internal oblique, transversus · sprinter out of blocks · rare

Nerveabdominal wall = lower intercostal nerves
✗ Wrong options: sciatic (hamstrings) · femoral (rectus femoris) · obturator (adductor longus) · superior gluteal (TFL)

Treatmentprotected WB + activity as tolerated, rest, analgesics, PT
✗ Wrong options: oncology work-up + biopsy · ORIF · abduction brace in 45° flexion · 120° knee flexion 24 h — quadriceps contusion

Surgerydisplaced > 3 cm or failed nonop

Articular Cartilage Defects of Knee

Knee & Sports · 5 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & pathomechanics

Incidence5–10% of people > 40 yr have high-grade chondral lesions · isolated defects in athletes est. 36% (OB)

Chronic ACL tearanterior lateral femoral condyle + posterolateral tibial plateau

OCD70% on posterolateral (lateral aspect of) medial femoral condyle

Mechanismacute trauma or chronic repetitive overload → softening, fissuring, flap tears, delamination

Thresholdimpaction > 24 MPa disrupts normal cartilage

Healinglimited spontaneous healing + propensity to worsen; defects isolated from blood supply / marrow → no repair response (basis of microfracture)

Overloaded cartilage (runner)chondropenia, chondrocyte apoptosis, subchondral bruising, sclerosis, fracture, necrosis; cartilage volume ↑ linearly with loading until a threshold

Genes & lab markers (collagen type of each repair tissue)

Tissue / procedure Collagen Note
Hyaline (articular) cartilage Type II Columnar organisation + lamina splendens (separates it from "hyaline-like")
Microfracture / drilling → fibrocartilage Type I > II (mostly I + III, some II) Stiffer, less durable → deteriorates over time
Microfracture (TO) Types I, II and III Fibrocartilage alone → mix of fibrocartilage + hyaline-like
ACI / MACI I + II, type II predominates "Hyaline-like"; ACI (TO) may give hyaline-like, hybrid or fibrocartilage (I + II)
OATS / mosaicplasty, OCA Type II Direct transfer of articular cartilage; chondrocytes viable
Particulated juvenile cartilage allograft Type II Live cells in native ECM
Fibrous tissue No type II Made by fibrocytes
Elastic cartilage — Ear, epiglottis, larynx

Labsonly to rule out inflammatory disease

3Presentation

Historyprecipitating trauma common · some found incidentally on MRI / arthroscopy

Symptomsasymptomatic vs localised pain, effusion, motion loss, mechanical symptoms (catching, locking) — esp. unstable / loose lesions

Examlook for background factors: laxity, malalignment, compartment overload; ROM, ligaments, gait

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
Standing AP, lateral, Merchant Rule out arthritis, bony defects; check alignment
Semiflexed 45° PA Most sensitive for early joint-space narrowing
Long-leg alignment Mechanical axis
CT Bone loss; TT-TG for patellofemoral joint
MRI Most sensitive for focal defects; FS T2, PD, T2 FSE ↑ sens / spec
dGEMRIC, T2 mapping Evolving — cartilage defects + repair
MRI after microfracture High fill rate = good short-term outcome
MRI ↑ T2 signal under defect Subchondral bone involvement / deficiency → favours OCA (✗ Wrong options: ACI)
MRI axial slices superimposed TT-TG > 20 mm = patellar maltracking

Grade Orthobullets TO version
0 Normal —
I Softening + swelling (probe) Softening + swelling

III Deep fissures to subchondral bone, > 1.5 cm diameter Fragmentation + fissuring, area > 0.5 inch
IV Exposed subchondral bone Erosion to bone

Outerbridge grade IVindication for cartilage restoration, not a failure risk factor

Grade Finding

1 Nearly normal — superficial lesions
2 Abnormal — < 50% cartilage depth
3 Severely abnormal — > 50% depth

Chondromalacia patellae — diagnosis & grading

Gold standard (TO)arthroscopy
✗ Wrong options: X-ray · MRI · CT

Modified Outerbridge — MRI (TO) FS PD finding
I Focal hyperintensity, normal contour
II Fissure or blister-like swelling reaching surface
III Focal ulceration + "crab meat" lesions
IV Full-thickness loss + reactive underlying bone

Tram-track sign (TO)mucoid degeneration of PCL
✗ Wrong options: crab meat

5Management

Decision factors & size thresholds

Nonop firstrest, NSAIDs, physio, weight loss when mild; viscosupplement, steroid, unloader brace — controversial, symptom relief, defect won't heal

Treatment spectrum (Alford) — marrow stimulation (MST) → ACI → osteochondral grafting (OCG, autograft / allograft)

Patient factorsage, skeletal maturity, demand, rehab tolerance · defect factors — size, location, contained vs uncontained, subchondral bone involvement

First correctmalalignment, ligament instability, meniscal deficiency (before / at time of cartilage surgery); patellofemoral → maltracking + malalignment

Femoral condyle defect (after correcting axis, ligaments, meniscus)
  • < 4 cm²→MICROFRACTURE or OATS (palliative if older / low demand)
  • > 4 cm²→OSTEOCHONDRAL ALLOGRAFT or ACI
Patellofemoral defect (after correcting maltracking)
  • < 4 cm²→MICROFRACTURE or OATS
  • > 4 cm²→ACI (microfracture if older / low demand)
Size / bone status (OB algorithm) Procedure
< 1 cm², no osseous defect Microfracture
< 1 cm², osseous defect OATS
1–2 cm², no osseous defect Microfracture or ACI
1–2 cm², osseous defect OATS
> 2 cm², osteochondral defect or AVN OCA or ACI + bone graft
Procedure Size range quoted (source)
Microfracture < 2 cm² / < 2 × 2 cm (Orthobullets, OB, TO) · < 1 cm² (OB patella, OB algorithm) · with OATS < 4 cm² (Orthobullets)
OATS < 2 cm², some 2–4 cm² (OB) · up to 4–6 cm² (OB, OCD chapter) · grafting up to 5 cm (TO)
ACI 1–10 cm² (OB) · 2–10 cm² large grade IV (TO) · > 4 cm² (Orthobullets)
OCA > 2 cm² (OB) · > 4 cm² (Orthobullets, OB) · > 6 cm² (OB, OCD chapter)
Threshold debate 4 cm² usual; some use 2 cm² (OB) — read the options

Operative criteria

Indication Detail
Failed nonop Symptomatic defect
Acute osteochondral fracture Full-thickness cartilage loss
Size (OB) Defects > 2 × 2 cm failing nonop
Arthroplasty instead > 55 yr (OB) · PF arthroplasty 40+ yr with isolated PF arthritis

Debridement / chondroplasty

Debridement / chondroplastyremoves loose flaps → relieves mechanical symptoms · short-term benefit 50–70% · simple, fast rehab · leaves exposed bone; natural history unknown

Chondroplasty for large PF defectonly older patients with diffuse degeneration
✗ Wrong options: young

Microfracture & marrow stimulation — fibrocartilage, outcomes & overgrowth

Principleperforate subchondral bone → marrow MSCs into defect → fibrocartilage · includes microfracture, abrasion chondroplasty, drilling
✗ Wrong options: true hyaline regeneration

Techniquestable vertical walls; remove calcified cartilage layer (✓ should be done); awl holes 3–4 mm apart; entry perpendicular (90°) to avoid skipping / hole collapse

Osseous overgrowthrisk ↑ with removal / violation of subchondral plate (over-aggressive debridement)
✗ Wrong options: more holes per area · small awls · 90° entry · calcified layer removal

Awl sizesmaller (1.0 mm) better than 1.2 mm in some studies

Drilling stepsdebride sclerotic bone → trim unstable cartilage edges → drill past subchondral plate (~4 mm) → enough coverage between holes for a mesenchymal clot

Drillingalters subchondral plate → micro-cysts + intralesional osteophytes (later fill with cancellous bone)

Benefitscheap, single-stage, arthroscopic; best for acute, contained lesions < 2 × 2 cm

Limitspoor if > 2 × 2 cm; not for bone defects or uncontained lesions (no rim); restricted WB 6–8 wk (Orthobullets) · ~6 wk (OB) · NWB 4–6 wk + CPM (Orthobullets OCD note)

Good short-term outcomehigh MRI fill rate, low BMI, short preop symptoms · patellar microfracture → poor

Durabilitygains maintained only 2–3 yr; not maintained long term

ACI / MACI — hyaline-like repair & patellofemoral indications

ACIcell therapy → autologous "hyaline-like" cartilage · arthroscopic harvest from low-load area → culture → inject under periosteal patch at 2nd (open) surgery

Needsfull-thickness cartilage margins, healthy subchondral bone
✗ Wrong options: significant osseous defect: < 8 mm deep OK (OB) · add bone graft if bone loss > 1 cm (OB, OCD chapter)

Limitsopen, 2-stage, prolonged protection · better histology than marrow stimulation; long-term ≈ microfracture

Periosteal patch (TO)harvested proximal tibia / distal femur, slightly oversized · cambium layer faces the defect (down to bone) · sewn watertight with interrupted 6-0 absorbable sutures + fibrin glue at margins · patch is chondrogenic + paracrine
✗ Wrong options: cambium away · sewn into defect · mixed with matrix

1st-stage harvest (TO)200–300 mg cartilage · cells expanded 2–3 wk (TO) · implanted after 3–6 wk (TO) — read the options

Collagen membrane (TO)replaced periosteum → avoids patch hypertrophy + harvest morbidity

ACI generation (TO) Features
1st (Brittberg 1994) 2-stage: arthroscopic biopsy → open / mini-open implantation under periosteal flap (PACI) or collagen membrane
2nd = MACI Autologous chondrocytes on a scaffold for expansion; 3D bioabsorbable scaffold press-fit (hyalograft C, bioseed-C) → all-arthroscopic implantation possible; NeoCart (bioreactor loading)
3rd Single stage; allogeneic tissue or stem cells; CAIS (minced autologous chondrocytes + marrow MNCs on polycaprolactone + PGA + PDS scaffold); De Novo ET (minced juvenile allograft); CARTISTEM (umbilical cord MSCs, hyaluronate gel)

3rd vs 1st generation (TO)all-arthroscopic, single-stage
✗ Wrong options: 2-stage · collagen cover · periosteal sheath

Generation conflictsMACI = 2nd generation (TO) vs 3rd generation, first to use scaffold (OB) · CAIS = 2nd-gen single-stage (one TO) vs 3rd-gen classic (other TO) — read the options

MACIcells cultured on porcine collagen membrane · fixed with fibrin glue or sutures · only FDA-approved cell therapy for cartilage (USA) · 2-stage, expensive · type II > I

5 cm² MFC defect, 32 yr (TO)ACI
✗ Wrong options: microfracture · UKA · mosaicplasty

ACI in PF jointJSN on Merchant view = contraindication · acceptable: grade 4 MFC / trochlea lesion, varus axis (corrected), concomitant Fulkerson AMZ · ACI not FDA-approved for patella (off-label)

PF defect + recurrent dislocation, TT-TG 26 mm, 2.2 × 2.1 cm, exposed boneMPFL reconstruction + autologous chondrocyte implantation + antero-medializing (Fulkerson) TTO
✗ Wrong options: lateralising TTO (↑ Q angle) · microfracture (< 1 cm² only) · PF arthroplasty (40+ yr)

PF lesionsinferior outcomes vs condyles (high shear) · TT-TG > 20 mm = maltracking → AMZ protects the repair · recurrent dislocation may avulse the MPFL patellar insertion (osseous fragment)

Osteochondral allograft — indications, contraindications & failure risk

Goallive chondrocytes in mature matrix + underlying bone · fresh, refrigerated grafts · bulk (screws) or shell / dowel press-fit · donor = cadaver hemicondyle · size + radius of curvature matched
✗ Wrong options: freeze-dried

Indicationslarge defects (> 2 cm² / > 4 cm²), subchondral bone loss / oedema / AVN, uncontained lesions, revision of failed techniques · single-stage

OCA over ACIdepth of osseous involvement
✗ Wrong options: footprint > 6 cm² · location · age · time since injury

Contraindicationsligament instability, meniscal insufficiency, uncorrectable malalignment, multicompartment / tricompartmental arthrosis, inflammatory arthropathy · ✓ defect > 2 cm² is an indication

Failure riskpatellofemoral joint defect (adverse biomechanics) · bipolar lesions
✗ Wrong options: unipolar · male sex · Outerbridge IV · concomitant AMZ

OutcomesPF worse than condyles (contact pressure) · > 80% return to activity in young · limits: availability, cost, infection / immune risk
✗ Wrong options: more easily available

Immune responseonly a concern with allograft · allografts cleansed in antibiotics before implantation
✗ Wrong options: OATS

Varus axis + large MFC lesioncorrect alignment before / at time of OCA
✗ Wrong options: isolated OCA

MFC 25 × 25 mm, 32 yrosteochondral allograft (ACI also correct if listed)
✗ Wrong options: 1–2 autograft plugs · microfracture · UKA · abrasion

MFC 1.7 × 1.3 cm (2.21 cm²) + loose bodies, neutral axisremoval of loose osteochondral bodies + osteochondral allograft transplantation to the MFC · loose bodies sit in suprapatellar pouch; hip-to-ankle film neutral, sunrise view normal
✗ Wrong options: osteotomy · microfracture (osseous defect) · OATS alone (loose bodies stay)

Osteochondral autograft (OATS) — graft fixation & donor site

Principlecylinders of normal cartilage + bone from low-load areas (periphery of trochlea, notch) press-fit into recipient socket · chondrocytes viable, cartilage heals, biopsy type II
✗ Wrong options: scaffold · replaced by fibrocartilage

Benefitsautologous, cheap, single-stage, arthroscopic possible · limits — size + donor-site morbidity, curvature matching

Fixation strengthinitially decreases in early healing, then increases with subchondral bone healing → delay WB 3 months; early non-WB motion

Donor sitedistal medial trochlea = lowest PF contact pressure + no tibiofemoral contact · also peripheral / superior lateral trochlea · grafts < 10 mm wide
✗ Wrong options: central trochlea · condyles (weight-bearing)

Ahmad map (figure)1 proximal medial trochlea · 2 medial condyle · 3 central trochlea · 4 distal medial trochlea ✓ · 5 lateral condyle

Procedure Indication Contraindication / risk
Maquet (anteriorisation) Distal pole lesions only Superior patellar arthrosis; elevate ≤ 1 cm → else skin necrosis
Fulkerson AMZ (anterior + medial) Lateral + distal pole lesions, ↑ Q angle, offload PF restoration, bipolar PF lesions Superior-medial patellar arthrosis, medial facet + MFC arthrosis, skeletal immaturity
Distal femoral varus osteotomy Valgus + lateral compartment chondral disease —
HTO (medial opening wedge) Varus-pattern disease Not if axis neutral

Scope before tubercle transfer — need intact proximal + medial cartilage

Anteriorised 2.5 cmskin necrosis / wound breakdown
✗ Wrong options: instability · nonunion · progression · fracture

Lateral FC + plateau chondromalacia, 10° valgus, 31 yrdistal femoral varus osteotomy · 5° valgus → 5-fold risk of progressing ≥ 1 grade in 18 months (Sharma)
✗ Wrong options: OAT · UKA · HTO · Fulkerson

Fixationneeds fragment with adequate subchondral bone · debride base, ± drill / local graft · absorbable or nonabsorbable screws · best: unstable OCD, open physes · lower healing when mature · headless nonabsorbable screws removed at 3–6 months

Acute patellar dislocation + osteochondral fragment + MPFL tearfragment fixation (ORIF) + MPFL reconstruction (best: 14-year-old female athlete, first-time dislocation, imaging shown in Figure D) · sites: patella + LFC · chronic, no fragment → OATS
✗ Wrong options: fixation without OC defect · partial-thickness chronic defect · bucket-handle tear · Outerbridge IV OA

Unfixable unstable MFC flap 1 × 1.5 cm, single procedure → type I + IImicrofracture

ROCK / De Smet (TO) Detail
Nonop protocol Stop impact sport, protected WB, unloader brace or cast · ≥ 3–6 months; healing on 6-month MRI → extend to 12–18 months
Strongest success predictor Younger age / open physes (boys < 14, girls < 12)
Other success predictors Small normalised lesion width; no cysts (< 1.3 mm may still heal at 12 months); extreme medial / lateral (coronal) or far posterior (sagittal) site
ROCK nomogram Age + normalised width + cyst size → > 48% healing probability at 6 months → continue nonop
Strongest failure predictor Subchondral cysts > 5 mm on MRI (fluid intrusion = instability) (✗ Wrong options: sclerotic rim (common, chronicity))
De Smet instability T2 fluid line ≥ 5 mm behind fragment · cysts ≥ 5 mm · focal cartilage defect ≥ 5 mm · fluid through cartilage into bone
Other failure signs Closing physes, mechanical symptoms, patella / LFC site, no progress after 3–6 months
Surgery options Trans- / retroarticular drilling (intact cartilage), internal fixation (unstable), MACI / OCA (unsalvageable)

Stable lesion (TO)no fluid behind fragment, firm on probing → failed conservative → drilling alone

Unstable but salvageable, immature (TO)circumferential T2 fluid, ballotable, minimally displaced → in situ fixation of the fragment using bioabsorbable screws, darts or compression screws ± graft
✗ Wrong options: drilling alone · excision + microfracture · OATS

Definitionprolonged ventricular action potential (QT) → arrhythmia · congenital (ion-channel genes) or acquired (electrolytes, K-channel blockers → ↑ intracellular positive charge)

Prevalence1 in 2,500–10,000 (Orthobullets) · 1 in 2,500; long QT in 0.42% of elite athletes (TO)

Whodiagnosed < 20 yr · rarer in females (Orthobullets) · SCD mostly in females < 40 yr (TO)

Type Gene / chromosome Channel Share Key fact
LQT1 KCNQ1, chr 11 K⁺ efflux (loss of function) 45% — commonest Adrenergic surge → swimming, diving into cold water (TO)
LQT2 KCNH2, chr 7 K⁺ 25–40% Most dangerous — most SCDs (females) (TO)
LQT3 SCN5A, chr 3 Na⁺ 5–10% —

LQT1–3 (TO)~95% of cases; 12 types (LQTS-1 to 12)

Acquired drugsantiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine), cisapride (TO)

Presentation (TO)palpitations, dizziness, unheralded syncope (polymorphic VT) · brief myoclonic jerks → misdiagnosed as epilepsy · most asymptomatic (Orthobullets)

Torsades de pointespolymorphic VT → VF → SCD · 50% asymptomatic · Romano-Ward syndrome (abnormal repolarization → torsades, VT, SCD)

Concussions (Mild Traumatic Brain Injury)

Knee & Sports · 9 / 61

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Definitionsubset of mild TBI → acute transient impairment of neurologic function 2° to an impulsive force transmitted to the head (blow to head, face, neck or elsewhere)

Functional, not structuralstandard CT / MRI normal in the vast majority
✗ Wrong options: MRI often diagnostic

LOCnot required for diagnosis · occurs in only ~10%

Incidence1.6–3.8 million sports concussions / yr (Orthobullets) · "nearly 4 million" (OB) · 5–9% of all sports injuries · ~6% of NCAA football injuries · rising (awareness, youth)

Who / whereTBI = leading cause of sport-related death · American football = majority · competition > practice

Pathophysiology — neurometabolic cascade

Step Clinical result
Abnormal neuronal ionic flux Headache, photophobia, phonophobia
Altered neurotransmitter release (glutamate) Impaired cognition, amnesia, slowed reaction time
Energy depletion (correcting imbalance) Vulnerable to second injury (second-hit)

After concussionre-injury risk significantly ↑ (biochemistry altered, neuroprotection disrupted)
✗ Wrong options: risk same as pre-injury

Risk factors & prevention (helmets, prior concussion)

Risk factor Fact
Prior concussion Strongest · 2–8× (Orthobullets) · 2–6× (OB) — read the options
Female Higher risk than males (✗ Wrong options: male gender) — possibly oestrogen / cerebral blood flow
Age < 18 (younger) Less "cognitive reserve" (✗ Wrong options: increasing age)
Player-to-player contact Football, wrestling, soccer, basketball highest
Mood / learning disorders, migraine, anxiety / depression Complicate diagnosis + recovery — not proven to predispose
Equipment quality No relationship established

Helmets / headgear↓ impact force · ↓ head + neck injuries in youth hockey, alpine, equestrian, cycling, motor sports

Equestrian injurieshelmets = greatest opportunity
✗ Wrong options: knee pads, wrist guards, boots, quick-release stirrups

Risk compensationprotective gear may ↑ injury by enabling dangerous technique

Rule changeswork when one clear mechanism · upper limb-to-head contact banned in American football (~50% of concussions) · red cards for high elbows (soccer)

Preparticipation evaluationnumber of prior concussions, symptoms, recovery length · low-impact injury + disproportionate symptoms → particularly vulnerable athlete

Genes & lab markers

Apolipoprotein Egenetic test under research (prevention)

CTE proteinstau, beta-amyloid, TDP-43 (after repetitive diffuse axonal injury)

Consensus guidelines (International Conference on Concussion in Sport)

Meets every 4 yearsconsensus statement · 1st 2001 · grading removed 2004 · all classification systems removed 2008 · latest focus = assessment tools + timing of return to play

SCAT origin (TO)2nd conference, Prague 2004

Zurich 2008 (3rd)no same-day RTP even if symptoms resolve · applies to minimal- and noncontact athletes · applies to children ≥ 10 yr (younger → age-appropriate checklists) · young elite athletes → more conservative · CT contributes little to early diagnosis (use only if structural lesion suspected) · multidisciplinary approach

3Presentation

Symptoms & mandatory signs

Headachemost common symptom — 70% · myofascial tension (posterior neck, base of skull) vs post-traumatic (forehead / vertex pressure)

Somaticdizziness, balance problems, nausea / vomiting, vision change, diplopia, tinnitus, photophobia, phonophobia

Cognitive"in a fog" / slowed, poor concentration, forgetful

Emotionallability, irritability, sadness · sleep — insomnia, drowsiness, more or less sleep

Mandatory signsLOC (~10%), lying motionless > 5 s, slow to get up, confusion / disorientation, clutching head, amnesia, vacant look / blank stare, motor incoordination, ataxia / gait instability → further evaluation ± removal (sport-specific)

Cervical muscle tendernessnot a concussion sign → C-spine evaluation, but no 5–10-day concussion protocol (✓ EXCEPT answer)

Handball player faints, plays on, progressively aggressive, can't recall last goal (TO)concussion → immediately remove from play area + Maddocks score
✗ Wrong options: counsel 15 min · electrolyte drink · "plays best aggressive"

4Diagnosis & Classification

Sideline evaluation

Primary surveyABC · altered mental status → assume C-spine injury (collar + board) · never leave player alone

Secondary surveyremove from field + immediate cognitive evaluation by licensed healthcare provider · no provider → remove entirely + urgent physician referral

Diagnosisclinical judgement = gold standard · no tool diagnoses concussion alone

Red flags — skull base fracture, diffuse axonal injury & emergent imaging

Red flag → ER for advanced imaging Not a reason for transport
Deteriorating mental status, restless, agitated, combative Transient unilateral UE numbness resolving (stinger)
Severe / worsening headache Headache alone, normal cognition
Focal deficit — unequal pupils, abnormal EOM, motor / sensory Mild headache + shoulder pain + prior concussion
Neck pain / tenderness (C-spine) Photophobia + dizziness < 15 min, no focal / cognitive signs
Bloody otorrhea, mastoid ecchymosis (skull fracture), blepharohematoma (eyelid haematoma)
GCS < 15, LOC, amnesia / confusion (OB list)

LOC + bloody discharge from external auditory meatusskull fracture → transfer to ER for advanced imaging
✗ Wrong options: SCAT5 · graduated RTP · practice tomorrow

Mastoid ecchymosis + eyelid haematoma, no LOCemergent transport to ED

Diffuse axonal injury (severe closed head injury)no return to football / contact sports
✗ Wrong options: return after 6 mo, 1 yr, 2 yr asymptomatic

Key radiology findings

Modality Fact
Imaging overall Usually unnecessary · indicated for red flags above, or subacute / chronic trauma with persistent symptoms
CT head Most used acutely · normal in vast majority · shows fracture, haemorrhage, contusion, mass effect, herniation
MRI brain Superior detail · DWI most sensitive to shear injury · standard MRI normal
Functional MRI ↑ cerebrovascular reactivity in acute post-concussive period
Negative CT Does not clear RTP · not diagnostic of concussion

Most sensitive test for deficits after mTBIneuropsychologic testing · its RTP role not fully defined
✗ Wrong options: head CT · MRI · skull radiographs · sideline assessment

Assessment tools — SCAT

SCAT fact Detail
Use Standardised tool, athletes ≥ 13 yr · Child SCAT for ≤ 12 yr (5–12) (TO)
SCAT5 on-field Red flags, observable signs, Maddocks questions (memory), GCS, C-spine assessment
SCAT5 off-field (private, quiet) Background, symptom evaluation, cognitive screen (SAC), neuro screen, mBESS, delayed recall, decision
SCAT5 additions (TO) On-field section, C-spine assessment, 10-word list (≥ 5 min between immediate + delayed recall), neuro screen
SCAT5 time Minimum 10 min — can't be done correctly in less (TO, OB key) · OB text: "< 10 min" / "on-field < 15 min" — read the options
SCAT history (TO) SCAT 2005 → SCAT2 2009 → SCAT3 2013 → SCAT5 2017 (5th conference)
SCAT6 (TO) Ideally within 72 h, up to 7 days · > 7 days → SCOAT6 / Child SCOAT6
SCAT6 immediate (TO) Observable signs, GCS, C-spine, coordination + ocular / motor screen, Maddocks
SCAT6 off-field (TO) Background, symptoms, cognitive screen, coordination + balance, delayed recall, decision

SCAT combines (TO)GCS (consciousness) + modified Maddocks (orientation) + PCSS (21 symptoms, 4 categories — somatic, cognitive, emotional, sleep — 7-point Likert) + SAC (orientation, concentration, immediate + delayed memory) + neck, balance, coordination exam

Boxing doctor — recovery from prior concussion, fit for sport? (TO)SCAT
✗ Wrong options: GCS · PCSS · SAC

Not a documentation tool (TO)SCAT · documentation = SOAP notes (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan of first aid), daily sideline injury report, training room treatment log, Daily Red Cross List (no / limited / full participation)

Test Assesses

SAC Orientation (month?), immediate + delayed memory (5 words × 3 trials + 1 at end), concentration (5 digits backwards, months in reverse) · pencil-and-paper · no reaction time, balance
BESS Balance — 3 stances (bipedal, unipedal, tandem) × 10 s

ImPACT baselinestable over 2 yr in college (no annual retest) · retest annually in high school / youth

Low baseline neuropsych scoreathlete's own reference → not a reason to withhold play (✓ EXCEPT answer)

Post-injury neuropsych testingnot required for all; no defined role in RTP criteria · RTP stays a clinical decision

5Management

Head trauma in athlete
  • Red flag (worsening GCS, focal deficit, otorrhea, Battle sign)→ER + CT
  • Any sign / symptom of concussion→remove, NO same-day RTP
    • rest 24–48 h→graduated RTP (≥ 24 h / stage, ≥ 1 wk)
  • Unilateral transient UE paresthesia, normal exam, no concussion signs → stinger→same-day RTP

Removal criteria — no same-day return to play

Remove from play (no same-day RTP) Not a criterion
Any sign / symptom of concussion ("if concerned at all") Low baseline neuropsych testing
No provider experienced in concussion present Cervical muscle tenderness alone
History of prior concussion Parental waiver / consent (doesn't permit RTP)
LOC · amnesia Normal neuropsych testing or imaging
Positive exertional stress test (symptoms recur with exertion)
Symptoms > 15 min

Same-day RTPcontraindicated in every diagnosed / suspected concussion, even if symptoms resolve · test to pass for same-game return → none
✗ Wrong options: neuro exam · SCAT5 · ImPACT · K-D · SAC · SOT clears

Only same-day RTPstinger: unilateral transient UE pain / paresthesia / deltoid weakness, complete resolution, normal exam, no concussion signs

✗ Wrong options: cervical muscle tenderness

✗ Wrong options: RTP on resolution · CT + MRI · "≥ 2 wk rest"

Graduated return-to-play protocol & timing

Stage Activity Goal
1 Symptom-limited activity Daily activities not provoking symptoms Reintroduce work / school
2 Light aerobic Walking, swimming, stationary cycling, HR < 70% max · no resistance ↑ HR
3 Sport-specific exercise Running or skating drills · no head impact Add movement
4 Non-contact training drills Complex drills (passing) · start progressive resistance / strength training Exercise, coordination, cognition
5 Full-contact practice Normal training Confidence, functional skills
6 Return to play Normal game play

Each stage≥ 24 h (✗ Wrong options: 12 h · 48 h · 72 h · 96 h) → earliest RTP = 1 week (✗ Wrong options: 30 min · 24 h · 4 wk · 2 mo) · usually 7–10 days (OB)

Number of steps6 (Orthobullets, 2012 consensus) · 5 (OB211942, counting asymptomatic day → full-contact practice) — same sequence

Symptoms recur at a stage24 h rest → drop back to previous asymptomatic stage

Correct sequencestationary bike → running on a track → running + catching a football
✗ Wrong options: squats / leg press before stage 4 · track before bike

14-yr-old, dizzy + can't focus after head clashRTP after ≥ 1-week graduated protocol
✗ Wrong options: negative CT · ImPACT back to baseline · later in game · next day

Confirmed concussion with LOCRTP after graduated protocol while symptom-free
✗ Wrong options: next day · after 7 days rest alone · neuropsychiatric clearance

1 wk later, headache + blurred vision at rest, cognition back to baselinewithhold from all contact — symptoms at rest = absolute contraindication
✗ Wrong options: graduated RTP · day-7 ImPACT · outpatient CT (symptoms may last up to 2 wk)

Friday concussion, still symptomatic → Mondaysub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise after baseline symptom reassessment
✗ Wrong options: strict rest until symptoms resolve · aerobic despite headache · accelerated drills · fixed 7 days regardless

Cognitive rest & predictors of prolonged recovery

Treatmentcognitive + physical rest 24–48 h → graduated RTP · no prolonged strict rest (weeks)

Cognitive restminimise concentration: reading, schoolwork, video games, texting, working online, chess → limiting video games ✓

Cognitive rest↓ symptom duration ✓ · ↑ activity in post-concussion period → prolonged symptoms (OB217826)

Early aerobic activity (days after injury)encouraged, speeds recovery (OB217914, OB219980) — must stay below symptom threshold
✗ Wrong options: delay aerobic ≥ 1 wk

Prolonged recovery predictorssubacute headache + depression symptoms ✓ · ADHD no longer thought a significant risk factor

Natural historycognitive deficits, balance + symptoms improve within the first 2 weeks · small % persistent ✓

6Complications

Second impact syndrome

Definitionsecond head trauma before first concussion's symptoms resolve — second hit can be trivial

Mechanismcatastrophic cerebral oedema from loss of cerebral autoregulation
✗ Wrong options: venous / arterial microvascular bleeding

Courserapid progression · brain stem often involved · CT shows oedema · poor prognosis · mortality ~50%
✗ Wrong options: gradual

Preventionrestrict RTP until symptom-free ✓ — the reason for no same-day RTP

Associationsmale, young age, American football
✗ Wrong options: leading cause of CTE · short-term memory loss

Postconcussion syndrome

Definitionpersistent symptoms (headache, confusion, lethargy) > 10–14 days adults · > 4 weeks children (younger → slower RTS)

ManagementRTP contraindicated · formal neuropsychiatric evaluation · pharmacotherapy controversial · self-limiting (vs CTE)

Intracranial haemorrhage

Subdural haematomamost common

Epidural haematomalucid interval before decline → neurosurgical decompression + seizure prophylaxis

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy

Definitionprogressive neurodegeneration from repetitive brain trauma · permanent
✗ Wrong options: temporary neuronal derangement

Onsetyears–decades later, midlife · mean 42 yr · boxing, football, hockey, wrestling
✗ Wrong options: by age 30

Early featuresbehaviour / affect: apathy, irritability, suicidal ideation, aggression, "short fuse", loss of impulse control · or cognitive: poor episodic memory, executive dysfunction, dementia

Latedepression, disinhibition + parkinsonism (bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity)

Pathologytau, beta-amyloid, TDP-43 · superficial cortical laminae II–III (Alzheimer: layer III and deeper) · gross changes present: cerebral atrophy, enlarged ventricles, diffuse senile plaques
✗ Wrong options: no gross changes

Diagnosispost-mortem neuropathology only · no consensus clinical criteria

45-yr-old ex-NFL running back, cognitive + mood + parkinsonismCTE
✗ Wrong options: early Alzheimer (rare in 40s) · Parkinson's (usually > 60) · ALS (no cognitive change) · FTD

✗ Wrong options: postconcussion syndrome

Discoid Meniscus

Knee & Sports · 10 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitionabnormal development → hypertrophic, disc-shaped meniscus

Incidence3–5% of the population · highest in Japanese + Korean populations (TO)

Sidelateral ≫ medial (✗ Wrong options: medial commonest) · bilateral in 25% (Orthobullets, OB) · 25–50% (OB) — read the options (✗ Wrong options: > 75%) · examine the other knee

Commonest causeof symptomatic clicking / clunking in a child's knee

Discoid medial (TO)much rarer · disc-shaped · linked with trauma / tears

Aetiology & pathology

Aetiologyfailure of apoptosis in utero (Orthobullets, OB) · the normal meniscus develops from a cartilaginous anlage and is never discoid during development (OB)

Aetiology traps✗ Wrong options: COL5A1 (female ACL rupture) · landing biomechanics · quadriceps dominance (ACL) · softening of cartilage with intact surface (OCD)

Tissuedisorganised type I collagen — fewer fibres, heterogeneous course, lost continuity (Atay, Papadopoulos) · TO: ↓ collagen density, mucinous change, ↑ thickness, enlarged surface, ↓ peripheral vascularity

Pathology traps✗ Wrong options: incomplete ossification of ACL tibial insertion (tibial eminence fracture) · patellar ossification variant (bipartite patella) · proximal tibial dyschondrosis (Blount) · cartilage sleeve–ossific nucleus separation (patellar sleeve)

Why it tears↑ thickness, poor tissue quality, instability / lack of peripheral attachments, ↓ vascularity

Tear site + patternmost tears posterior or middle (Kramer) · commonest pattern horizontal (TO) · OB cases: longitudinal LM tear, radial tear

3Presentation

Symptomspain, clicking, mechanical locking · often symptomatic in adolescence · most children asymptomatic

Snapping knee syndromecommonest presentation of a symptomatic discoid · classic for the unstable (Wrisberg) variant · clunk going flexion → full extension · TO: "meniscal thud" at terminal extension (10–20°)

Age (TO)3–4 y: often painless snapping · 8–10 y: pain with activity, more acute

Exammechanical symptoms most pronounced in extension · loss of extension (lacks 10°, ROM 10–85°) · lateral fullness, lateral joint line tenderness

Painless clunk at 5–6 y, no traumadiscoid lateral meniscus (abnormal meniscal morphology)
✗ Wrong options: ACL agenesis (hypoplastic LFC, shallow notch, absent tibial spine) · medial plica (older athletes) · grade IV chondral flap (rare < 9 y) · PVNS · osteomyelitis (systemically ill)

12 y, snapping, lacks 10° extension, wide lateral jointdiscoid meniscus
✗ Wrong options: OCD · medial plica (medial snapping) · Osgood–Schlatter (tibial tubercle) · Sinding-Larsen–Johansson (inferior pole patella)

Study Finding
Radiographs (AP + lateral) Normal in most children · severe discoid: widened lateral joint space (up to 11 mm), squaring of lateral femoral condyle, cupping of lateral tibial plateau, hypoplastic lateral intercondylar spine

MRI sagittal / coronal Thick, flat meniscus across the whole lateral compartment · ↑ lateral meniscus-to-tibia width ratio · tear in symptomatic cases
MRI pitfalls (TO) Vacuum phenomenon mimics a tear in a discoid · Wrisberg type mimics a floating meniscus

Algorithms

Discoid meniscus (OB / Orthobullets)
  • Asymptomatic, no tear (incl. incidental at arthroscopy)→observe / do nothing
  • Pain, mechanical symptoms, tear→arthroscopic saucerization ± repair
    • Unstable / detached rim (Wrisberg)→saucerization + stabilization (repair)
  • Total meniscectomy (open or arthroscopic)→avoid — early OA
Discoid lateral meniscus (TO)
  • Asymptomatic→nonop, close follow-up
  • Child (usually complete), mechanical symptoms→partial meniscectomy ± repair
  • Adult, complete, mechanical symptoms→partial meniscectomy ± repair
  • Adult, incomplete
    • Pain ± mechanical symptoms→partial meniscectomy ± repair
    • Clicking only→nonop, close follow-up

Observation — asymptomatic discoid

Painless clicking, 8 y, incomplete, no tearobservation only
✗ Wrong options: diagnostic arthroscopy · saucerization · + microfracture · + stabilization

Direct blow, 8 y, asymptomatic discoid on MRI, normal X-rayobservation
✗ Wrong options: debridement + repair · ligament reconstruction · cast at 45° · immobiliser + NWB 6 wk

Incidental, untorn discoid at arthroscopy, 38 y with medial paindo nothing surgically to the lateral meniscus · not treated prophylactically
✗ Wrong options: saucerization · meniscectomy · repair · microfracture

Operative criteria

Operate (saucerize ± repair) Do not operate
Persistent pain, recurrent locking, swelling Asymptomatic discoid without tear
Mechanical symptoms / loss of extension Incidental finding at arthroscopy
Meniscal tear or meniscal detachment Painless clicking only (TO: adult incomplete)

Saucerization ± repair / stabilization

Indication for saucerizationsymptomatic meniscal tear
✗ Wrong options: asymptomatic abnormal shape · valgus instability · varus malalignment · hyperextension

11 y, 6 months snapping, 10° extension lossarthroscopic saucerization ± meniscal repair
✗ Wrong options: PT strengthening · NWB 6 wk · open lateral meniscectomy — historical · microfracture

9 y, partial central tear of stable discoidarthroscopic saucerization (partial meniscectomy) · repair only for peripheral instability
✗ Wrong options: total lateral meniscectomy (poor long-term results) · transplant · repair of central tear · cast 6 wk

13 y, torn discoid, effusion, failed 4 wk PTarthroscopic stabilization (repair vs partial meniscectomy) + saucerization
✗ Wrong options: hinged brace · meniscectomy alone (premature OA) · open saucerization

Watanabe I with radial tear, locking, 14 ypartial meniscectomy ± repair
✗ Wrong options: observation · repair only (leaves discoid tissue to re-tear) · complete meniscectomy · transplant (viable tissue present)

Techniquedebride to an anatomic-looking meniscus · repair if detached (Wrisberg) · saucerization = remove central disc, keep peripheral crescent

Rimsaucerize to a 6–8 mm peripheral rim — keeps function, avoids re-tear of larger remnants

Saucerization alone vs with repaircomparable ROM, pain, complications · Carter: stabilization doesn't change outcomes or complications
✗ Wrong options: repair inferior

Small kneesall-inside repair difficult in young children (small knee, deep posterior perforation risk)

Outcomes

Saucerizationsuccessful in 93% (28 / 30 knees); rest needed complete meniscectomy for complex tears (Good) · full flexion > 135°

Long-term degenerative change (OB) Rate
Arthroscopic saucerization ~20%
Partial meniscectomy ~40%
Complete meniscectomy ~90%

Lee (< 15 y)partial meniscectomy → better radiographic results / less OA than subtotal / total
✗ Wrong options: similar degenerative change

Total meniscectomy — TO view vs OB view

TO< 16 y: total meniscectomy may give the longest symptom-free period · Wrisberg type → total meniscectomy (subtotal leaves an unstable rim) or saucerization + suture rim to capsule · stable complete / incomplete → defer unless grooving / chondromalacia · hypermobile medial segment, intact periphery → subtotal meniscectomy / saucerization

ConflictTO above vs OB / Orthobullets: avoid complete meniscectomy (~90% degenerative change); repair / stabilize a detached Wrisberg rim with saucerization — read the options

X vs Y

Complete / incomplete Wrisberg type
Shape Disc / semilunar Near normal
Posterior attachment Present Absent (Wrisberg MFL only)
Stability Stable; symptomatic when torn Hypermobile
Presentation Asymptomatic until tear Snapping knee, younger, no trauma
Treatment Saucerize ± repair if symptomatic Saucerize + stabilize (OB) · total meniscectomy (TO)

5Management

Auricular haematoma

Mechanismblunt shear separates perichondrium from cartilage → blood collects

First step in EDotoscopic evaluation (TM rupture; rule out skull fracture)
✗ Wrong options: compressive dressing + PCP referral · formal surgical decompression · needle decompression before otoscopy · head MRI

Treatmentaspiration (urgent needle decompression) + wrapping (compressive dressing) to prevent re-accumulation · formal surgical evacuation → recurrent or delayed cases · prevent with headgear

Untreatedcauliflower ear (fibrous / abnormal cartilage), perichondritis, infection, necrosis

Nasal septal haematoma

Whatsub-perichondrial / subperiosteal septal haematoma (submucosal vessel rupture) · uni- or bilateral (bilateral → severe trauma) · any age
✗ Wrong options: mostly children

Commonest symptomnasal congestion / obstruction (~95%) · exam: purple-red bulging septum
✗ Wrong options: epistaxis

Treatmenturgent decompression (I&D) under local anaesthesia + anterior packing
✗ Wrong options: phenylephrine packing (that's for epistaxis)

I&D preventsseptal cartilage (chondral) avascular necrosis → saddle nose · septal abscess within 72 h (common, not unlikely)
✗ Wrong options: deviated septum · recurrent epistaxis · olfactory nerve damage · turbinate swelling

Injury Key finding Treatment
Traumatic mydriasis Dilated pupil, contusion of iris sphincter, transient Bed rest
Corneal abrasion Fluorescein stain + UV light Topical antibiotics + NSAIDs, patch, non-urgent ophthalmology
Hyphema Blood in anterior chamber (haze) — may mean vitreous / retinal injury Patch + ER / emergent ophthalmology
Ruptured globe Sunken eye, vitreous exudate Emergent
Orbital wall fracture Extraocular muscle entrapment Emergent
Retinal detachment Bright flashes, stabbing pain, field cut Emergent
Traumatic optic neuropathy ↓ acuity, ↓ colour vision, field cut Emergent CT

Red-flag symptomsvision loss, ↓ acuity, floaters / flashers, diplopia

Boxer: hyphema + ↓ acuity + ↓ colour vision + field cutemergent CT
✗ Wrong options: patch + ophthalmology in 2 days · fluorescein · high-dose steroids before CT · observation

Traumatic optic neuropathyblunt 78% / penetrating 22% · sports + MVA · optic canal fracture on CT = poor prognosis · treatment controversial (steroids, optic canal decompression, sheath fenestration) · children: only 29–44% improve

Most serious acute complicationairway obstruction
✗ Wrong options: blood loss · CVA (carotid injury, rare) · periodontal disease (late) · hearing loss

Airwayintubation often impossible → surgical airway
