Avulsed toothmedical emergency · survival depends on time out of socket + periodontal ligament damage

Handlinghold by crown, never root · rinse debris with water / saline · never brush or scrub
✗ Wrong options: toothbrush · hydrogen peroxide

Replant immediatelyimmediate repositioning / replantation → bite on towel → dentist / ER
✗ Wrong options: wait for dentist · emergency root canal

If not replantedkeep moist: milk (whole), saline, saliva / buccal fold, buffered solution kits · rinse with saline → milk = usual answer
✗ Wrong options: ice · water · carbonated drink

Childrenreplanting or carrying in mouth → aspiration risk

Dentistas soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour

Contraction types – isokinetic, isotonic, isometric & eccentric

Type Definition Example Fact asked
Isotonic Constant muscle tension (force) as length changes · improves motor performance Free-weight biceps curls · leg extensions + curls Concentric + eccentric are isotonic · force–velocity (force constant)
Isometric Constant length, tension ∝ external load · causes hypertrophy (Orthobullets) Push against an immovable object · plantarflex against a wall 15 s Length–tension relationship
Concentric Muscle shortens, tension ∝ load Curl with elbow flexing · slow single-leg heel rise —
Eccentric Muscle lengthens under constant force Curl with elbow extending · "negative" of a lift Most efficient strengthening · highest muscle forces
Isokinetic Constant velocity, variable resistance (✗ Wrong options: constant effort at variable speed) Cybex / dynamometer · bike at constant pedal velocity, varied resistance Objective strength testing in rehab · force–velocity (velocity constant)
Plyometric Rapid eccentric → concentric (stretch-shortening) Box jumps, bounding, hopping Power sports · late rehab
Open chain Distal end moves freely Seated leg extensions + curls —
Closed chain Distal end fixed Squat with planted foot, leg press —

Eccentric = injury contractionmuscle strain at myotendinous junction · DOMS · distal biceps rupture (forced eccentric load, + hook test)
✗ Wrong options: isometric · concentric · isokinetic · plyometric

Achilles tendinitis rehab after rest + CAM booteccentric strengthening: rise on both legs on a 1-inch board, lower slowly on the injured leg only + gastrocnemius-soleus stretching · avoid steroid injection
✗ Wrong options: box jumps (plyometric) · wall push (isometric) · slow single-leg rise (concentric) · delay rehab

Overstretched musclesarcomeres generate little active tension → < 30% maximal force

Isokinetic in tennis (TO)slow + fast speed isokinetic → maximal resistance at every point of ROM, uniform strength, concentric + eccentric · add core strengthening (lower back + hip) → kinetic-chain power transfer
✗ Wrong options: ballistic · plyometric (power, added once baseline strength exists) · fartlek (trains energy systems, not muscle)

Characteristic Closed chain Open chain
Distal segment Fixed against considerable resistance Free in space

Muscle injury healing – TGF-β & early mobilisation

Injury Key facts
Soreness (DOMS) Oedema + inflammation in connective tissue → ↑ intramuscular pressure · type IIB · eccentric · starts at MTJ, spreads · cytoskeletal disruption · peaks 24–72 h (Orthobullets)
Strain Myotendinous junction, eccentric contraction · inflammation → fibrosis
Contusion Blunt → haematoma · ECM within 2 days, peaks 5–21 days · myositis ossificans most apparent at 4 wk
Laceration Near MTJ, abnormal contour · dense scar via myofibroblasts ← TGF-β · regeneration + reinnervation unpredictable, incomplete

✗ Wrong options: VEGF

Immobilisation after muscle injury≤ 3–5 days, then progressive strengthening + stretching · immediate motion → large dense scar, poor fibre penetration · 2 wk → atrophy limiting outcome, ↑ fatty infiltration, less scar, less regeneration, disorganised fibres

Immobilisation (Orthobullets)atrophy, ↓ tension, ↑ fatigability, fatty infiltration · faster in single-joint muscles · non-linear (most in first days; myofibril loss) · worse without tension → quadriceps > hamstrings when knee held in extension

Exertional Compartment Syndrome

Knee & Sports · 13 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitionexercise-induced, reversible ischaemia of muscle within a compartment

Rank2nd commonest exercise-induced leg syndrome after medial tibial stress syndrome

Whomales > females, 3rd decade, runners · long-distance runners + military recruits (TO) · paediatric CECS → more common in females in running sports (OB)

Sitesleg commonest, then thigh + forearm (OB) · forearm 2nd (another OB) · volar forearm with repetitive gripping

Leg compartment involved Share
Anterior ~70% — most common (Orthobullets) · anterior (TO)
Anterior + lateral 10% (Orthobullets) · 95% of CECS in anterior + lateral (TO)
Posterior Less predictable surgical outcome; more often linked to PAES (accessory medial gastrocnemius head)

Pathophysiology

Mechanismlocal metabolism can't clear metabolic waste · ↑ muscle volume in a non-compliant closed compartment (TO)

Muscle swelling (OB)fibres swell up to 20× resting size → 20% ↑ muscle volume and weight

Aetiology (OB)limited osseofascial expansion, ↑ fascial hernias, arteriole dysregulation · ↓ capillary density vs asymptomatic

Fascial hernias40% of ECS vs 5% asymptomatic (Orthobullets) · palpable in 40–60% (TO) · near the intermuscular septum of anterior + lateral compartments, where the SPN exits

Risk factors – anabolic steroids (TO)

Risk factor (TO) Why
Anabolic steroids ↑ muscle volume
Creatine ↑ muscle volume
Eccentric exercise ↓ fascial compliance
Rear-foot landing / over-pronation Differential loading of individual muscle groups

Traps (TO)✗ Wrong options: inversion + supination of foot on landing · "most recover with activity modification, eccentric exercise + stretching" · posterior + medial calf pain as commonest symptom

3Presentation

Symptomsaching / burning or cramping leg pain · paraesthesias over dorsum of foot · reproduced by exercise, relieved by rest · often bilateral (vs acute CS)

Timingstarts at a predictable time / distance / intensity · ~10 min into exercise, resolves ~30–40 min after stopping · patient can predict how long pain lasts

Exam at restmost likely normal
✗ Wrong options: Tinel at fibular neck · firm compartments · 1st web numbness · weak dorsiflexion

Exam findings when present↓ sensation 1st web space, ↓ active ankle dorsiflexion (drop foot)

Exam after provoking exercise (TO)tender muscles, pain on passive stretch, firm compartments, palpable fascial hernia

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
Radiographs Normal — exclude other pathology
MRI Not diagnostic — excludes others: marrow oedema = tibial stress fracture, ring-enhancing collection = abscess
Near-infrared spectroscopy Muscle deoxygenation; normal within 25 min of stopping
Compartment pressures Required / gold standard

Diagnosis – pressure measurement protocol & thresholds

Protocollimb relaxed + consistent position · rest, 1 min post-exercise, 5 min post-exercise (± 15 min, some authors)
✗ Wrong options: 30 min continuous · rest + 1 min only · 60 min continuous

Stryker catheter (TO)commonest device · TO protocol = pre-exercise + 5 min after exercising to severe symptoms

Forearm (OB)simulated grip activity → forearm compartment pressures
✗ Wrong options: CTA · MRA · EMG / NCS · angiography

Diagnostic criteria

Time point Orthobullets / OB Pedowitz (OB, TO) TO (FNB)
Rest (pre-exercise) > 15 mmHg ≥ 15 > 15 (✗ Wrong options: > 10)
1 min post-exercise > 30 mmHg ≥ 30 > 30 (✗ Wrong options: ≥ 20)
5 min post-exercise > 20 mmHg ≥ 20 > 20
15 min post-exercise > 15 mmHg (some authors) — —

How many criterialisted with "and" (Orthobullets) · "one or more" (Pedowitz, TO) · "or" / "and/or" (OB) — any one value above threshold = consistent in the MCQs

Values in the options Verdict
Rest 10 · 1 min 35 · 5 min 25 Normal rest, ↑ 1 + 5 min (OB)
17 · 32 · 21 · 16 (rest, 1, 5, 15 min) Confirms ECS (OB)
5 min = 25 Most consistent (✗ Wrong options: rest 10 · 1 min 15 / 25 · 5 min 15) (OB)
Anterior 25 at 5 min Positive (✗ Wrong options: superficial posterior 10 at 15 min) (OB)
Pre 18 · 1 min 58 · 5 min 33 All point to CECS (TO)

5Management

Exertional compartment syndrome
  • First line, ≥ 3 months→activity modification, NSAIDs, rest / ice / stretching
    (leg: rarely effective; works only if activity stopped completely)
  • Forearm, no treatment yet→NSAIDs + PT (stretching, endurance)
  • Refractory→fasciotomy of involved compartments

Nonop successforearm PT ~80% vs leg PT < 50% (OB) · all CECS get a nonop trial first

Definitive (TO)fasciotomy in non-responders · mainstay = subcutaneous fasciotomy (OB)

Incision Releases Landmark
Lateral Anterior + lateral 12–15 cm above lateral malleolus · protect SPN · may see hernia
Medial Posterior compartments (if pressures ↑) Mid-tibia, posterior border
Endoscopic Same Smaller incisions, similar complications

Structure at risk (single anterolateral incision)superficial peroneal nerve crossing near the anterior / lateral fascial border
✗ Wrong options: sural (posterolateral) · saphenous (medial) · peroneal artery (deep) · posterior tibial artery (posteromedial)

Successanterior > 80% · deep posterior ~60% · not a "home run" (multifactorial) · no op vs nonop trials

Recurrence / failureup to 20% at mean 2 yr · fibrosis / scar · risk = isolated (anterior + lateral) release · four-compartment fasciotomy ↓ reoperation

Not risk factors (OB)age < 23 (better success + satisfaction), higher pre-op pressures, bilateral involvement

Sportsmotocross, rock climbing, gymnastics, rowing (repetitive gripping) · volar compartment commonest

Gymnast, 5-min pressures 25 + 32, untreatedNSAIDs, activity modification, PT
✗ Wrong options: endoscopic / open fasciotomy · fasciectomy · observation

Differential – popliteal artery entrapment

Traps✗ Wrong options: intraseptal SPN entrapment (gives CECS-type symptoms) · flexor digitorum accessorius longus → tarsal tunnel · popliteal thromboembolism

1Basics

Epidemiology & risk factors

Causeheat gain > heat loss (production > dissipation)

When / who↑ in warmer months · highest in American football, running, cycling, adventure races

Risk factorspoor heat acclimatisation, dehydration, sleep deprivation, prior heat illness · conditioning, body composition, protective equipment, environment

Football preseason~74% of EHI = heat cramps · peak in first 14 days (esp. first 7) · risk ↑ when WBGT ≥ 82°F (27.8°C)

Spectrummild (heat oedema, rash, cramps, syncope) → moderate (exhaustion) → severe (heat stroke) · heat cramps don't predispose to heat stroke

3Presentation

Spectrum of exertional heat illness

Condition Key features Treatment
Heat syncope Transient LOC, peripheral vasodilation, ↓ cardiac output, normal temperature · rapid recovery supine Supine + legs elevated, fluids
Heat cramps / EAMC Painful spasm of large muscles · ↓ hydration, ↓ Na + Cl · random muscles, spasms 1–3 min Stretching + oral fluids with NaCl
Heat exhaustion Can't continue · core < 39°C (102.2°F) · no CNS dysfunction · profuse sweat, pale moist skin, nausea, vomiting, headache, weakness Cooling, oral rehydration, monitor · loosen clothes, ice axilla + groin, cool sprays
Hypernatraemic heat exhaustion Inadequate water replacement · thirst, oliguria Water
Heat stroke Hyperthermia + CNS dysfunction + loss of thermoregulation ± multi-organ failure Immediate cold-water immersion
Exertional rhabdomyolysis Muscle pain, weakness, ↑ CK, myoglobinuria Cooling, aggressive IV fluids, ± dialysis
Condition Key features Treatment
Exercise-associated collapse (EAC) Conscious collapse after finishing · loss of venous return on stopping · normal mental status, temp, vitals · most common in marathon tent (59–85%) Rule out serious causes → oral fluids + Trendelenburg → discharge
Exercise-associated postural hypotension SBP falls ≥ 20 mmHg standing vs supine
Exercise-associated hyponatraemia Na < 135 + mental status change · dilutional Severe → EMS + IV hypertonic saline

Heat exhaustion core temp< 39°C (102.2°F) (Orthobullets, OB) · 98.6–104°F (OB211458) — read the options

Heat stroke — definition, CNS dysfunction & cold-water immersion

Key discriminator from heat exhaustionCNS dysfunction ✓
✗ Wrong options: temp > 38°C · hypotension / dehydration · cramps + dizziness (dizziness isn't CNS dysfunction) · profuse sweating

CNS signsconfusion, disorientation, bizarre behaviour (often first sign), staggering / ataxia, seizures, delirium, coma · CNS depression = most important marker

Heat stroke core temperature Source
> 40°C (104°F) Orthobullets (printed "> 102.2°F or 40°C"), ACSM / AFP (OB)
> 41°C (105.8°F) OB1428, OB8705
> 105°F OB211458
May reach 106–110°F (41.1–43.3°C) OB8735

Sweatingclassic teaching: anhidrosis, hot dry skin (OB "hallmark") · exertional heat stroke often sweat-soaked, pale (OB219812) · sweating is an inconsequential criterion (OB211458) · dry, flushed skin → non-exertional / classic heat stroke

Temperaturerectal = only reliable · not oral, temporal, axillary, auricular (ACSM — don't use for diagnosis)

Trigger for immediate coolingcollapse + mental status change · rectal > 40°C + any CNS change → cool
✗ Wrong options: temporal temp 39.4°C · anhidrosis · tachypnoea · hypotension (both conditions can show collapse, hypotension, tachypnoea)

5Management

Athlete collapses in heat
  • Mental status change (± rectal > 40°C) → heat stroke→cold-water immersion ON SITE
    • then IV fluids + EMS→cool to 39°C first, transport second
  • Alert, sweating, temp < 39°C → heat exhaustion→shade, cool, oral fluids
  • Conscious, normal temp + vitals after finishing → EAC→oral fluids, Trendelenburg
  • Endurance event, heavy water intake, confused → hyponatraemia→hypertonic saline

Heat stroke treatment

First steprapid cooling: ice / cold-water immersion = most effective whole-body method
✗ Wrong options: IV fluids first · acetaminophen (antipyretic COX block, no effect) · supine + leg elevation (heat syncope) · IV antibiotics · benzodiazepines / Valium (may worsen) · electrolyte or low-osmolarity drinks (cramps / syncope) · warm bath · reverse Trendelenburg

Cooling target0.2°C / min to 39°C · other: cooling blankets, evaporative (fans, sprays), ice to large muscle groups, internal cooling, cool IV fluids

Cool first, transport secondwhole-body cooling on site before evacuation unless other medical emergency (Orthobullets, ACSM, OB219812) · OB8735 key = transport to ED with IV fluids + cooling during transfer — choose immersion if offered

Outcomecooling within 1 h of onset → usually full recovery · on-site immersion safe (half-marathon: 68% treated on site, 59% discharged home)

ThenIV resuscitation + treat complications · EMS activation

RTP after heat strokeno evidence-based guideline · rest 7 days → gradual increase over next month → cleared when heat tolerance returns (medically supervised)

Exercise-associated hyponatraemia & collapse

Ironman, 60°F, heavy bottled-water intake, collapseshyponatraemia
✗ Wrong options: hypernatraemia · hypothermia · subendocardial MI · berry aneurysm

Causeexcess free (hypotonic) water not replacing sweat Na losses · usually > 3 h ingestion · endurance athletes (triathlon, ultra-marathon, marathon)

Na thresholds< 135 (Orthobullets prints mg/dl; OB mEq/L) · up to 10% of ultradistance athletes ≤ 135 mEq/L (mostly asymptomatic) · symptomatic usually ~125 mEq/L

Presentationmental status change, peripheral paresthesias, extremity swelling

Correctionsevere acute → rapid correction (avert brainstem herniation) · mild → oral salty solutions · too-rapid correction → central pontine myelinolysis (OB) — read the options

Preventionfluid balance · sports drinks (4–8% carbohydrate) for exercise > 1 h · water best early; electrolyte drinks later prevent dilutional hyponatraemia

Soldier collapses after 2-mile run, conscious, rectal 37.9°C, BP drop 10 mmHg, recoversexercise-associated collapse
✗ Wrong options: heat stroke (no CNS change) · cramps · postural hypotension (needs ≥ 20 mmHg) · hyponatraemia

Wet bulb temperaturethermometer wrapped in a wet cloth → reflects evaporative (sweat) cooling capacity in heat + humidity

Wet bulb temperature Action
82–86°F 1:1 practice : rest
> 86°F Postpone / cancel participation (✗ Wrong options: > 75 · > 83 · > 90 · > 93°F)

Other preventionheat acclimatisation (gradual ↑ activity in heat), hydration, activity modification, immersion tub on site at high-risk events

Risk factors

Group Risk factors
Demographic Female, caucasian, older age · poor baseline fitness (TO)
Activity Military, track / cross-country, high training volume · sudden ↑ training intensity (TO)

Anatomy & biomechanics

Proximal femurneck-shaft angle 130 ± 7° · anteversion 10 ± 7° · calcar = strongest part (dense posteromedial bone)

Head blood supplyMFCA predominant · LFCA · artery of ligamentum teres (~10%) · ↑ displacement → ↑ vascular disruption

Capsular ligamentsiliofemoral (Y of Bigelow, AIIS → IT line) resists ER + extension · ischiofemoral resists IR · pubofemoral resists abduction + ER in extension

Load3–5× BW jogging · 8.4× BW running

Muscle strainabductors → highest compressive strain superolateral neck · extensors / flexors → tensile vs compressive strain posterior / anterior cortex · rectus femoris (knee extensor) loads neck least

Compression side Tension side
Site Inferomedial neck (calcar) Superolateral neck
Propagation Starts inferomedial → superiorly · 45° → stable oblique Starts superolateral → inferiorly · 90° to cortex → unstable transverse
Cause Compressive load Bending; abductors fatigue
Risk Low (if < 50%) High — displaces
Rx Nonop if < 50% Screw fixation

5Management

Femoral neck stress fracture on MRI
  • Compression, line < 50%, no effusion→NWB / protected WB + activity restriction
  • Compression, line > 50% or effusion or progression→percutaneous cannulated screws
  • Tension side→percutaneous screw fixation (urgent)
    (MRI stress change without line → nonop per Orthobullets)
  • Displaced→urgent ORIF, anatomic reduction

Finding Treatment
Compression, line < 50% Nonoperative — NWB / protected WB, activity restriction
Tension-side stress change, no line (MRI) Nonoperative (Orthobullets)
Tension-side fracture Cannulated screw fixation
Compression, line > 50% Cannulated screws (or strict NWB + weekly X-rays — Shin)
Compression + hip effusion Cannulated screws (8× progression)
Progression of compression fracture Cannulated screws
Displaced ORIF — cannulated screws or sliding hip screw
TO treatment table Incomplete (< 50% width) Complete (> 50% width)
Compression Conservative — unless significant pain or can't straight-leg raise Surgical — cannulated screws or DHS
Tension Surgical — DHS Surgical — DHS
Displaced — Immediate reduction + fixation — DHS ± derotation screw
Atypical tension Conservative Surgical — DHS

Implant choice conflict3 cannulated screws, inverted triangle (Orthobullets, OB) · DHS for tension-side (TO table) — read the options

Initial management – protected weight bearing

Compression < 50% — NWB vs protected WBNWB + activity modification (TO; ✗ Wrong options: protected WB with crutches · screws · bed rest + calcium / vitamin D) · crutches with protected WB (OB; ✗ Wrong options: skeletal traction · calcium · ORIF · pulsed US) — read the options

Nonop protocol (Orthobullets)NWB 6 wk → ↑ 25% BW per week to painless FWB → unrestricted at 3–4 months · 75–100% heal and return

OB protocolprotected WB + close observation 6–8 wk · cessation of running until healed

Nonop consrefracture (case reports), progression

No rolecorticosteroids, calcium, pulsed ultrasound, skeletal traction in acute FNSF

Low-risk stress fracture (TO)relative rest + activity modification · not healed or symptoms > 4–6 wk → immobilisation + NWB or surgery

High-risk incomplete fracture (TO)immobilisation + strict NWB · worsening / progression → fixation · complete high-risk fracture → strongly consider surgery

Tension vs compression side – surgical fixation

Tension sidehigh risk of displacement → percutaneous screws as soon as diagnosed (Shin & Gillingham) → avoids displacement + harms of bedrest, allows early crutch WB
✗ Wrong options: cam / pincer arthroscopy · NSAIDs + ↓ mileage · PWB

Nonop tension siderare reports: strict NWB with 3+ wk bed rest then prolonged crutches

Compression > 50%percutaneous screw fixation
✗ Wrong options: oncology referral · valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy · arthroscopic labral repair · I&D

Recruit, 10% weight loss, compression line 60%compression-sided; surgical fixation
✗ Wrong options: complete fracture · crutches only · tension-sided

Deciding factorcompression vs tension side + % width · bone density not important

Displaced fatigue fractureurgent surgery

Screw techniquethree 7.0 / 7.3 mm cannulated screws, inverted triangle (> two): inferior calcar (highest load to failure), posterosuperior, anterosuperior · start at or above lesser trochanter (avoid stress riser) · parallel, maximal spread · threads in head, not across fracture · washer vs GT penetration · percutaneous or mini-open lateral

Screw outcomesprevent displacement · outcomes ≈ nonop lower-risk FNSF · more military separation

Screw complicationscutout, varus collapse, implant failure, neck shortening, nonunion

ORIF of displaced FNSF

Principleanatomic reduction + early surgery ↓ AVN

Approach Interval Note
Smith-Petersen (anterior) Superficial TFL (SGN) / sartorius (femoral) · deep gluteus medius (SGN) / rectus femoris (femoral) — internervous Best view of whole neck · implants via separate lateral incision
Watson-Jones TFL / gluteus medius (both SGN) — intermuscular Same incision for reduction + implant · poor subcapital view

Reduction aidsK-wire / Schanz joysticks, pointed clamps, medial buttress plate · fix with cannulated screws or DHS · autograft vs nonunion

ORIF complicationsinfection, AVN, nonunion, cutout, malreduction, implant failure · lower return to activity than nondisplaced

Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI)

Knee & Sports · 16 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & natural history

Definitionabnormal femur–acetabulum contact → labral damage, chondral injury, progressive hip pain

Whodeformity common + often asymptomatic · symptomatic with extreme ROM (ballet, gymnastics, martial arts) · hockey goalies, gymnasts, dancers → labral tears (repetitive FADIR)

Onsetactive young adult, slow-onset groin pain, often after minor trauma

Elite athletesprone to cam → linked to ↑ training intensity during skeletal development

Natural historyearly hip dysfunction + arthritis · FAI = most common cause of OA in nondysplastic hips
✗ Wrong options: Perthes · traumatic labral tear · repetitive high-impact sport · dashboard injury

Anatomy (capsule, labrum, ligamentum teres)

Acetabulumilium + ischium + pubis · femoral head anteverted 15° relative to condyles

Capsular ligamentsiliofemoral (Y ligament of Bigelow), ischiofemoral, pubofemoral

Iliofemoralstrongest capsular ligament → restrains extension + ER → key restraint vs microinstability · cut during capsulotomy

Labrumhorseshoe fibrocartilage, joined inferiorly by transverse acetabular ligament · ↑ acetabular volume + suction seal

Labral sealnegative intra-articular pressure, retains synovial fluid · no labrum → ↑ cartilage loading + ↓ resistance to distraction

Ligamentum terescotyloid fossa → femoral head · negligible blood supply in adult

Ligament arrangementiliofemoral, pubofemoral + ischiofemoral form a helical spiral around the proximal femur

Cam vs pincer pathomorphology & chondrolabral damage patterns

Cam Pincer
Side Femoral Acetabular
Typical patient Young athletic males Active middle-aged women
Site Anterolateral neck / anterosuperior head-neck junction Anterosuperior acetabular rim
Morphology ↓ head-neck ratio, aspherical head, ↓ femoral offset, femoral neck retroversion AS rim overcoverage, acetabular retroversion, protrusio, coxa profunda
Mechanism Aspherical head (radius > acetabulum) jams in → shear at chondrolabral junction Normal neck abuts abnormal rim → crushes labrum
Labrum Chondrolabral separation — outside-in detachment, anterosuperior Intrasubstance tear / contusion (coup)
Cartilage Delamination anterosuperior — precedes labral tear Contrecoup posteroinferior acetabulum (head levered back)
X-ray Pistol grip, ↑ alpha angle, ↓ offset ratio Crossover sign, posterior wall sign, ↑ LCEA

FAI (TO)dynamic conflict: early abutment of proximal femur on acetabulum · intra-articular impingement = cam or pincer

Cam (TO)aspherical antero-superior head-neck junction rotates in → compression + shear at chondrolabral junction → chondrolabral separation, labral degeneration, cartilage detached from subchondral bone

Pincer (TO)excessive acetabular wall → labrum compressed between femoral neck and rim

Mixed cam + pincermost common type (up to 80%)

Only one lesion neededcam or pincer alone can cause symptoms

SCFEepiphysis displaced posteriorly → prominent anterior neck, ↓ IR → cam / pistol grip (variable patterns) · externally rotated limb

After PAOacetabulum may become retroverted → pincer

FAI labral tearsanterosuperior, 10–2 o'clock

Pathologic anatomy of cammorphologic abnormality of femoral head · impingement in flexion
✗ Wrong options: acetabular retroversion (pincer) · posteroinferior labral tears · femoral anteversion · osteonecrosis

Cam pathology in a gymnast↓ femoral head-neck offset
✗ Wrong options: AS rim overcoverage (pincer) · neck anteversion (cam = retroversion) · ↑ head-neck ratio · spherical head

Horizontal growth plate signpistol grip + epiphyseal scar extending lateral to the best-fit circle of the head → cam

Lesion pattern seen Means
AS cartilage delamination → then labral tear at chondrolabral junction Cam ✓
AS labral tear at labral-capsular junction → then delamination Wrong order
Posteroinferior acetabular cartilage lesion Pincer contrecoup
Posterosuperior acetabular eburnation · posterosuperior head fraying OA
Non-spherical head + AS chondral-labral separation (scope) Cam ✓
Anterior labral contusion + intrasubstance tear + posteroinferior chondral softening Pincer ✓
Lateral acetabular cartilage softening + partial labral detachment Cam
Posteriorly oriented acetabulum + AS labral tear Retroversion (pincer)
Non-hemispherical acetabulum + hypertrophic labrum Dysplasia
Tense iliopsoas + anterior labral tear · tear at 4 o'clock + bursal inflammation Internal (iliopsoas) impingement
AS femoral head cartilage flap + haemarthrosis AVN
Gluteal enthesopathy + bursal scarring GTPS (lateral pain, abductor weakness)
Ligamentum teres tear + patulous anterior capsule Hip instability

3Presentation

Symptoms

Painactivity-related groin pain ↑ with hip flexion · worse with prolonged sitting / driving · better standing / lying · deep groin pain on squatting

Mechanicalclicking / popping (may be absent) · gluteal or trochanteric pain from aberrant gait

Byrd C sign (TO)patient cups hip: index finger over anterior hip + thumb over posterior trochanteric region → intra-articular hip pathology
✗ Wrong options: knee · ankle · shoulder

Intra-articular injection relieftemporary relief confirms intra-articular source

Clinical examination – FADIR & loss of internal rotation

Hallmark↓ flexion + ↓ internal rotation (flexion < 90°, IR < 5°)
✗ Wrong options: ↑ ER · ↑ abduction · ↓ ER · ↓ adduction

Anterior impingement test (FADIR)supine, hip passively flexed 90°, adducted, internally rotated → deep groin pain
✗ Wrong options: abduction / ER combinations

Posterior impingement testextension + ER → occasionally positive

FADIR in FAImost sensitive exam · positive in cam, pincer and AS chondrolabral tears

Exam finding Points to (not FAI)
Stinchfield — groin pain on resisted hip flexion Femoral neck fracture, iliopsoas tendonitis, abscess
FABER pain Lumbar spine, iliopsoas, sacroiliitis (not routine for FAI)
Trendelenburg gait Abductor weakness
Half sit-up pain + pubic ramus tenderness Athletic pubalgia
Greater trochanter tenderness Trochanteric bursitis
Pain with axial loading, female athlete triad Femoral neck stress fracture
Symphysis tenderness, resisted adduction / abduction Osteitis pubis
Pain on resisted hip flexion / sit-up Adductor / hip flexor strain

Key radiology findings

View / study Technique Use
AP pelvis + true lateral Lateral with hip in 15° IR Recommended routine views (Orthobullets)
Frog-leg lateral — Alpha angle (Orthobullets method)
45° modified Dunn (TO) Supine, 45° flexion, 20° abduction, neutral rotation Best view for cam (✗ Wrong options: frog-leg · cross-table lateral · 90° sitting view)
Cross-table lateral (TO) Hip in 10° IR Anterior head-neck offset ratio
90° Dunn / seated (TO) Seated, 90° flexion, 20° abduction, neutral rotation Beta angle

Bone scan — Not for FAI (used for FNSF when MRI impossible)

MRA triad (Kassarjian)AS labral tear + AS cartilage lesion + ↑ alpha angle

Cam on MRIaxial T2: loss of sphericity of anterior head-neck (alpha angle measurable, e.g. 80°) · fluid-sensitive images: labrum separated from chondral surface · coronal T1: no neck oedema
✗ Wrong options: stress fracture

Alpha angle method (other OB views)best-fit circle on head + line along neck axis → angle where head exits the circle · AP, frog-leg lateral or Dunn

Radiographic measurements

Measurement How Normal Abnormal
Alpha angle Line head centre → neck centre + line head centre → point where head loses sphericity (anterolateral head-neck junction) < 42° (Orthobullets) · ≈ 42° (TO) · < 55° (one OB) > 42° head-neck offset deformity · > 50–55° cam · > 50° diagnostic (one OB)
Head-neck offset ratio (anterior head line − anterior neck line) ÷ head diameter > 0.17 < 0.17 cam · < 0.15 → 95% PPV for FAI (TO, Beaulé)
Beta angle (TO) Acetabular rim–head centre line vs head centre–loss of sphericity line (Wyss, open MRI) — < 30° → impingement (cam, pincer, mixed) (Brunner)

ACEA (Lequesne) False profile Over 20° (Orthobullets) · 25–50° (OB) < 20° structural instability / dysplasia
Tönnis (roof) angle Acetabular index (inclination) Above 0° (Orthobullets) · 0–10° (OB) < 0° ↓ inclination → overcoverage (pincer) · > 10° ↑ inclination → dysplasia

✗ Wrong options: alpha angle · beta angle · anterior head-neck offset ratio

Pincer/acetabular retroversion – crossover sign

Normal AP pelvisanterior rim runs medially + distally, diverging from the more vertical posterior rim · walls meet superolaterally

Crossover signanterior rim line crosses posterior rim line ("figure 8") → crossing occurs more distally → acetabular retroversion → pincer · the two wall lines should never cross normally (two OB explanations word it as the posterior wall crossing over the anterior)

Seen onAP pelvis / AP hip · hip AP normal head-neck + popping in gait extension → AP pelvis shows crossover
✗ Wrong options: normal film · ↑ femoral offset · SI sclerosis · coxa valga

Crossover = ?excessive acetabular retroversion
✗ Wrong options: low acetabular index · deficient anterior column · labral detachment · pelvic discontinuity

Crossover in FAIretroversion in pincer
✗ Wrong options: retroversion in cam · protrusio (head medial to ilioischial line) · femoral anteversion / retroversion (CT)

Other pincer signsposterior wall sign, protrusio, coxa profunda, ↑ LCEA, negative Tönnis angle

Pincer AP pelvisbilateral acetabular over-coverage + cephalad retroversion · bilateral cam + crossover = mixed

FAI types

Type Defect Classic sign
Cam Femoral head-neck (aspherical) Pistol grip, alpha > 50–55°
Pincer Acetabular overcoverage / retroversion Crossover sign
Mixed Both — most common (up to 80%) Both

Condition Discriminator
Femoral neck stress fracture Female athlete triad / energy deficiency · axial-load pain, no impingement · linear lucency / sclerosis of inferior or posteromedial neck · T2 oedema
DDH Shallow acetabulum, ↓ anterolateral coverage, low CEA, hypertrophic labrum
Os acetabuli Unfused secondary ossification centre of anterosuperior acetabulum
Iliopsoas tendonitis / internal impingement Resisted hip flexion pain · Rx tenotomy

Osteitis pubis Central pain, symphysis tenderness · peri-symphyseal sclerosis + osteolysis · NSAIDs, rest
AVN Insidious, pain with impact / inclines, risk factors, not end-range
Displaced femoral neck fracture ORIF (young) · arthroplasty (old)
Other Ischiofemoral impingement, adductor strain, athletic pubalgia, lumbar radiculopathy, hip instability

Compression-sided FNSF (distractor)NWB if < 50% neck · percutaneous screws if > 50%

5Management

Symptomatic FAI
  • Minimal symptoms, no mechanical symptoms→activity modification, PT, NSAIDs
  • Failed nonop, mechanical, non-arthritic→arthroscopic osteoplasty + labral repair
    (no viable labrum → labral reconstruction)
  • Large femoral deformity (residual SCFE / Perthes)→open surgical hip dislocation (Ganz)
  • Significant acetabular retroversion / dysplasia→periacetabular osteotomy
  • Arthritic, end-stage→THA (resurfacing vs THA controversial)

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Nonoperative Minimal symptoms, no mechanical symptoms — always first
Arthroscopic osteoplasty Symptomatic + mechanical, failed nonop, non-arthritic
Labral repair Viable tissue, tear at chondrolabral junction (vascular acetabular margin)
Labral debridement Intrasubstance tears
Labral reconstruction No viable labral tissue
Open surgical dislocation Previous gold standard · preserved cartilage, correctable deformity, reasonable expectations · residual SCFE / Perthes
PAO Acetabular deformity with significant retroversion · dysplasia
THA Arthritic, end-stage
Hip preservation contraindicated Tönnis grade 2–3 or < 2 mm joint space (Harris)

Treatment – nonoperative first

Initial Rxactivity modification + NSAIDs + PT (core / hip strengthening, kinetic chain) — even pro athlete with labral tear on MRI

PT to ↑ passive IRavoid: worsens impingement + chondrolabral damage

Untreated cam FAI, pro footballeractivity modification + NSAIDs
✗ Wrong options: open dislocation (more morbidity) · isolated labral repair (leaves cam) · PAO (no acetabular deformity)

Hockey player, 3 wk pain, no mechanical symptomsactivity modification, PT, NSAIDs
✗ Wrong options: bone scan · any surgery yet

Arthroscopic osteoplasty with labral repair

Failed 12 wk PT + NSAIDs, cam + labral teararthroscopic labral repair + femoral osteoplasty
✗ Wrong options: more PT · surgical dislocation (slower return) · debridement · PAO (no dysplasia)

Arthroscopic over openless soft-tissue trauma, ↓ AVN risk, quicker return · equivalent results to open

Repair vs debridementrepair / reconstruction → better PROMs (HHS, SF-12, VAS) + less pain
✗ Wrong options: ↑ OA risk · no difference · ↑ pain · ↑ nerve injury

Always treat bonelabral debridement or repair alone → suboptimal; address cam / pincer as well · femoral osteotomy no role · minimal arthritis → arthroplasty not indicated

Pincer + AS chondrolabral tear, failed 6 mo PTpincer osteoplasty + labral repair
✗ Wrong options: cam osteoplasty (no cam) · labral reconstruction · more PT + isolated repair

Cam + labral detachment, minimal arthritisfemoroacetabular osteoplasty + labral repair
✗ Wrong options: debridement · femoral osteotomy · hemi / THA

Mixed FAI, wrestler with Trendelenburg + IR 10°hip arthroscopy + osteoplasty
✗ Wrong options: abduction orthosis · DEXA · bone scan · osteotomy

Hockey goalie, failed PT + iliopsoas bursa injectionFADIR reproduces pain → femoroacetabular osteoplasty
✗ Wrong options: PAO (dysplasia) · iliopsoas tenotomy (internal impingement / snapping) · FABER · loose body removal

Techniquecapsulotomy to reach peripheral compartment (cam) · trim head-neck · rim trim → labral refixation if destabilised · debridement vs repair vs reconstruction

Evidence caveatlong-term halt of arthritis unproven (Gerdeman)

Open surgical hip dislocation (Ganz)

Approachlateral decubitus, Kocher-Langenbeck incision, gluteus maximus split → digastric trochanteric flip (fragment mobilised anteriorly) → capsulotomy → anterior dislocation, ligamentum teres transected

Advantagewide exposure, preserves external rotators + MFCA → no ↑ AVN

Cam + anterior labral tear (classic)anterior transtrochanteric dislocation + labral repair + femoral osteoplasty
✗ Wrong options: THA · arthroscopic debridement alone · arthroscopic repair alone · posterior dislocation

Alternativedirect anterior approach → limited posterior acetabular view · combined arthroscopic + limited open → early results promising

Complicationtrochanteric hip pain

Adolescent, open treatmentmedian 7 months
✗ Wrong options: 4–6 wk · 3 mo · 12 mo · 16 mo

Hamstring Injuries

Knee & Sports · 17 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence30% of new lower-extremity injuries in athletes · ↑ 4% / yr in soccer over ~15 yr

Sportsrapid acceleration: soccer, track and field, football · sprinters, gymnasts (TO)

Most common muscle injury in athletes (TO)biceps femoris
✗ Wrong options: adductor longus · gastrocnemius · rectus femoris

Two-joint muscles (TO)exposed to acceleration / deceleration forces → hamstrings, quadriceps, gastrocnemius most often injured

Which hamstring (TO)biceps femoris ~83% > semimembranosus ~12% > semitendinosus ~5%

Site — adultmyotendinous junction (MTJ) = most common rupture site, sprinting

Site — skeletally immatureischial tuberosity avulsion · also water skiers · 10% of pelvic avulsion fractures in the skeletally immature (Orthobullets) · ischial tuberosity ~50% of pelvic apophyseal avulsions (OB, Rossi — see AIIS / ASIS chapters) — read the options

Risk factors

Previous hamstring injury×6 reinjury risk (weak scar) → greatest predictor of proximal avulsion

Strengthhamstring : quadriceps ratio < 0.6 · side-to-side difference > 10–15%

Otherinadequate warm-up · ↓ hip extension (Orthobullets) · ↓ baseline hip flexion (OB) · leg-length difference (shorter leg = tighter hamstrings) · ↑ age, high training demand, ↑ BMI, tight hip flexors (OB)

Anatomy

4 musclessemimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris long head + short head · gracilis is NOT a hamstring (pubic origin) (OB) · TO text lists "semitendinosus and gracilis medially, biceps femoris laterally" — read the options

Originall from ischial tuberosity except short head (linea aspera)

Footprintconjoint tendon (ST + BF long head) medial (inferomedial / posteromedial), BF more proximal than ST · SM = separate, most lateral (superolateral / anterolateral), slightly proximal · SM closest to sciatic nerve

Muscle Insertion Nerve
Semimembranosus Posterior medial tibial condyle Tibial division of sciatic
Semitendinosus Superomedial tibia — pes anserine Tibial division
BF long head Fibular head Tibial division
BF short head Fibular head, BF long head, lateral capsule Common peroneal division

Blood supplyinferior gluteal + profunda femoris arteries

Distancesorigin ~6 cm proximal to inferior border of gluteus maximus · sciatic nerve 1.2 cm lateral to origin · pudendal nerve 2–3 cm superomedial

Biomechanicscross hip + knee (except short head — knee only) · BF long head + SM most active in hip extension · ST + BF short head most active in knee flexion

Muscle regeneration — satellite cells

Satellite cellsdormant in muscle until injury → regenerate skeletal muscle + new satellite cells
✗ Wrong options: osteoblast signalling · periosteum · chemotherapy binding · sonic hedgehog = limb bud

2Mechanism

Mechanism & origin anatomy

Hip flexion + knee extensioneccentric contraction at end of swing phase (maximal fibre elongation) → biceps femoris
✗ Wrong options: sartorius · rectus femoris · adductor magnus · TFL

Intramuscular / MTJ injurysudden take-off phase of running · acute injuries usually BF

Chronic repetitive stretchhip flexion + knee extension → proximal semimembranosus (OB)

Older patientssame hyperflexion in slips and falls, water-skiing

Adolescent hurdlerischial tuberosity avulsion = "hurdler's fracture" · same mechanism in adult → MTJ rupture
✗ Wrong options: muscle belly · tendinous insertion · ramus fracture · sports hernia

Hamstring strain (TO) Type I Type II
Mechanism High-speed running Slow stretch — hip flexed + knee extended (high kicking, splits)
Site BF long head, proximal MTJ Semimembranosus near ischial tuberosity
Acute loss of function More marked Less dramatic
Rehabilitation Shorter Longer

Tennis leg (TO)medial head of gastrocnemius torn at muscle belly–aponeurosis junction

Historysudden posterior thigh pain running / kicking / jumping ± "pop" · pain with sitting = proximal avulsion

Ecchymosisposterior thigh → proximal avulsion or high-grade MTJ tear · latent ecchymosis appears ~1 week after injury (haematoma tracking)

Palpable massmiddle ⅓ posterior thigh → MTJ rupture

Gait"stiff-legged" (avoids hip + knee flexion)

↑ Popliteal anglehip 90°, knee 90° → extend knee slowly → angle at pain vs other side

Strengthprone knee flexion at 90° weak · resisted knee flexion prone painful (TO)

Neuromay have peroneal weakness (foot drop)

Provocative test (pain = +) Method Sens / spec
Puranen-Orava Heel on raised surface, reach for toes 0.76 / 0.82

Modified bent-knee stretch Same, rapid full extension 0.89 / 0.91 — best

5Management

Hamstring injury (MRI: tendons + retraction)
  • MTJ / single tendon / 2 tendons < 2 cm→NONOPERATIVE
  • 2 tendons > 2 cm, young active→OPEN REPAIR
  • 3-tendon / complete proximal avulsion→OPEN REPAIR (acute)
  • Partial avulsion, symptoms > 6 months→REPAIR TO ISCHIAL TUBEROSITY
  • Bony avulsion→by displacement
    • < 2 cm → PROTECTED WB 4 wk→PT
    • > 2 cm or chronic symptomatic→ORIF

Nonoperative care

Indicationsmost injuries · all single-tendon tears · 2 tendons < 2 cm retraction · MTJ rupture · less active / comorbid

Regimenrest, ice, NSAIDs, protected WB 4 wk → stretching + strengthening · heals in up to 6 wk · OB: WBAT, gentle stretching, over 4–6 wk
✗ Wrong options: NWB 6 wk

Single tendon < 2 cmruptured tendon scars to intact tendons

Returnstrength ≥ 90% of contralateral

Modalitiesmassage, ultrasound, electrical stimulation

PRPacute strains, high-level athletes · within 24–48 h, US-guided · RTP 3–5 days earlier (NFL, low-level data)

Operative criteria

Tendon repair ORIF
Proximal avulsion ruptures Bony avulsion > 2 cm displaced (fragment big enough for hardware)
Partial avulsion, failed nonop 6 months Chronic symptomatic bony avulsion
2 tendons > 2 cm retraction, young (< 50 y) active
3-tendon tears (all avulsed)

Complete tearsnonop → poorer outcomes → repair · acute complete > chronic partial for improvement after surgery

Arthroscopyno intra-articular pathology · endoscopic repair = case reports only

Proximal avulsion — surgical indications & repair

22-yr sprinter, complete proximal avulsion retracted > 5 cmsurgical repair first-line
✗ Wrong options: ATFL signal = low ankle sprain → rest, ice, early rehab · PCL avulsion → nonop, quadriceps strengthening · partial cuff tear → NSAIDs + PT · compression-sided femoral neck stress fracture < 50% width → activity restriction + NWB

Hurdler, 3 tendons avulsed (BF, SM, ST)open surgical repair of all tendons to the ischial tuberosity
✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs + NWB 6 wk · stretching · CT · hip arthroscopy

42-yr, acute 3-tendon tear, massive retraction, no bony fragmentprimary suture-anchor repair + 4–6 wk PWB ± brace · bracing optional
✗ Wrong options: ORIF · Achilles allograft + sciatic neurolysis · PRP + NWB · crutches 6 wk

Partial avulsion, ischial pain at 6 monthsrepair to ischial tuberosity
✗ Wrong options: sciatic decompression · labral repair · repair to intertrochanteric crest / femoral shaft (nonanatomic)

Approachprone, knee free to flex · transverse incision in gluteal crease → "T" extension distally for large retracted / chronic tears · fascia usually intact; vertical fascial incision → haematoma

Footprintscrape with elevator / curette, avoid burr (sciatic) · 4–6 suture anchors, knee flexed

Chronic, unable to re-approximateAchilles allograft bridge (≈ acute results, small studies)

Post-opPWB 4–6 wk, knee flexed 40° ± knee / hip brace

ORIF techniquedirect reduction, partially / fully threaded screws + washers ± suture anchors / interference screws

Outcomes80% RTS at 6 months · complications up to 23% (23.17%) · chronic > acute (< 6 wk) complications · 91% return of strength after operative repair (OB)

Surgical nerve risk (sciatic, pudendal)

Nerve Position vs ischial tuberosity Fact
Sciatic 1.2 cm lateral Most commonly injured in repair · neurolysis just lateral to hamstring sheath · transient palsy (retraction)
Pudendal 2–3 cm superomedial Aggressive Hohmann superomedially → sexual dysfunction, dyspareunia, impotence, pain sitting / defecating → use glenoid retractors
Posterior femoral cutaneous Lateral, beside sciatic With inferior gluteal artery deep to gluteus max · transient posterior thigh numbness
Inferior gluteal Below piriformis, under gluteus max Retracted with gluteus max · 5 cm cephalad to its inferior border
Superior gluteal Far superolateral Exits above piriformis (OB) · "inferior to piriformis, then superior" (other OB) — not in field
Nerve to obturator internus Medial, with pudendal Rarely encountered

Rehabilitation & recurrence prevention (eccentric training)

Phase (TO) Exercise
Acute (painful) Isometric (no joint movement), ice, compression, elevation, NSAIDs as needed
Subacute (pain-free walking) Isotonic = concentric + eccentric → emphasis on eccentric: Askling L-protocol + Nordic hamstring curls
Adjunct Lumbopelvic stability (balance board), adductor + glute strengthening

Recurrent hamstring injury, 15-yr footballer (TO)eccentric training
✗ Wrong options: balance board · isotonic · isometric

Nordic hamstring exercisekneel, heels held, lean forward to prone + return · ↓ injuries 50–70%

Preventionadd abdominal, hip + quadriceps strengthening · correct hamstring–quadriceps imbalance

Recurrent sprinter returning — advise (TO)work on hamstring strength · assess hip position while running · lumbopelvic control · false: "avoid high-speed training" — sprinter must train at high intensity

Terminal swing (TO)hip max flexion ~30° → controlled by hamstrings + glutes; hamstrings slow the extending knee before heel strike → eccentric load = injury phase · hip adductors switch eccentric → concentric

Anterior pelvic tilt (TO)strains lumbar spine + hamstrings, impairs gluteal function → lumbopelvic control prevents recurrence

Compartment Traction? Contents
Central Yes Acetabular fossa, head articular surfaces, ligamentum teres, rim + labrum, AIIS + capsule

Zona orbiculariscircular ring of capsule · landmark for iliopsoas tendon lying immediately deep to it
✗ Wrong options: pectineus · sartorius · adductor brevis · rectus femoris

Stabilityproximal–middle capsule incl. zona orbicularis → greatest influence on stability during distraction (Ito)

Byrd C sign (TO)index finger over anterior hip + thumb over posterior trochanteric region → intra-articular hip pathology
✗ Wrong options: knee · ankle · shoulder

Key radiology findings (pre-arthroscopy screen)

Measurement Normal Implication
Tönnis grade (OA) 0–1 Grade 2–3 → contraindication (failure, conversion to THA)
LCEA > 25° (28° normal) < 20° → dysplasia (e.g. 15°)
ACEA — < 20° → dysplasia
Tönnis (roof) angle 0–10° (5°, 8° normal) > 10° → dysplasia (e.g. 15°)

5Management

Setup, positioning & joint access

Kit70° arthroscope, long cannulas + guides, flexible instruments · fluoroscopy + arthroscopy towers both visible

Positionsupine or lateral decubitus, fracture / dedicated table · well-padded perineal post

Traction~50 lb to distract · Trendelenburg ↓ force needed

Accessspinal needle at AL portal into central compartment under fluoroscopy (avoid head + labrum) → saline distension or venting (air arthrogram) → guidewire, cannula, scope → later portals under direct vision

Portals & nerve injury (LFCN, sciatic)

Portal Location Use At risk
Anterolateral (AL) 2 cm anterior + 2 cm superior to anterosuperior GT (Orthobullets) · 1 cm proximal + 1 cm anterior to GT tip (TO) First (fluoroscopy, only blind portal) · primary viewing Superior gluteal nerve (> 4 cm proximal, TO) · chondrolabral injury = biggest risk (TO)
Anterior (AP) Line down from ASIS × line across top of GT, moved lateral · ~6 cm distal to ASIS through sartorius + rectus femoris (OB) Central compartment (4:30–8:30 o'clock) LFCN + lateral femoral circumflex artery · femoral NV bundle if medial
Distal anterolateral (DALA) 3–5 cm distal to AL · traction off, neutral or 45° flexion Peripheral compartment (neck) Ascending branch LFCA
Mid-anterior (MAP) Between anterior and AL As anterior —
Posterolateral (PL) 1 cm posterior + 1 cm proximal to posterosuperior GT tip (Orthobullets, TO) · 2–3 cm posterior to GT tip (OB) · neutral rotation Posterior joint Sciatic nerve (2.9 cm) · deep branch MFCA (> 1 cm) (TO)

LFCA distance (TO)femoral nerve + ascending LFCA ~4 cm · terminal LFCA branches as close as 2 mm · transverse LFCA branch 10.1 mm (OB)

Medialised anterior portalno better view · ↑ risk to femoral vessels + LFCN (Thorey) · too medial → femoral nerve

✗ Wrong options: AL portal → SGN · traction → pudendal · fluid extravasation · orthosis

Sciatic nerve + rotationER brings sciatic closer to PL portal → never ER during entry; IR moves it away (OB, Orthobullets) · ↑ risk with IR or ER (TO) — read the options

Standard central portalsAL, anterior, PL (Byrd) · reference for all others

Complications mostly due totraction
✗ Wrong options: lateral positioning · supine positioning · DVT · HO

✗ Wrong options: obturator (no scrotal supply) · LFCN (anterolateral thigh) · pudendal from DALA portal

Hip Labral Tear

Knee & Sports · 19 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & etiology

Commonest associationacetabular dysplasia = highest incidence (Orthobullets, OB) · FAI = most common cause of labral pathology (another OB) — read the options

Whoall ages · commonly active females

Siteanterosuperior (chondrolabral junction) — low collagen content + fibres parallel to chondrolabral junction · FAI tears 10–2 o'clock

Asymptomatic69% of asymptomatic adults have a labral tear on MRI · 73% some hip pathology (Register) → a tear alone ≠ indication for surgery

CausesFAI, dysplasia (floppy / redundant / enlarged labrum), trauma (dislocation / subluxation), capsular laxity (↑ translation), degeneration (edge loading)

Effecttear ↓ resistance to motion → initially relative hip instability ✓ · commonest associated lesion: chondral injury

Trapstears are related to DJD (✗ Wrong options: unrelated) · occur with or without abnormal morphology (✗ Wrong options: only with)
✗ Wrong options: caused by ligamentum teres lesions · posteroinferior quadrant

Dysplasia vs FAI labrum (Leunig)both tear anterosuperior · labrum enlarged in 12 dysplastic hips, none with FAI → anterosuperior rim = initial fatigue site

Consequence↑ friction, cartilage consolidation + strain → accelerated degeneration (Safran)

Anatomy

Shapehorseshoe, continuous with transverse acetabular ligament

Two partsarticular = fibrocartilage · capsular = dense connective tissue

Vascularityfrom capsule + synovium at acetabular margin → only peripheral ⅓ vascularised

Innervationhighly innervated (mechanoreceptors + nociceptors) · nerve to quadratus femoris + obturator nerve

Functionadds 22% surface area + 33% volume · negative-pressure suction seal → retains synovial fluid, frictionless motion

3Presentation

Symptomsmechanical pain + snapping (internal snapping), locking, vague groin pain · pain with sitting (anterior pathology)

Provocative test Manoeuvre
Anterior labral tear Flexed + ER + abducted → extension + IR + adduction (painful catch)
Posterior labral tear Flexed + adducted + IR → abduction + ER + extension
FADIR Positive in AS chondrolabral tear and cam FAI

Element Grading

Hip labral tear
  • All patients first→rest, NSAIDs, PT, steroid injection
  • Failed nonop→hip arthroscopy (+ treat FAI)

    • tear not amenable to repair→labral debridement
    • irreparable labrum→labral reconstruction

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Outcome
Nonoperative Initial treatment for all No long-term data
Arthroscopic repair Failed nonop + full-thickness tear at labral-chondral junction Better healing + function than partial labrectomy
Arthroscopic debridement Failed nonop + tear not amenable to repair 70–85% short-term relief
Labral reconstruction Failed nonop + irreparable labrum Allograft ≈ autograft PROMs

Treatment – arthroscopic repair

Failed rest, PT, NSAIDs + 1-day injection reliefarthroscopic treatment of labral tear ± FAI
✗ Wrong options: repeat injection · pinning (no fracture) · loose body removal · PAO (no dysplasia)

Address causeboth labrum and FAI bone must be treated for symptomatic gain · AP pelvis may show retroversion

Repair techniqueknotless suture anchors preserve labral anatomy

Debridementremove unstable labrum + synovitis · limited WB × 4 wk · flexion + abduction limited 4–6 wk

Approach (Matsuda)open dislocation, mini-open and arthroscopy all improve pain + function · open → highest complication rate · mini-open → LFCN injury · all-arthroscopic ≥ others, fewest major complications

Dysplasia labrum FAI labrum
Labrum Hypertrophic / floppy / enlarged Normal size, crushed / separated
Site Anterosuperior Anterosuperior
Bony fix PAO Osteoplasty

1Basics

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

Whoadolescents + young adults · F > M · PF pain = most common condition affecting adolescents (OB) · mainly adolescent females

Pain generatorunclear, multifactorial · roughened / damaged undersurface cartilage of patella · biologic, mechanical + emotional causes (OB)

Proposed factorslimb malalignment, muscle weakness, chondral lesions, maltracking (narrow contact points → ↑ PF contact pressure → pain) · dynamic valgus = excessive medial movement of limb in weight bearing (OB)

Pain receptorsanterior fat pad + joint capsule = highest potential · subchondral bone weak

Miserable malalignmentfemoral anteversion + genu valgum + external tibial torsion / pronated feet → ↑ Q-angle · assess tibial + femoral rotation

Associations & aetiology (TO)

Associated with chondromalacia (TO)rheumatoid arthritis, alkaptonuria, recurrent haemarthrosis

EXCEPT (TO)ankylosing spondylitis

Aggravated byclimbing or descending stairs · theatre sign (prolonged sitting, knee bent — long car rides, back seat) · squatting / kneeling · rising from a deep seat

Exampain on patellar compression with ROM or resisted (open-chain) knee extension · crepitus · quads atrophy · full ROM, no effusion, stable ligaments

Study Finding / use
X-ray (AP, lateral, notch ± Merchant) Often normal · chondrosis, shallow sulcus, patella alta / baja, lateral tilt

MRI Best for articular cartilage · T2 best · abnormal cartilage = high signal · only if intra-articular / intra-osseous lesion suspected

Grade Cartilage
0 Normal
I Surface intact, heterogeneous, high signal
II Fissures + fragmentation extending down to articular surface
III Partial-thickness defect, focal ulceration
IV Exposed subchondral bone

  • All patients→rest, NSAIDs, quads (VMO) + core + hip PT, ≥ 1 yr
  • Failed rehab + Outerbridge 2–3→arthroscopic debridement
  • Tight lateral retinaculum + lateral tilt→lateral retinacular release
    (severe, failed extensive PT → realignment osteotomy / MPFLR)

Mainstayrest, rehab, NSAIDs for minimum 1 year · NSAIDs > steroids · activity modification

✗ Wrong options: FAI hip series · CT for TT-TG · Graston / ASTYM / iontophoresis (chronic tendinopathy) · chest CT + oncology

✗ Wrong options: steroid injection · MRI · diagnostic arthroscopy · patellar taping (adjuvant only)

Exercise that ↑ pain (TO)leg extension = open chain against resistance in functional range → ↑ contact pressure
✗ Wrong options: leg press · squat · lateral step

Best quads exercises (TO)closed kinetic chain (mini-squat, lateral step, high-saddle cycling) in 0–30° (minimal pressure) · leg press tolerated · mini-squat + hip adduction (ball) favours VMO

Least PF stress (TO)CKC restricted to 0–45° + OKC restricted to 90–45°
✗ Wrong options: OKC full 90–0° · CKC 60–90° + OKC 30–0° · deep squats 0–90°

Procedure Indication
Arthroscopic debridement (mechanical, radiofrequency) Outerbridge grade 2–3 chondromalacia

Fulkerson (anteromedialisation) ↑ Q-angle, instability (controversial) · not with superior medial arthrosis (scope first) or skeletal immaturity

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence2–15% of knee overuse injuries · most common cause of lateral knee pain in runners + cyclists (TO)

Whorunners, cyclists, repetitive flexion–extension · first seen in US Marine recruits (1975); skiers, hockey, basketball, soccer (TO) · slightly more common in women (TO)

Anatomy

Origincontinuation of tensor fascia lata (Orthobullets) · distal fascial continuation of TFL + gluteus medius + gluteus maximus (TO)

InsertionGerdy tubercle (lateral tibial plateau) + partly lateral femoral supracondylar ridge (TO) · runs superficial to vastus lateralis

Innervationsuperior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) · synergists = hip abductors

Function (TO)knee extensor < 30° flexion, flexor > 30°; moves posterior to lateral epicondyle with flexion · anterolateral stabiliser (OB)

MechanismITB shifts forward + back over lateral femoral condyle / epicondyle → friction, tension, inflammation · also compression + bursal inflammation (OB)

Impingement zone30° of knee flexion = knee angle at foot strike (TO)

Pathoanatomycompression / irritation of tissue deep to ITB (TO: highly innervated fat pad under ITB) · cysts or bursitis of lateral synovial recess · condylar bone oedema · ITB itself rarely abnormal

Associatedpatellofemoral syndrome (tight ITB) · medial compartment OA (↓ medial joint space → varus) · greater trochanteric pain syndrome

Presentation & running risk factors

Risk factors Orthobullets TO
Training Sudden ↑ intensity / mileage, poor shoe support Tilted surfaces, hills, abrupt training change, downhill running

Biomechanics Quads–hamstring imbalance, ↑ landing force, ↑ knee flexion at heel strike ↑ hip adduction, ↑ knee IR + IR velocity, ↑ knee flexion at heel strike, ↑ maximal foot inversion

✗ Wrong options: ↑ foot eversion · ↑ knee external rotation · ↑ hip abduction

✗ Wrong options: lateral meniscus tear · LCL tear · lateral hamstring strain

Infection Return to play
CA-MRSA After 72 h on antibiotics (e.g. TMP-SMX) (OB) · cover lesions · NCAA bacterial: no new lesions 48 h + 72 h antibiotics + no exudative lesions (OB)

Small Topical mupirocin

Nonopprogressive ROM, quadriceps + hamstring strengthening · 6 wk casting heals but → stiffness · unrecognised PLC → progressive varus / hyperextension laxity

Procedure Indication
Nonop Isolated grade I / II, no instability at 0°

Meniscal Cysts

Knee & Sports · 29 / 61

1Basics

Definitionlocal collection of synovial fluid within or next to the meniscus, most often from a meniscal tear

Incidenceno general-population data · 1–4% of knee MRIs · no age trend

Associationmeniscal tear — almost always present, the most common associated lesion (TO) · also articular cartilage injury, ACL tear (Orthobullets) · TO: false: "common with ACL tear"

Type Site Usual tear
Perimeniscal Small fluid collection within the meniscus · medial → posterior horn · lateral → anterior horn / mid-portion Radial or vertical
Parameniscal (e.g. Baker) Extruded outside the meniscus — most common · usually between semimembranosus + medial head of gastrocnemius Horizontal or complex

Sidemedial slightly commoner, 2:1 (Orthobullets — literature conflicting) · medial > lateral on recent radiology reviews; lateral was the old teaching (TO)

Lateral meniscal cysts (OB)myxoid degeneration spreading from the meniscal centre outward · horizontal cleavage tears · most often from a middle-third LM tear
✗ Wrong options: discoid meniscus · PLC injury · vertical tears · popliteus tear

2Mechanism

One-way valvethe tear lets synovial fluid out, not back → fluid concentrates into gel-like material

3Presentation

History± recent trauma · may be asymptomatic

Symptomspain at the medial / lateral joint line or back of knee · locking + clicking · delayed / intermittent swelling · weakness or claudication (neurovascular impingement)

Exampopliteal mass, best seen in extension · joint line tenderness · palpable mass · crepitus

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Radiographs Normal in young patients with acute meniscal injury or cyst
MRI Most sensitive test for both the cyst and the tear · cyst = bright T2
MRI mimics Necrotic tissue, nerve sheath tissue, pus look like cysts on T2 → IV contrast may be needed

Parameniscal cyst on MRIimplies a meniscal tear (Meniscal Tears chapter)

5Management

Meniscal cyst
  • Small perimeniscal or parameniscal→rest, NSAIDs, physiotherapy (first line)
  • Isolated Baker cyst, young patient→aspiration + US-guided steroid injection
  • Tear communicates with joint, not repairable→arthroscopic partial meniscectomy + decompression
  • Symptomatic parameniscal / tear not open to joint→open posterior cyst excision

Nonopfirst line · trial to gauge pain response · may work with degenerative tears

Aspiration + steroidfor isolated Baker cyst in the young · poor results in older patients with degenerative tears + cysts

Arthroscopic debridement, decompression + partial meniscectomyperimeniscal cyst with a tear not amenable to repair (complex, degenerative, radial) · decompress fully · incomplete resection → recurrence · repair the meniscus if the tear allows (Orthobullets summary)

Tear doesn't open into joint (OB)arthroscopy followed by open cystectomy

Open posterior excisionprone, curved incision over popliteal fossa · interval medial gastrocnemius ↔ semimembranosus · sharp dissection of cyst down to capsule · incomplete resection → recurrence

How it's asked

"Lateral meniscal cyst — associated pathology?"middle-third lateral meniscal tear

"True about meniscal cysts (TO)?"most common associated lesion is a meniscal tear

Meniscal Tears

Knee & Sports · 30 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

Incidencevery common · most common indication for knee surgery · ↑ risk in ACL-deficient knees

Medial > lateraloverall · exception: acute ACL tear → lateral tears commoner (alpine skiers: LM > 4× MM) · chronic ACL → medial (PH MM = secondary restraint)

ACL + meniscal injury (TO)meniscal tear in > 50% of acute and > 80% of chronic ACL tears

Acute tearsyoung athletes · twisting on a loaded, flexed knee

Degenerative tearsolder (> 40 y, loss of elasticity) → posterior horn medial meniscus

Commonest pattern (TO)radial in a normal meniscus · horizontal in a discoid meniscus

Meniscal structure & collagen (TO)

Feature (TO) Fact
Arteries Medial, lateral + middle geniculate (from popliteal) → perimeniscal capillary network in synovium / capsule
Vascular rim Peripheral 10–30% of MM, 10–25% of LM (Orthobullets: MM 20–30%)
Avascular part Remaining 65–75% fed by synovial fluid diffusion / mechanical pumping (joint motion)
Age Fully vascular prenatal → just after birth · 10–30% at age 10 · peripheral 10–30% at maturity = red-red
Nerves Posterior articular branch of posterior tibial nerve + terminal obturator + femoral · lateral capsule = recurrent peroneal branch of CPN
Nerve fibres Concentrated in the periphery + anterior / posterior horns (✓ horns rich in mechanoreceptors)
Mechanoreceptors Ruffini endings, Pacinian corpuscles, Golgi tendon organs
ECM Water 72%, collagen 22% + cells
Collagen Type I predominates (+ II, III, V, VI) · collagen = up to 75% of dry weight · collagen (type I) gives tensile strength (✗ Wrong options: type II)
Fibres Type I circumferential in deep layers (parallel to periphery) · radial superficially
Hoop stress Axial load → tensile stress along circumferential fibres (✓ generated on axial loading)

Why peripheral tears heal↑ blood supply (geniculate vessels at capsular attachment)
✗ Wrong options: elasticity · type I / II collagen · GAG (distribution similar, no effect on healing)

2Mechanism

O'Donoghue unhappy triad (TO)

Triad (TO)ACL + MCL + medial meniscus · lateral force on knee with foot fixed · O'Donoghue 1950
✗ Wrong options: LCL · PCL · lateral meniscus

Later arthroscopic studies (TO)lateral meniscus tear commoner with acute ACL tear → triad questioned

Bucket handle (TO)twisting injury, fixed leg with flexed knee struck by another player

Root tearMMPRT: low-energy attritional · descending stairs / downhill, rising from a seat, deep squat → pop · LPRT: with ACL (high energy)

3Presentation

Symptomspain localised medial / lateral · mechanical (locking, clicking), esp. squatting · delayed / intermittent swelling · effusion

Joint line tendernessmost sensitive physical examination finding

Locked kneecannot actively or passively extend (past 40°, past 30°, ROM 20–90°) → displaced bucket handle in notch · MRI indicated with mechanical symptoms or locked knee

Root tearpop in loaded flexion (rising from seat, stairs) · posteromedial JLT · less catching / locking than flap tears (meniscus extrudes) · exam lacks specificity
✗ Wrong options: exam = gold standard

Test Technique Positive
McMurray (Orthobullets / OB) Flex knee, hand on joint line, rotate tibia, bring flexion → extension Palpable pop / click + pain · ER → medial, IR → lateral
McMurray (TO) Knee > 90° flexion, full IR (LM) or full ER (MM); more flexion → more posterior segments Thud / click felt (sometimes heard)
Apley Prone, 90° flexion, axial compression Pain with ER (MM) / IR (LM)
Thessaly Standing on affected limb, twist IR / ER at 5° then 20° flexion Joint line pain, locking / catching
Ege Squat with knees max ER or IR Pain / click

✗ Wrong options: body of MM · discoid LM · anterior horn LM

✗ Wrong options: MM · popliteus · proximal tib-fib · pes bursitis

Exam trapsno valgus end-point = MCL · no varus end-point = LCL · apprehension = patellar instability · posterior drawer + quadriceps active test = PCL · pivot shift (clunk with flexion, IR, valgus from extension) = ACL · 3-quadrant lateral translation + J-sign = patellar dislocation · posterior sag = PCL

MCL sprainpain with valgus stress at 30° (isolates superficial MCL), medial gapping

Plica syndromemedial parapatellar pain, palpable cord

Zone Distance from MCJ (TO) Blood supply Healing (TO)
Red-red (outer third) 0–3 mm Rich > 90% — repair all

Algorithms

  • Degenerative, older→nonop first (rest, NSAIDs, PT)
    ("noninferior" to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy)
  • Young, locked knee / displaced bucket handle→arthroscopic reduction + repair
  • Peripheral vertical / longitudinal, young→repair
  • Root tear→root repair (see below)
  • Complex, degenerative, flap, white-white→partial meniscectomy
Posterior root tear
  • Minimal arthritis (KL ≤ 2), BMI < 35→transtibial pull-out root repair
  • With ACL tear→ACL reconstruction + root repair
  • Established arthritis→arthroplasty (UKA / TKA)

Meniscus

Knee & Sports · 31 / 61

1Basics

Function

Load transmissioncarries 50% of load in extension, 85% in flexion · ↑ congruency → ↑ contact area → ↓ point loading

Shock absorptionmeniscus more elastic than articular cartilage

Hoop stressvertical compressive load → circumferential "hoop" tension in the circumferential fibres → load spread, ↓ femorotibial contact stress

Stabilitydeepens the tibial surface · secondary stabiliser · posterior horn MM = main secondary stabiliser to anterior translation · menisci become primary stabilisers in the ACL-deficient knee

Lateral meniscusless stabilising · 2× the excursion of the MM

Other roles (OB)proprioception, lubrication, nutrition of the joint, cartilage protection / OA prevention

Composition & collagen

Tissuefibroelastic cartilage (fibrocartilage): collagen, proteoglycan, glycoproteins, cells

Water65–75% (Orthobullets) · 72% water + 22% collagen (OB, TO)

Collagen sharetype I = 90% of meniscal collagen (Orthobullets, OB) · type I = 75% of ECM dry weight (TO) · + II, III, V, VI · collagen gives tensile strength

Predominant type (TO)type I
✗ Wrong options: type II · "type II in red-red + type I elsewhere" · "type I in red-red + type II elsewhere"

Zonal collagen (TO)red-red: type I (like ligament / tendon) · white-white: more type II (like hyaline cartilage) (false: "type II predominates in red-red")

Collagen Tissues
Type I Meniscus (fibrocartilage), ACL, annulus fibrosus, bone, tendon
Type II Articular (hyaline) cartilage (✗ Wrong options: same as meniscus)
Fibre layer (OB) Orientation Role
Superficial network + lamellar layer Radial Structural integrity; tie fibres together
Central main layer Circumferential (longitudinal), parallel to periphery Converts compression → hoop stress; captured by vertical mattress sutures

Horizontal cleavage tear (OB)usually excised (avascular inner zone, degeneration) · Ahn: all-inside vertical mattress + notch drilling (marrow) → 91% healing

Gross anatomy

Medial meniscus Lateral meniscus
Shape C-shaped, semicircular, triangular cross-section Near circular — horns close together, next to ACL
Length (TO) 40–45 mm — longer / "larger"; ~27 mm wide 32–35 mm — shorter
Width (Orthobullets) 9–10 mm 10–12 mm
Thickness 3–5 mm 4–5 mm
Plateau covered (TO) 51–74% — less 75–93% — more
Horns (TO) Posterior horn ≫ anterior Horns equal
Fixation Rigid peripheral (coronary) fixation → less mobile Fewer capsular attachments → more mobile
AP displacement (OB) 0.43 mm 0.66 mm
Artery (Orthobullets) Medial inferior genicular → peripheral 20–30% Lateral inferior genicular → peripheral 10–25%

Kinematicsboth menisci move anterior with extension, posterior with flexion · MM: less anterior translation in extension + less posterior movement in flexion
✗ Wrong options: more translation · fewer capsular attachments

TO "not true" trap"MM larger than LM" ✓ (longer) · "LM covers more surface" ✓ · "PH MM larger than anterior horn" ✓ · "type II predominates in red-red" (false)

Attachments

Transverse (intermeniscal) ligamentjoins the anterior horns of MM + LM

Transverse ligament on MRIits junction with the anterior horn LM mimics a tear on sagittal images → follow it over successive images
✗ Wrong options: LM / MM tear · anterior meniscofemoral ligament (a posterior structure) · ligamentum mucosum

Ligamentum mucosum (infrapatellar plica)best on sagittal · intercondylar notch → anterior fat pad

Coronary (meniscotibial) ligamentsfix the meniscus peripherally to the tibia

Meniscofemoral ligamentsfrom the posterior horn LM into the PCL / MFC near the PCL insertion · Humphrey = anterior to PCL · Wrisberg = posterior · both in 46%, at least one in 100% (TO)

Blood supply & healing

Middle genicular arteryposterior horns (+ posterior capsule, ACL, PCL) → primary supply to PH MM
✗ Wrong options: medial inferior / superior genicular · lateral geniculates

Inferior geniculatesmedial inferior → peripheral 20–30% MM · lateral inferior → peripheral 10–25% LM · anastomose anteriorly → fat pad, synovium, patellar tendon · lateral superior + inferior → lateral retinaculum

Perimeniscal capillary plexus (TO)from superior + inferior medial / lateral geniculates · menisci lose vessels after birth → only peripheral 10–25% perfused at maturity (TO; meniscal-tears TO: 10–30%)

Central 75%nourished by diffusion from synovial fluid · limited / no intrinsic healing

Peripheral 25% (red zone)heals by fibrocartilage scar · fibrochondrocyte = healing cell · tears < 4 mm from periphery heal best

Innervationperipheral two-thirds: type I + II nerve endings · posterior horns: highest mechanoreceptor density

5Management

Meniscal root tear — tibial fixation

Root tearbiomechanically = total meniscectomy (loss of hoop tension → ↑ peak contact pressure) → chronic pain, instability, rapid OA · an independent tear subtype

52 y, PH MM root tear, no arthritis on X-rayfixation to the tibia (root repair) = gold standard
✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs + PT · partial meniscectomy · total meniscectomy (Fairbank changes) · UKA (only if arthritis)

Nonop (Krych)poor outcomes, worsening OA, > 33% arthroplasty at mean 32 months

Partial meniscectomy vs repair (Chung)repair better clinically + radiologically · lower arthroplasty at 5 y

Age (LaPrade)transtibial double-tunnel pull-out improves < 50 and > 50 y equally, medial or lateral

Pre-existing / rapid arthritisUKA / TKA

TKA after unrepaired root tear — cross-check> 33% at 32 months (OB, here) · ~30% at 5 y · up to 28% at 3.2 y (OB, Meniscal Tears chapter) — read the options

X vs Y

Red zone (peripheral 25%) White zone (central 75%)
Blood supply Geniculate capillary plexus Diffusion only
Collagen (TO) Type I More type II
Healing Fibrocartilage scar (fibrochondrocyte) Little or none

"Root tear, no arthritis — definitive treatment?"fixation to the tibia

Neck Injuries in Athletes

Knee & Sports · 32 / 61

1Basics

Spectrum & epidemiology

Spectrumligament sprain → burner / stinger → spear tackler's spine → cervical fracture → transient quadriplegia → quadriplegia

Whocontact sports, football + rugby · better protective gear → ↓ incidence · 9–15% of ~12,000 new spinal cord injuries / yr from contact / collision sports

Catastrophic~6 quadriplegic events / yr (US high school + college football; more at college level)

Highest rate of cord injurybilateral facet dislocation

Predisposing conditions (↑ severity, may bar play)

Underlying conditionsprevious C-spine trauma (fracture, ligament injury), cervical stenosis, congenital odontoid hypoplasia, os odontoideum, Klippel-Feil anomalies

2Mechanism

Spear tackling & axial loading

Mechanismaxial load (compression) on a flexed neck · most injuries during tackling

Spear tackling (leading with crown of helmet) — most common mechanism of neck injury in football → gradual cervical stenosis + loss of lordosis

Catastrophic injuryaxial loading of the subaxial spine during spear tackling → fracture, dislocation, ligament disruption
✗ Wrong options: arm-tackle traction root avulsion (neurotmesis, most severe "stinger") · lateral bending · flexion-distraction / whiplash cut block · face-mask rotation

Boden series (196 catastrophic injuries, 13 yr)subaxial 95, C1-C2 9, combined 7, unknown 41 · 43 cord neurapraxia, 1 root avulsion · defensive backs + spear tackling = greatest risk

# Spear tackler's spine — all 4 criteria
1 Developmental cervical canal stenosis
2 Persistent straightening / reversal of lordosis
3 Post-traumatic radiographic abnormalities
4 Documented spear-tackling technique

Spear tackler's spinecontraindication to contact sports

3Presentation

On-field management of suspected cervical spine injury

Assume spinal injuryany athlete with lost or altered consciousness

Most important prehospital stepmaintain neutral cervical alignment
✗ Wrong options: assess off field first · high-dose steroids (weak evidence, surgeon's discretion)

Prone player, can't move limbs
  • 1→log-roll SUPINE with C-spine stabilised
  • 2→remove FACEMASK (airway)
  • 3→remove helmet + shoulder pads together (if safe)
  • 4→hard collar, controlled backboard (log-roll)
    (equipment kept: towel rolls taped beside helmet)

(✗ Wrong options: Traps — hard collar with helmet still on) · keeping player prone · helmet off before facemask

Helmet + padsNATA now allows on-field removal of both by trained personnel if neutral alignment kept (Orthobullets, Mills consensus) · older advice: remove facemask, retain helmet (Schroeder & Vaccaro) · cadaver C5-6: helmet alone → kyphosis, pads alone → lordosis, both retained → neutral — remove or retain together

Examinspect deformity · palpate spinous processes (step-off, pain) · motor, sensation + reflexes in all 4 limbs

Transient quadriplegia (cervical cord neurapraxia)

Featuresneurapraxia of the cord → bilateral upper + lower limb pain, paresthesia, weakness → resolves minutes–hours (Orthobullets) · 10 min–48 h (OB, stinger chapter)

Mechanismhyperextension, hyperflexion or axial load · 3 of 16 NFL disc herniations presented with transient paresis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Fact
Radiographs — indications Recurrent stingers · neurologic symptoms / transient quadriplegia · C-spine trauma series
Canal diameter (SAC) Normal ~17 mm · < 13 mm = stenosis · < 10 mm = absolute stenosis (OB)
Torg-Pavlov ratio Canal ÷ vertebral body (sagittal) · normal 1.0 · stenosis < 0.8 (Orthobullets) · < 0.82 (Pavlov + Torg original)
Torg ratio limits Technique dependent, low PPV / not predictive, inaccurate in large athletes (big bodies skew ratio)
Torg ratio < 0.8 prevalence 49% of asymptomatic pro football players
MRI Bilateral neurologic symptoms → stenosis, loss of CSF around cord, cord signal change
"Functional" stenosis Loss of CSF / cord deformation on MRI or CT myelogram — bone ratios alone can't define it

Torg original datacanal 14 mm in symptomatic athletes vs 18.9 mm controls

SAC at injury level vs deficit10.5 mm complete · 13.1 mm incomplete · 15.9 mm root · 16.7 mm none
