Osgood Schlatter's Disease (Tibial Tubercle Apophysitis)

Knee & Sports · 33 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

Definitionosteochondrosis / traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle → paediatric anterior knee pain

Whoboys > girls · bilateral 20–30% · jumpers (basketball, volleyball), sprinters, soccer, gymnastics, track · non-athletes too

Ageboys 12–15 yr (Orthobullets, OB) · boys 5–12 yr (OB) · girls 8–12 yr — read the options

Causerepetitive pull of extensor mechanism / patellar tendon · growth spurt: bone lengthening outpaces muscle–tendon flexibility → ↑ tension on apophysis

Patellar tendon strain ratio↓ in OSD (elastography, Enomoto: 18 vs 42 legs) → less compliant tendon → force reaches tibial tubercle faster

Anatomy — tibial tubercle ossification

Age Tubercle
< 11 yr Cartilaginous
11–14 yr Apophysis forms (secondary ossification centre)
14–18 yr Apophysis fuses with tibial epiphysis
> 18 yr Epiphysis + apophysis fused to tibia

3Presentation

Symptomsdull anterior knee pain, worse with kneeling, jumping, squatting, stairs · often bilateral

Examenlarged, tender tibial tubercle · pain on resisted knee extension (most painful) · no effusion, no limp, stable knee

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Lateral knee X-ray Irregularity + fragmentation of tibial tubercle · early: apophysis separation · late: fragmentation + intratendinous ossicles · may be normal
X-ray role Diagnosis is clinical; films rule out other causes
MRI Not essential · soft-tissue swelling, thickened oedematous inferior patellar tendon, fragmented ossification centre
Mature patient Persistent ossicle after tibial epiphysis fuses

Diagnosis & differential (Sinding-Larsen-Johansson, sleeve fracture)

Condition Distinguishing fact
Osgood-Schlatter Tibial tubercle tenderness, chronic, walks normally
Sinding-Larsen-Johansson Chronic apophysitis / minor avulsion of inferior patellar pole; 10–14 yr, esp. cerebral palsy
Patellar sleeve avulsion Inferior pole tenderness, cortical elevation of inferior patella, can't walk
Tibial tubercle avulsion fracture Acute, ambulation difficulty
Tibial spine avulsion Acute, can't bear weight, big effusion, Lachman +
Bipartite patella Normal variant (failed fusion of 2 ossification centres); painless, incidental
Others Jumper's knee, proximal tibial osteochondroma, Lyme (isolated effusion), plica, fat-pad impingement, infection, malignancy

5Management

Osgood-Schlatter
  • First line→NSAIDs, rest, ice, activity modification, strapping, quads stretching
    • severe, not responding→CAST 6 WEEKS
  • Skeletally mature + persistent symptoms (~10%)→OSSICLE EXCISION ± TUBERCLEPLASTY

Nonop outcome90% complete resolution · self-limiting but resolves only when growth stops (physeal closure)

Persistent pain60.5% still had knee pain at median 3.75 yr (Guldhammer) → "self-limited" dogma questioned

Cast complicationquadriceps wasting

Persistent symptomatic ossicle — excision

Surgery indicationspain localised to tubercle, limits activity, failed nonop, persists into skeletal maturity

Procedureossicle excision + tubercleplasty (resect prominence) → relieves symptoms, return to sport expected
✗ Wrong options: never indicated · prednisolone injection · hamstring lengthening · RTS unlikely

Surgical outcome (Pihlajamäki) Result
178 military recruits, 10 yr 85% no pain at operative site · 75% back to full activity
107 patients (117 knees), median 10 yr Good Kujala / VAS, no long-term harm · but 39% still pain on kneeling
Mital (16 knees) Only 1 did not return to sport → combine excision + tubercleplasty

Osgood-Schlatter Sinding-Larsen-Johansson Tibial tubercle fracture
Site Tibial tubercle Inferior patellar pole Tibial tubercle
Onset Chronic, activity-related Chronic Acute
Walking Normal Normal Difficult
X-ray Fragmentation, ossicles Inferior pole fragmentation Displaced fracture

Causeshereditary, traumatic, vascular (multifactorial) · adult form → vascular · microtrauma · mechanical (discoid meniscus, tibial spine impingement) (OB)

Cascadesoftening of cartilage with intact surface → early cartilage separation → partial detachment → osteochondral separation + loose bodies

Study Finding / use

Tunnel (notch) view Knee flexed 30–50° — shows posterior condyle lesion
X-ray sign Well-circumscribed sclerotic subchondral bone + radiolucent halo; sclerosis = poor prognosis
MRI Size, subchondral bone + cartilage status, signal around lesion, loose bodies → stability
MRI unstable Fluid (high T2) behind / circumferential to fragment (rim sign), fluid breaching cartilage / breaks in cartilage + oedema; cysts deep to lesion = subchondral involvement
Bone scan Open physes + activity behind lesion → 100% healed; closing physes → none (Paletta)
Arthroscopy Gold standard for instability — break in cartilage or mobile flap on probing

Stable Unstable

Intact surface, no fragmentation on MRI Synovial fluid behind lesion on MRI

Epidemiology

Whowomen : men 3 : 1 · women < 55 yr with risk factors · found after knee arthroscopy in middle-aged women

Group Risk factors
Classic Alcoholism, steroids (endogenous or exogenous), sickle cell, hypercoagulable states, trauma
Dysbaric Decompression sickness ("the bends")
Marrow-replacing Gaucher disease
Systemic SLE, inflammatory bowel disease, transplant patient
Infective / drugs Viruses (CMV, hepatitis, HIV, rubella, rubeola, varicella), protease inhibitors (HIV)

Mechanism↓ blood flow to bone secondary to risk factors

Spontaneous osteonecrosis (SONK)likely a subchondral insufficiency fracture · also linked to meniscal root tear

Painwith weight bearing, especially sitting → standing

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
X-ray (first line) AP, lateral, Merchant · wedge-shaped lesion · diagnostic only in advanced disease
MRI Most useful · highest sensitivity + specificity · needed for early / subclinical disease
MRI signal T1 dark · T2 bright (marrow oedema)

Differential diagnosis

Condition Distinguishing fact
Osteochondritis dissecans Lateral aspect of MFC, males 15–20 yr (this note) · 10–15 yr, median 13 (OCD chapter) — read the options

Occult fracture / bone bruise Trauma, weak bone, overuse

Osteonecrosis of the knee
  • All→NONOP FIRST (NSAIDs, limited WB, quads, activity modification)

  • Large area / collapse / multiple compartments→TKA

Overallobservation + treat the underlying systemic condition · surgery for advanced disease with severe subchondral collapse

Procedure Indication

MPFL tear sitepatellar insertion commonest (Orthobullets) · femoral attachment common avulsion site (OB) · soft-tissue avulsion most common pattern; midsubstance + soft-tissue avulsion > bony avulsion (OB) — read the options

Fragment originmedial patellar facet (most common) > LFC / lateral trochlear ridge · transverse patella fracture not associated
✗ Wrong options: lateral facet · odd facet · medial / central trochlea

Radiograph after self-reduced dislocation, 3 quadrantsFigure C = medial patellar facet fragment
✗ Wrong options: A lateral facet fracture · B knee dislocation · D LFC fracture (less common) · E inferior pole / transverse fracture

Fragment on X-ray + large effusionnext = magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs + PT · aspiration + cortisone · ORIF · arthroscopy before MRI

Fragments missed on X-rayup to 40% of first dislocations have large fragments → MRI

12-yr-old, 1st dislocation, large fragment in lateral recess + partial MPFL tear on MRIarthroscopic loose body removal versus osteochondral fragment fixation
✗ Wrong options: aspirate + brace · PT · immediate isolated MPFLR · TTO + MPFLR ± trochleoplasty

Fixationscrews / pins if enough bone; else removal (arthroscopic or open)

Vertical intra-articular patella fracture after dislocation (TO)internal fixation (ORIF)
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopy · cylinder cast · patellectomy

Patella fracture (TO) Rule
Commonest mechanism Direct impaction on flexed knee; indirect = eccentric quads contraction
Nonop Displacement < 4 mm, step-off < 2 mm, active SLR intact → brace ~10° flexion, neutral rotation (avoid baja)
Surgery Displacement > 4 mm and / or step-off > 2 mm, extensor disruption
Other ORIF Open fracture, articular gap > 3 mm, loose bodies, osteochondral fractures, paediatric sleeve fracture

MPFL repair vs reconstruction

MPFL repairacute first-time dislocation with bony fragment / avulsion with intact midsubstance · within first few days · no studies prove it beats nonop · not after many dislocations (attenuated tissue)

MPFL reconstructionrecurrent instability without significant malalignment · autograft or allograft

Graftgracilis or semitendinosus (stronger than native), two-tailed · open physes → medial quadriceps turndown on suture anchors (no femoral tunnel, TO)

Graft choiceall equal rates of postoperative instability (allograft = autograft = quadriceps = synthetic) · infection + PROs also equal

Complications (TO)knee stiffness, patella fracture, continued instability · femoral graft position is critical

MPFL reconstruction – femoral tunnel malposition

Femoral tunnel Result
Too proximal ("high and tight") Graft tight in flexion → loss of flexion / failure, overconstrains medially
Too distal ("low and loose") Graft loose in flexion
Too posterior Not tighter in flexion than a proximal tunnel
Schöttle point Correct — anteroproximal quadrant

Proximal tunnel traps✗ Wrong options: tight in extension (minimal MPFL tension in extension) · lateral tilt · patella baja · cause = cam-shaped distal femur

Tensionat 30° flexion (OB)

Operative criteria

Finding Procedure
Recurrent, no significant malalignment Isolated MPFLR
TT-TG > 20 mm (CT) · TT-PCL > 24 TTO (AMZ / Elmslie-Trillat) ± MPFLR
Patella alta, CDI > 1.2 Distalisation ± MPFLR
Dejour B or D Trochleoplasty + MPFLR ± TTO
Dejour A or C MPFLR ± TTO
Femoral anteversion > 25° Femoral derotation osteotomy + MPFLR
Lateral tilt > 20° / tight lateral retinaculum Lateral release (TO) / lengthening (OB) + MPFLR
Genu valgum > 10°, ≥ 6 mo growth Guided growth (8-plate, staples)

Surgical selection – isolated MPFL vs tibial tubercle osteotomy (TT-TG) vs trochleoplasty

Isolated MPFLR (TO)TT-TG ≤ 20 mm, normal or Dejour A trochlea, CDI < 1.2, tilt < 20°

Isolated MPFLR (OB)IS < 1.2, TT-TG < 20 mm, sulcus < 140°, negative crossing sign · e.g. Insall-Salvati ratio 1.15, TT-TG distance 15 mm, sulcus angle 138°, negative crossing sign
✗ Wrong options: sulcus 150° + crossing · TT-TG 21 · IS 1.3 · IS 1.25 + TT-TG 20 + sulcus 150°

Best isolated-MPFLR candidaterecurrent patellar dislocation, 3 quadrants lateral translation at 30 degrees knee flexion, presence of J sign, TT-TG of 15mm
✗ Wrong options: first-time (surgery controversial) · TT-TG 24 → consider TTO

Residual instability after isolated MPFLRsevere trochlear dysplasia = most important predictor · failure risks: dysplasia, ↑ TT-TG, age < 20 · IS ratio + tibial slope not factors

14-yr-old recurrent, TT-TG 20, sulcus 150°presence of trochlear dysplasia places him at risk for recurrent instability
✗ Wrong options: MPFLR alone poor (it does well) · IS 1.2 protective (normal) · age protective · slope 15°

✗ Wrong options: MPFL repair (attenuated) · TTO medialisation / distalisation · trochleoplasty

3rd dislocation, mild valgus, CDI 1.2, TT-TG 14.5 mm, mild dysplasia, wants fast RTSMPFL reconstruction
✗ Wrong options: MPFL repair · TTO alone · MPFLR + TTO (longer recovery, no proven benefit) · lateral release

TT-TG 20 exactlyisolated MPFLR still good · some add TTO only if > 20 · TTO importance controversial

TTO thresholdusually not done if TT-TG < 15–20 mm (e.g. 13 mm → no TTO)

Tibial tubercle osteotomy (Fulkerson / AMZ)

Fulkersonoblique osteotomy → tubercle anterior + medial (anteromedialisation, AMZ) · medialisation restores TT-TG, anteriorisation unloads PF · cut long (> 5 cm) + thick (> 0.75 cm) for 2 screws (OB)

Indication (OB)TT-TG > 20 mm (e.g. 25mm) + recurrent instability ± cartilage restoration
✗ Wrong options: open apophysis · medial defect · sulcus 165° · tilt 25°

Indication (TO)grade 3 and 4 chondromalacia patella and recurrent patellar dislocation (lateral facet or distal pole arthritis) + TT-TG > 20 mm
✗ Wrong options: habitual dislocation · grade 1–2 · Osgood-Schlatter

Contact pressures after AMZ↑ proximal & medial → proximal / medial facet arthritis = contraindication · medial patellar defect = relative contraindication
✗ Wrong options: distal · lateral

Correction targetTT-TG 10–15 mm, never < 10 (Orthobullets) · ~10 mm (TO) · TO: medialisation = TT-TG − 20 mm

Other TTOs (TO)Elmslie-Trillat = direct medial · Maquet = direct anterior · TTO when TT-TG > 20, ↑ TT-PCL, CDI > 1.2

Distalisation (TO)for CDI > 1.2 → target CDI 1 on C-arm · usually ~10 mm bone removed

Open tibial apophysisabsolute contraindication → growth arrest → recurvatum · paediatric: preserve physis

TTO complications (TO)tuberosity nonunion, painful hardware, tibial shaft fracture · longer recovery

Skin approachmidline incision → infrapatellar branch of saphenous nerve → inferolateral numbness

Trochleoplasty

Best suited (TO)Dejour type B and D (spur)
✗ Wrong options: A + B · B + C · C + D

Indications (TO)high-grade dysplasia + instability / maltracking, no established OA · revision with residual instability · rarely done in USA

Not for (TO)flatness alone (spur must be present) · type A (no trochlear procedure) · type C (lateral facet elevating instead)

Contraindications (TO)open physes, PF arthrosis

Complications (TO)arthrofibrosis / stiffness (most frequent) · trochlear shingle fracture propagation (brittle subchondral bone in PF arthritis)

Techniquesarthroscopic or open sulcus deepening · open recession wedge

Recurrent + Dejour D (cliff + spur)MPFL reconstruction with trochleoplasty
✗ Wrong options: MPFL repair ± VMO · TTO alone · MPFLR alone (residual instability)

Lateral release – lateral patellofemoral angle

Isolated lateral releasenot indicated for instability → iatrogenic medial instability

Lateral lengthening vs releaselengthening: better outcomes, less quadriceps atrophy, less medial instability · only for excess tilt / tightness after medialisation

2nd dislocation, 3 quadrants, J sign, tight lateral retinaculum, TT-TG 13, CDI 1.15MPFL reconstruction + lateral retinacular lengthening
✗ Wrong options: isolated release / lengthening · MPFLR + release · AMZ TTO

Main indication for isolated releaselateral patellar (facet) compression syndrome, no instability

Measurement for lateral releaselateral patello-femoral angle (negative tilt) on CT / sunrise
✗ Wrong options: congruence angle · Q-angle · sulcus angle · patellar height

Congruence + sulcus anglesassess malalignment + instability, not release

Other bony procedures

Guided growthgenu valgum > 10° + instability + ≥ 6 months growth · tension band 8-plate or staples (more rigid, faster)

Femoral osteotomy (TO)severe valgus → distal femoral osteotomy · anteversion > 25° → supracondylar derotation + MPFLR · hemiepiphysiodesis in immature valgus

Recurrent dislocation Nonop 15–60% at 2–5 yr · highest if 1st dislocation < 20 yr

TTO / trochleoplasty Nonunion, tibial fracture / arthrofibrosis, shingle fracture

1Basics

Risk factors & diagnosis

Incidenceup to 20% of jumping athletes (Orthobullets) · prevalence 8.5% in non-elite athletes (OB) — volleyball highest (14.4%), soccer lowest (2.5%)

Whoadolescents / young adults · M > F (2:1) · quadriceps tendinopathy = older adults

Risk factorspoor quadriceps + hamstring flexibility · hamstring tightness · male, younger, taller, heavier, type of sport (jumping) · patellar hypermobility · quadriceps atrophy · hard surfaces · ↑ training frequency

Predisposing factor (OB)hamstring tightness
✗ Wrong options: female · ↑ quadriceps strength · soft surfaces · low-frequency training

Risk factor EXCEPTolder age
✗ Wrong options: male · higher weight · quads / hamstring inflexibility · type of sport

Witvrouw vs Zwerver (OB)inflexibility = only significant factor; height, weight, age, Q-angle, LLD, strength not (Witvrouw) · younger, taller, heavier = risk (Zwerver) — read the options

Malalignmentnot strongly associated · malalignment → generalised PF syndrome, maltracking

Mechanismrepetitive forceful eccentric contraction of extensor mechanism · jumping, acceleration / deceleration, deep flexion

Histologydegenerative, not inflammatory · micro-tears at bone-tendon junction of inferior pole · angiofibroblastic + mucoid degeneration
✗ Wrong options: intra-substance inflammatory reaction

Theory (Rath, OB)impingement of deep tendon fibres on inferior pole · flexion + quads contraction ↓ pain

Sinding-Larsen-Johansson & jumper's knee – site (TO)

Jumper's knee (TO)tendinitis at tendo-osseous junction of lower (inferior) pole of patella · common in jumpers
✗ Wrong options: superior pole

Tooth sign (TO)periosteal reaction on anterior surface of patella · seen in jumper's knee (TO)

Jumper's knee treatment (TO)eccentric quads strengthening, avoid provoking activity, taping, deep transverse friction massage, cryotherapy

Sinding-Larsen-Johansson (TO)osteochondrosis of inferior pole of patella · often bilateral · overuse traction by patellar tendon on partly cartilaginous lower pole · active adolescents 10–14 yr

SLJ clinical (TO)pain + tenderness at lower pole of patella (↑ loading in flexion), subpatellar oedema · later tendon thickening, fragmentation of lower pole, bursitis

SLJ EXCEPT (TO)pain at lower end of patellar tendon (false) — pain is at proximal tendon / inferior pole

3Presentation

Symptomsinsidious anterior knee pain at inferior border of patella · early: after activity · late: during activity · "movie theater sign" (prolonged flexion)

Examswelling over tendon, tenderness inferior pole · local soft-tissue oedema but no effusion, no apprehension, no crepitus

Basset's signtender at distal pole in full extension, not in full flexion → tenderness greater in extension than flexion ✓

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
X-ray (AP, lateral, skyline) Usually normal · chronic: inferior traction spur (enthesophyte)
Ultrasound Tendon thickening, hypoechoic areas
MRI (chronic, surgical planning) Tendon thickening (more diagnostic than oedema) · ↑ signal on T1 + T2 at proximal tendon (✗ Wrong options: decreased) · loss of posterior fat-pad border (chronic) · partial tear

Blazina classification

Stage Orthobullets (3 phases) OB illustration (4 stages)
I Pain after activity only Pain only after sports
II Pain during and after activity Pain at start, goes after warm-up, returns with fatigue
III Persistent pain with or without activity (↓ performance) Constant pain at rest and with activity
IV — Complete rupture of patellar tendon

Stage IIIpain at rest + with activity · surgical indication if refractory

5Management

Patellar tendinopathy
  • Early / Blazina I–II→rest, activity modification, quads strengthening, eccentric PT
  • Blazina III, in season→eccentric PT + rest from sport and jumping
  • Refractory / Blazina III / partial tear→surgical excision + repair

Nonoperative care – eccentric training & rest

First lineice, rest, activity modification, PT (quads + hamstring stretching, eccentric programme, quadriceps strengthening, isometric + short-arc work) · NSAIDs, moist heat, ultrasound, phonophoresis

Offloadingtaping or Chopat's strap ↓ tension across patellar tendon

Eccentric = isotonic with muscle lengthening ✓
✗ Wrong options: plyometric · isotonic shortening = concentric · isometric

As effective as surgeryeccentric training · also works for Achilles insertional tendinopathy
✗ Wrong options: electrotherapy · concentric · massage · taping (none proven)

Most recommended exercise (TO)decline squat · 3 × 15 reps, twice daily, single-leg eccentric squat, upright torso, on a decline board
✗ Wrong options: plyometric · treadmill protocol · concentric loading

Why eccentric (TO)promotes tendon remodelling (collagen) · ↓ recurrence

Plyometric (TO)rapid eccentric stretch → concentric of same muscle (jumping, hopping) · builds power · late rehab · early → can exacerbate (OB)

Corticosteroid injectioncontraindicated → patellar tendon rupture · no benefit at 6 months (eccentric + heavy slow resistance keep effect)

PRP / sclerosing agentsexperimental, inconsistent · PRP not first line

18-yr-old, 6 wk, plays through painrest, activity modification, quadriceps strengthening
✗ Wrong options: low-dose steroid · PRP · arthroscopic debridement · no sport until pain-free (complete rest → weakness + inflexibility)

Blazina III, in season, pain at resteccentric PT + rest from sport and jumping · playing through season → no improvement
✗ Wrong options: steroid · debridement without nonop trial · PRP · sclerosant

Refractory cases – surgical debridement

IndicationsBlazina stage III, chronic pain / dysfunction refractory to nonop, partial tears · severe tendinopathy, extensor disruption

Techniqueopen or arthroscopic · resect angiofibroblastic + mucoid degenerative tissue · bone abrasion at insertion · suture repair / anchors

Rehabimmobilisation in extension → progressive ROM · WBAT

Outcome80–90% return to sport · aching 4–6 months · 89% normal / near normal at 12 months (OB)

18 months pain, can't jump, MRI partial teardebridement and repair
✗ Wrong options: cast · aggressive eccentric overload · ice + play on · steroid

Persistent pain with and without activity, failed PT (pole vaulter)surgical excision of the affected tissue
✗ Wrong options: concentric stretching · intratendinous / intra-articular steroid · patellar chondroplasty

X vs Y

Jumper's knee Sinding-Larsen-Johansson
Lesion Tendinopathy (degenerative) Osteochondrosis of lower pole
Age Adolescent / young adult athlete 10–14 yr
Site Tendo-osseous junction, inferior pole Inferior pole (proximal tendon)
Imaging Thickening, ↑ T1 / T2 signal · tooth sign (TO) Fragmentation of lower pole
Patellar tendinopathy Quadriceps tendinopathy
Age Adolescents / young adults Older adults

Patellar Tendon Rupture

Knee & Sports · 39 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology & risk factors

Incidencerare, < 1 / 100,000 / yr

Who3rd–4th decade (Orthobullets) · < 40 yr (OB) · males in 30s–40s · M > F

Quadriceps vs patellarquadriceps tendon rupture more common (2:1) · quadriceps > 40 yr, patellar < 40 yr

Systemic (→ bilateral)diabetes, SLE, RA, chronic renal disease · also infectious + metabolic disorders

Localpatellar degeneration (most common) · previous injury · patellar tendinopathy

Drugscorticosteroid injection · chronic steroids · anabolic steroids

Pathobiologyend-stage chronic tendon degeneration → eccentric load on a diseased tendon

Anatomy & biomechanics

Extensor mechanismquadriceps tendon → patella → patellar tendon → tibial tubercle

Blood supplyinfrapatellar fat pad + retinacular (medial + lateral inferior geniculate arteries)

Forces3× BW ascending stairs · 17× BW to rupture a normal tendon

After TKAapproach disrupts extensor blood supply → poorer healing · acute → primary repair · chronic → allograft reconstruction

2Mechanism

Mechanismtensile overload: sudden quadriceps contraction with knee flexed (jumping, missing a step) · eccentric load (basketball, football, soccer)

Flexion anglegreatest tendon force at > 60° flexion · PT : QT force ratio > 1 at < 45°, < 1 at > 45° (distal-pole contact gives quads advantage at low flexion)

Pattern Fact
Avulsion ± bone from inferior pole of patella Most common · strain at tendon-bone interface 3–4× midsubstance
Midsubstance Less common · reconstruction / augmentation if poor tissue
Distal avulsion from tibial tubercle Least common

Associatedtibial tubercle avulsion, patella fracture, TKA extensor mechanism rupture

3Presentation

Historyjump / sudden quads contraction, "pop" · infrapatellar pain, immediate swelling, can't weight-bear · may mimic ACL (buckling, giving way)

Inspectionhigh-riding patella, large hemarthrosis + ecchymosis, palpable gap below inferior pole

Straight leg raisecannot actively SLR or hold passively extended knee · retinaculum intact → active extension with a few degrees of lag

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
X-ray — AP + lateral at 30° flexion (± merchant) Patella alta in complete rupture
MRI Most sensitive · partial vs complete · site, degeneration, associated injury · not needed for complete tear
Ultrasound Detects + localises · operator-dependent

Diagnostic criteria — patella alta indices

Index Calculation Normal Rupture (alta) Baja
Insall-Salvati Tendon length (Y) ÷ patellar length (X) 0.8–1.2 (~1) > 1.2 (e.g. 1.3) < 0.8 → quadriceps rupture
Blackburne-Peel Plateau line → lower articular margin (Y) ÷ articular length (X) 0.5–1.0 > 1.0 (e.g. Y/X 1.1) < 0.5
Caton-Deschamps Anterior tibial plateau → lower articular margin (Y) ÷ articular length (X) 0.6–1.3 > 1.3 (Orthobullets) · > 1.2 (OB) < 0.6

Ratio trapsX/Y inverted ratios are meaningless · IS 0.95 and CD 1.1 = normal

Most reliable indexInsall-Salvati (highest intra- + inter-observer reliability on X-ray, CT, MRI; Verhulst) · Blackburne-Peel most useful — articular-surface based (Seil) — read the options

Diagnosiscomplete tear = exam + X-ray · partial tear may need MRI

Classification

Type Features Treatment
Incomplete Extensor mechanism intact Nonop possible
Complete Patella alta + palpable defect Surgical repair

5Management

Patellar tendon injury
  • Partial, extensor mechanism intact→brace locked in extension 6 wk, weight bearing
  • Complete, acute→primary repair within 2 wk
    (suture anchors: less gap formation)
  • Chronic > 6–8 wk / degenerate / poor tissue→tendon reconstruction

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Complete rupture, tendon can be approximated Primary repair (end-to-end, transosseous, suture anchors)
Subacute > 2 wk Repair + quadplasty / scar release
Chronic > 6–8 wk, severely disrupted / degenerate tendon Reconstruction
Midsubstance tear, poor tissue Reconstruction / graft augmentation
Revision or chronic Achilles allograft

Treatment – primary repair (suture anchors vs transosseous)

Timingrepair within 2 weeks → prevents extensor mechanism contracture · timing = most important prognostic factor

End-to-endneeds a cuff of tissue on both sides · often not feasible (rupture at inferior pole, no proximal stump) · nonabsorbable locking sutures

Transosseous#5 nonabsorbable sutures through 2 trans-patellar tunnels, tied over top · ± cerclage wire / tape patella → tubercle

Suture anchors≥ 2 anchors · less gap formation (0.9–4.1 mm vs 2.9–10.3 mm transpatellar) · ↑ pull-out strength / ultimate load to failure (Orthobullets, OB) · load to failure not different, gap still less (Danaher, OB) — read the options

Anchor vs transosseous — no differencere-operation rate, infection, PROMs, return to sport, release from care

Re-rupture~8% transosseous vs 1–2% anchors (Orthobullets) · 7.5% vs 0% (O'Dowd, OB)

Best for gap formation (footballer)suture anchor repair
✗ Wrong options: end-to-end · rehab then autograft · Achilles allograft · transosseous

Anchor construct vs bone tunnelsincreased pull-out strength
✗ Wrong options: ↓ re-operation · ↓ infection · better PROMs · quicker RTS

High load to failure + less gapprimary repair with suture anchors
✗ Wrong options: 2 or 3 transosseous tunnels · end-to-end · gracilis reconstruction

24-yr-old, patella alta after reboundprimary surgical repair
✗ Wrong options: PT then BPTB reconstruction · brace at 30° · medialising TTO + lateral release · arthroscopy

40-yr-old, alta on X-rayopen surgical repair
✗ Wrong options: MRI first · ice + observation · PT · arthroscopic repair

CKD + T2DM, 1 wk after fallprimary repair of injured structure
✗ Wrong options: + AMZ tubercle transfer (no instability) · immobilisation (partial tears only) · hamstring reconstruction first · CTA (pulses present)

Partial tear, extensor intacthinged brace locked in extension 6 wk, weight bearing · progressive active flexion / passive extension

Tendon reconstruction

Graftsipsilateral semitendinosus / gracilis, central quadriceps tendon-patellar bone autograft, contralateral BPTB autograft or allograft, Achilles allograft

Techniquetendons through transosseous holes in patella + tibial tubercle → circle graft · retracted patella → quadplasty, scar release

Postoperative rehabilitation

Bracelocked in extension, immediate weight bearing, 6 wk · brace-free by 6 wk

Early motionfrom 7–10 days · passive extension + active flexion
✗ Wrong options: any active extension

ROM exercisesheel slides (active closed-chain flexion) · prone open-chain flexion · both with passive extension

Active extensionnone for at least 4–6 wk (OB) · permitted at 3 wk (Matava, OB) — read the options

Lateropen-chain strengthening (leg extensions) + weight-bearing resistance (squats, lunges, leg press)

Goalsfull extension + 120° flexion by 6 wk · full RTS at 6 months (100% return at 6 months with cerclage repair, OB)

Chainsclosed = distal segment fixed (squat, leg press, pull-up) · open = distal free (leg extension, hamstring curl) · open → more shear · open terminal knee extension = most anterior shear

6Complications

Complication Fact
Knee stiffness Most common · risk: delayed surgery, delayed ROM · MUA if flexion < 120° at 6–12 wk · lysis of adhesions if < 120° after > 12 wk
Quadriceps atrophy 2nd most common · doesn't compromise strength return · PT
Re-tear ~8% transosseous / 1–2% anchors · acute + good tissue → repair · chronic / poor tissue → reconstruction
Infection ~2%
Delayed repair Functioning extensor but persistent quads atrophy + ↓ flexion

PCL Injury

Knee & Sports · 41 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence5–20% of all knee ligament injuries · rare in isolation → usually multiligament (PLC, ACL), knee dislocation

Sports (TO)football, soccer, rugby, skiing → highest incidence of PCL tears

Anatomy

Origin (femur)anterolateral medial femoral condyle · broad crescent-shaped footprint · arthroscopic view from anterolateral portal shows AL + PM bundle origins on MFC

Insertion (tibia)posterior tibial sulcus below (distal to) the articular surface
✗ Wrong options: superior to articular margin

Size38 mm long × 13 mm diameter · 30% larger than ACL · strength 2500–3000 N · resists 95% of posterior tibial displacement

Synovial status (TO)cruciates = intra-articular, extrasynovial (own blood supply, not fed by synovial fluid) · collaterals = extra-articular, extrasynovial · menisci = intra-articular, intrasynovial (fed by synovial fluid)

Blood supplymiddle geniculate artery + fat pad

Meniscofemoral ligamentsPCL lies between them · Humphrey anterior, Wrisberg posterior · arise posterior horn lateral meniscus → insert into PCL substance

Bundle Tight in Fact
Anterolateral (AL) Flexion Strongest · main posterior stabiliser at 90° · "PAL" = PCL Antero-Lateral · reconstructed in single-bundle
Posteromedial (PM) Extension Reciprocal to AL
✗ Wrong option: anteromedial / posterolateral — ACL bundles (distractor)

Biomechanics

Functionprimary restraint to posterior tibial translation · prevents hyperflexion / sliding · isolated injury → greatest instability at 90° flexion

Popliteussynergistic with PCL → controls ER, varus, posterior translation (see PLC)

2Mechanism

Most common overalldirect blow to proximal (anterior) tibia, knee flexed (dashboard) (TO, OB)

Most common in athletesfall on flexed knee with foot plantarflexed → posterior force on tibia
✗ Wrong options: foot dorsiflexed · blow to back of tibia · ER-valgus or IR-varus twist

Other (TO)non-contact hyperflexion > hyperextension (both less common) · hyperextension (stepping into hole) · rotational with varus / valgus · hyperextension often ACL + PCL

Clue in stemscars over anterior proximal tibia + dorsum of ankle / forefoot → foot plantarflexed + blow to tibia → PCL (can extend knee → not patella fracture, patellar tendon or tubercle avulsion; Lachman negative → not ACL)

3Presentation

Historyhigh vs low energy · posterior knee pain · instability subtle / asymptomatic if isolated · ask about dislocation / nerve injury

Diagnosis mainly clinical (TO)posterior drawer; MRI best test for cartilage, ACL, meniscus but not PCL (TO) · MRI = confirmatory study (Orthobullets) — read the options

Clinical tests (posterior drawer, sag, quadriceps active, dial)

Test Technique / positive Meaning
Posterior drawer (90°) Posterior force on proximal tibia · most accurate for PCL Isolated: > 10–12 mm neutral, 6–8 mm IR · combined: > 15 mm neutral, > 10 mm IR
Posterior sag sign Hips + knees 90°, ankles supported → tibia sags Normal medial plateau 10 mm anterior to MFC; absent / posterior step-off = +
Quadriceps active test Quad contraction at 90° Anterior reduction of tibia = +
Reverse Lachman Posterior translation near extension PCL
False Lachman Posterior subluxation mimics ↑ anterior travel PCL (✗ Wrong options: ACL)
Varus / valgus at 0° Laxity Collateral + PCL (cruciate)
Varus / valgus at 30° only Laxity Isolated MCL / LCL
KT-1000 / KT-2000 Arthrometer Less accurate than for ACL

Dial test (TO)

Dial result (ER asymmetry vs other side) Lesion
> 10° at 30° only Isolated PLC
> 10° at 30° AND 90° PLC + PCL
ER 15° more at 30°, further ↑ at 90° (TO) PCL + PLC
2° asymmetry / symmetric at 30° + 90° No PLC → isolated PCL

Threshold> 10° (Orthobullets, OB) · 10–15° (OB) · 15° (TO supine description) — read the options

Prone dial (TO)thigh–foot angle in prone position (angle between sagittal plane of sole and body)
✗ Wrong options: foot–leg angle · tibial tuberosity angle supine · foot divergence

Supine dial (TO)leg over edge of bed, stabilise distal femur, hold heel → max ER at 30° → note tibial tuberosity position → repeat at 90°

Combined exam (OB)2B reverse Lachman + sag + varus at 0° / 30° + negative dial + negative reverse pivot → PCL + LCL
✗ Wrong options: complete PLC (needs + dial / reverse pivot)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
AP + supine lateral X-ray Avulsion fractures (acute) · posterior tibiofemoral subluxation · chronic → medial + PF arthrosis
Lateral stress view (knee 70°) Asymmetric posterior displacement · becoming gold standard for diagnosing + quantifying · side-to-side > 12 mm → PCL + PLC
Kneeling stress X-ray Quantifies posterior translation
Sagittal CT Tibial PCL bony avulsion fragment
MRI Confirmatory · essential to plan concomitant injuries in avulsions (TO)

PCL grading

Grade (posterior tibial subluxation at 90°) Injury Translation
I Partial tear 1–5 mm
II Complete isolated tear 6–10 mm · anterior tibia flush with femoral condyles
III Row blank in source table —

Veltri (OB)isolated PCL < 10 mm posterior laxity → nonop · > 10 mm or combined → reconstruct

5Management

PCL injury
  • Isolated grade I / II→protected WB + quadriceps rehab (RTS 2–4 wk)
  • Isolated grade III → immobilise in extension 4 wk→quadriceps strengthening
    (surgery if bony avulsion or young athlete)
  • Bony tibial avulsion (displaced > 5 mm)→ORIF (Burks–Schaffer posteromedial)
  • Combined (ACL / PLC / grade III MCL or LCL)→PCL reconstruction + all lesions
  • Chronic, functionally unstable / varus→reconstruction ± medial opening-wedge HTO

Nonoperative management – quadriceps rehabilitation

Principlequadriceps strengthening (knee extensors) pulls tibia anteriorly → counteracts PCL deficit · ACL-deficient knee → hamstring rehab
✗ Wrong options: hamstrings · hip · gastroc-soleus

Grade II protocol (OB)relative protection 10–14 days → ROM + gentle closed-chain quadriceps strengthening · global strengthening at 4–6 wk · RTS at full ROM + strength

Quadriceps-first, possibly definitive (OB)isolated PCL rupture → closed-chain quad strengthening (foot fixed) · no clear prognostic factors
✗ Wrong options: ACL rupture (hamstring rehab) · patellar tendon rupture · bucket-handle meniscal tear · meniscal root tear (surgery)

Prone ROMflexion done prone → limits posterior sag

Avoidresisted hamstring until healed (4–6 wk) · plyometrics early · prolonged immobilisation
✗ Wrong options: long leg cast 4 wk → stiffness · 12 wk in extension

Isolated grade II exam (OB)2+ posterior drawer, 1+ stable Lachman, negative dial, no valgus laxity → PT with quadriceps focus · persistent anterior / medial pain or "loose" → reconstruct later
✗ Wrong options: delayed or acute reconstruction

Grade III isolatedrelative immobilisation in extension 4 wk + limited daily ROM → quad strengthening

Tibial avulsion – ORIF

Tibial-sided avulsion (TO)most common form of isolated bony PCL disruption · mechanism: dashboard > sports hyperextension

Displaced > 5 mm (TO)surgical fixation (arthroscopic or open) · MRI to plan concomitant injuries
✗ Wrong options: long leg cast in full extension 4 wk

Young active, displaced (OB)ORIF of fragment · nonop historically → loss of motion · good results with repair of avulsions
✗ Wrong options: reconstruction · hinged brace + therapy · HTO

Examisolated PCL: posterior drawer 11 mm neutral / 7 mm IR, stable varus / valgus, negative dial

Burks–Schaffer approach (TO)posteromedial approach for PCL avulsion · prone · horizontal limb over popliteal crease + vertical limb over medial gastrocnemius
✗ Wrong options: ACL avulsion · TA repair

Interval (TO)medial gastrocnemius – semimembranosus → blunt finger dissection to posterior capsule · ligate middle geniculate artery if needed · preserve tibial nerve motor branch to medial head gastrocnemius · retract medial gastrocnemius laterally (protects NV bundle) · vertical capsulotomy

Operative criteria

PCL repair / reconstruction indicated Nonop
Combined: PCL + ACL or PLC Isolated grade I, II
PCL + grade III MCL or LCL Isolated grade III (unless avulsion / young athlete)
Isolated grade II / III with bony avulsion
Isolated chronic, functionally unstable
Chronic deficiency + varus → HTO

Reconstruction technique – graft tensioning, tibial inlay, killer turn

Graftusually allograft (Achilles, BPTB, hamstring, tibialis anterior) · no technique clearly superior · results < ACL reconstruction, residual posterior laxity common · midsubstance primary repair fails · success needs concomitant ligaments addressed

Single-bundlereconstruct anterolateral bundle · tension at 90° flexion (ACL tensioned nearer extension; closest to isometric)
✗ Wrong options: 0° · 30°

Double-bundleAL at 90°, PM in extension · biomechanical advantage; clinical advantage unproven · useful with PCL + PLC (rotational control; PLC grafts loosen)

Transtibial (arthroscopic)drill anterior → posterior · accessory posteromedial portal 1 cm above joint line, posterior to MCL (saphenous nerve branches at risk) · fix graft at 90° with anterior drawer · risk to popliteal vessels

Posteromedial corner view70° arthroscope through notch (modified Gillquist) or posteromedial portal

Tibial inlay (open)posteromedial incision between medial gastrocnemius + semimembranosus · graft bone block fixed directly to posterior tibia · screw within 20 mm of popliteal artery · ORIF of avulsions

Killer turn (TO)sharp (~90°) bend of graft around proximal posterior tibia at tibial tunnel exit → abrasion, thinning, elongation → main cause of residual laxity + graft failure · Markolf: thinning 40.6%, elongation 65.3% (9.8 / 15 mm)

Reduce killer turn (TO) Mechanism
Tibial inlay (Jakob, Berg) No tibial tunnel · posterior arthrotomy · anatomic · bone-to-bone healing
Anterolateral tibial tunnel ↓ angulation, no ↑ translation vs anteromedial (theoretical: ↓ compressive force → ↑ translation)
Tunnel 15–20 mm deep from posterior tibial margin (jig) ↑ tunnel angle → smaller turn
Tunnel exit lower in footprint One acute turn → two smoother turns
Aperture fixation (interference screw) no suspensory (endobutton) "bungee cord" micromotion · stiffer construct
Smooth aperture Punch / rasp
All-inside Half tunnels (sockets) · bone stock · ↓ tunnel widening / convergence · ↓ "windshield effect"
✗ Wrong option: tunnel exit superiorly (upper half of fossa) Does NOT avoid it
✗ Wrong option: transtibial in place of inlay Does NOT help (transtibial causes it)

Inlay vs transtibial (OB)only advantage = eliminates the 90° killer turn
✗ Wrong options: less invasive · cosmesis · shorter time · faster rehab · better clinical results · normal kinematics

Rehabilitation after PCL reconstruction (OKC vs CKC)

Earlyimmobilise in extension, protect against gravity · early motion prone · focus on quadriceps

Avoidresisted hamstring curls (prone / OKC) → posterior pull on tibia stresses graft

4 wk post-op, highest posterior shear (TO)OKC resisted hamstring curls 0–90° (esp. deep flexion > 60°)
✗ Wrong options: CKC leg press 0–60° · OKC quad extension 90→0° · CKC wall squat 0–45°

Allowed (OB, TO)quadriceps activation · closed-chain terminal extension · non-WB resisted extension 60°→0° · prone passive flexion + active terminal extension · ankle pumps · CKC up to 60°

PCL + PLC post-op (OB)no active flexion, active extension 90→0° · hinged brace + crutches, partial WB first 4 wk

Kinetic chain (TO, Steindler 1955) OKC CKC

Patellofemoral 90–45° → lower PFJ force than deep CKC 0–45° → lower PFJ force than OKC
TKA SLR, terminal extension (supplement) Early sit-to-stand, partial squat
Fracture Strength when WB restricted Axial load → callus (Wolff's law)

Combined PCL / PLC / LCL injuries & slope-increasing osteotomy

Dial + at 30° and 90°, sag signPCL + PLC
✗ Wrong options: ACL only · PCL only · PLC + ACL (dial + at 30° only + Lachman)

Chronic PCL + PLC, varus thrust, 10° varusHTO to INCREASE slope + correct varus, then PCL + PLC reconstruction
✗ Wrong options: bracing · PCL alone · ACL + PCL (high failure if coronal alignment untreated)

✗ Wrong options: decreased · posterior

✗ Wrong options: anterolateral · anteromedial · supraclavicular

Loss of motion (TO)most common complication of PCL reconstruction · flexion loss > extension loss (10–20° flexion loss) · graft malposition / inadequate rehab

Piriformis Muscles Syndrome

Knee & Sports · 42 / 61

1Basics

Sciatic nerve anatomy relative to piriformis

Normal exitinferior to (deep / anterior to) piriformis, superior to superior gemellus · via greater sciatic foramen

Commonest patternsingle nerve anterior to piriformis · 79% (OB, Pokorny) · 96% (TO) — read the options

Atypical anatomy~21% (Pokorny, 91 cadavers)

Commonest variant14%: nerve splits above piriformis → one branch anterior + one through the muscle (OB) · usually peroneal part pierces, tibial part runs below / above (TO) · whole nerve may pass through the belly (TO)

Short external rotators (superior → inferior)piriformis, superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus, obturator externus, quadratus femoris

Pathophysiology

Definitionsciatica-like pain from extrapelvic sciatic nerve compression at the hip · aka back pocket / wallet sciatica (TO)

Siteanterior to piriformis or posterior to obturator internus / gemelli at ischial tuberosity level (Orthobullets) · in piriformis at greater sciatic notch (TO)

Primary (TO)anatomic: split piriformis, split sciatic nerve, anomalous nerve path · Orthobullets adds bipartite piriformis, tumours, inferior gluteal artery aneurysm

Secondary (TO)trauma, LLD, cerebral palsy, narrowed sciatic foramen · macrotrauma to buttock (spasm) · microtrauma / overuse (long-distance walking, running, dancing) · wallet in back pocket

FAI link↓ IR → short external rotator contracture → sciatic compression

3Presentation

Painposterior gluteal pain radiating down back of leg, burning / aching

Pattern (TO)worse rising after sitting / squatting > 15–20 min · pain on IR (cross-legged sitting) · improves with ambulation, worse with rest

Referred (TO)spasm stresses sacrotuberous ligament → pudendal compression → groin / pelvic pain · fibular (peroneal) branch compression → paraesthesia sacrum → buttock → posterior thigh

Test (TO) Positive when
FAIR (Orthobullets) Flexion, adduction, IR stretches piriformis → reproduces symptoms
Pace sign FAIR recreates sciatic symptoms
Piriformis sign Supine, foot lies externally rotated · active return to midline → pain
Freiberg sign Pain on passive hip IR
Beatty test Side-lying on unaffected side, lifts top knee ~4 inches → sciatic pain
Lasègue Hip + knee 90°, extend knee → posterior thigh pain

4Diagnosis & Classification

ImagingX-ray unremarkable · hip MRI usually unremarkable · lumbar MRI to exclude spinal cause · EDS document sciatic impairment

Differential – ischiofemoral impingement

Dancer, buttock pain → at rest, pain on hip extension + ER, quadratus femoris oedema (TO)ischiofemoral impingement
✗ Wrong options: FAI · piriformis syndrome · quadriceps tendinopathy

IFI definition (TO)chronic groin / buttock / hip pain + narrowed space between lesser trochanter and ischial tuberosity

Ischiofemoral distance on axial MRI (TO)normal > 2 cm · < 1.3 cm critical

MRI (TO)quadratus femoris ↑ T2 signal, fibres intact · QF oedema can compress / displace sciatic nerve → radicular pain

Causes (TO)iatrogenic after hip surgery, hip trauma, ischial exostosis, primary in young athletes

IFI test (TO)pain on extension + adduction + ER (one TO explanation) · extension + abduction + ER (other TO explanation) · tenderness over ischiofemoral space

IFI treatment (TO)NSAIDs, guided steroid injection, PT → failure: endoscopic resection of lesser trochanter

Condition (TO) Key features Treatment
Ischiofemoral impingement Buttock pain, extension + ER, QF oedema, distance < 1.3 cm NSAIDs, injection → LT resection
Piriformis syndrome Buttock → posterior leg, worse with sitting, FAIR / Pace Stretch, NSAIDs → release + neurolysis
Snapping hip — internal Anterior click · iliopsoas over iliopectineal eminence Stretch → iliopsoas release / lengthening
Snapping hip — external More common · lateral · ITB over greater trochanter Stretch → ITB release / lengthening
Snapping hip — intra-articular Labral tear, loose body · dynamic USG / MRI Arthroscopic loose body removal + labral repair
Iliopsoas tendinopathy Musculotendinous junction · pain on active flexion, stairs, getting out of car Rest, stretch, NSAIDs, PT → release at LT / lengthening
Iliopsoas tendonitis after THR Groin pain on active flexion · painful SLR, passive SLR pain-free CT-guided steroid + stretch → iliopsoas tenotomy

Snapping hip (TO)coxa saltans / dancer's hip · ballet dancers, extreme flexion + abduction · extra-articular more common than intra-articular · resistant extra-articular → local steroid into sheath

Iliopsoas bursa (TO)largest bursa in the body · 3 causes of bursitis: RA, acute trauma, overuse

Snapping hip sign / extension test (TO)palpate inguinal crease, flex → abduct + ER → back to neutral → palpable click

Iliopsoas after THR — diagnosis (TO)cross-table lateral shows cup prominent beyond anterior rim (snapping over anterior lip) · relief after USG / CT-guided local anaesthetic into iliopsoas sheath confirms

5Management

Piriformis syndrome
  • First line→rest, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, ice, PT stretching, steroid injection
  • Refractory→piriformis release + external sciatic neurolysis

Nonoperativestretch piriformis + short external rotators · strengthen abductors + adductors (TO) · corticosteroid injection near piriformis · early conservative Rx most effective (TO)

Surgeryonly after failed conservative care · release piriformis tension + explore sciatic notch for fibrous bands / constrictions

Plicae

Knee & Sports · 43 / 61

1Basics

Embryology & pathology

Origin (TO)embryonic knee divided by synovial folds → absorbed by 3–4 months → single cavity · partial resorption → persistent septations = synovial plicae (visible at arthroscopy)

Mediopatellar plica (TO)not a septum remnant (Ogata & Uhthoff) · linked to lateralised patella = remnant of mesenchyme that was larger medially

Prevalencemedial patellar plica in 5–55% of people; few symptomatic (OB) · mere presence ≠ symptoms (TO)

Plica syndromepainful impairment from thickened, inflamed synovial fold (usually medial) · 50% give history of blunt anterior knee trauma · repetitive sport, direct trauma, other knee pathology

Inflamed plica (TO)fibrotic, thickened, inelastic → snaps over femoral condyle or under patella → pain, synovitis of condylar margins, chondromalacia patellae / cartilage wear

Plica anatomy, types & symptomatic plica

Plica Course Key fact
Infrapatellar = ligamentum mucosum Intercondylar notch → infrapatellar (Hoffa) fat pad; narrow femoral origin (anterior notch), widens, anterior to ACL Most common / most frequently seen at arthroscopy; rarely symptomatic
Suprapatellar Anterior femoral metaphysis → medial joint wall (TO) · → posterior quadriceps tendon above patella (TO) · medial → lateral wall of suprapatellar space (Orthobullets); between joint + suprapatellar bursa Most persistent; impinges superomedial trochlea in flexion; usually asymptomatic
Medial (mediopatellar, Lino band, shelf) Medial joint wall → synovium over infrapatellar fat pad (from suprapatellar origin) Most common cause of plica syndrome; most significant / most symptomatic; abrades MFC
Lateral Lateral wall, lateral patellar facet → infrapatellar region; thin, 1–2 cm lateral to patella Least common; existence controversial; asymptomatic

Frequency order (TO)infrapatellar > suprapatellar > mediopatellar · Orthobullets: ligamentum mucosum most common

Conflictinfrapatellar = most common plica (TO, Orthobullets) vs medial = most common type + most symptomatic (TO FNB 2023) — read the options; most symptomatic = medial in all sources

Multiple plicaenot uncommon in one patient

3Presentation

Symptomsanterior / anteromedial knee pain, snapping, popping, clicking with repetitive flexion–extension, buckling, pain on sitting, crepitus, swelling · worse with poor quadriceps tone / muscle imbalance

Cyclist (TO)tenderness on undersurface of medial patellar facet; deep flexion + full extension painful

Exammedial parapatellar tenderness · painful palpable cord rolled + popped under the finger · band painful with flexion–extension with tibia internally rotated · McMurray negative

Provocative testknee held in full extension, examiner flexes against resistance, then pushes patella medially palpating medial border → pain ± click = positive

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Finding
Clinical Diagnosis is primarily clinical
MRI Detects plica but low sensitivity, non-specific · order only after failed conservative treatment
MRI symptomatic plica (TO) Thick ± synovitis (normal plica thin)
MRI Sakakibara C (TO) Axial FS PD hypointense band covering anterior MFC
MRI suprapatellar (TO) Sagittal: band-like low-signal structure posterior to patella
Arthroscopy Gold standard for diagnosis + treatment; arrow on PF view from inferolateral portal = plica (✗ Wrong options: loose body · meniscus · retinaculum · OCD)
Arthroscopy, suprapatellar (TO) Almost never diagnosed — complete plica suggested only by a short suprapatellar pouch (or needle enters bursa)

Sakakibara classification of medial plica

Type (TO) Arthroscopic appearance Symptoms
A Cord-like elevation in synovial wall Unlikely
B Shelf-like, does not cover anterior MFC Unlikely
C Large shelf covering anterior surface of MFC Trapped between MFC + patella → thick, hard → cartilage damage
D Fenestrated (central defect) Trapped → cartilage damage

Types C + D (TO)impinge medial patellar facet cartilage in flexion + MFC cartilage in extension → arthroscopic resection = treatment of choice

Untreated medial plica syndrome (TO)can cause Outerbridge grade IV chondral lesions (subchondral bone exposed)

Misfiled TO items (Brodie abscess, carpal tunnel tests)

Brodie abscess (TO) Fact
Site / age Proximal tibia, children + young adults
Course Indolent; mild–moderate local tenderness; intermittent pain worse at night, > 2 wk; low-grade fever
Labs WBC, ESR, CRP normal or mildly ↑
X-ray Cavity at metaphyseal–epiphyseal junction + rim of reactive new bone
Diagnosis / organism Bone biopsy confirms · S. aureus commonest
Treatment Curettage + bone grafting under an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic cover (✗ Wrong options: curettage alone · observation · needle aspiration)
Carpal tunnel syndrome (TO) Fact
Not a CTS test Murphy (✗ Wrong options: Phalen · Durkan · Semmes-Weinstein)
Pathology Carpal tunnel pressure > 30 mmHg
Commonest causes Idiopathic > hypothyroidism > pregnancy
Risk factors Female, obesity, pregnancy, hypothyroid, RA, trauma (distal radius fracture / malunion, carpal dislocation), repetitive motion, acromegaly, age, menopause, CRF, space-occupying lesion, OCP, CHF, diabetes, smoking, alcohol, mucopolysaccharidosis (children)
Symptoms Pain, numbness, paraesthesia first 3 digits + lateral half of 4th; thenar atrophy
Riche-Cannieu anastomosis Deep ulnar → recurrent motor median branch → thenar strength preserved
Sensory tests 2PD (fails at 5 mm), Semmes-Weinstein = most sensitive (early), vibrometry, texture, hand diagram = most specific
Phalen Dorsal hands together 30–60 s
Durkan Thumb pressure over carpal tunnel just distal to wrist crease → symptoms within 30 s
Tinel Tapping over nerve → tingling
CTS-6 Score > 12 → 80% probability
Imaging X-ray limited · MRI if mass · US CSA > 10 mm² at pisiform / proximal TCL
NCV Distal sensory latency > 3.5 ms, motor latency > 4.5 ms, CV < 52 m/s (less specific than latencies)
EMG Traditional gold standard (AAOS: limited recommendation) · ↑ insertional activity, sharp waves, fibrillations, fasciculations, complex repetitive discharges

Plica syndrome
  • First line→ACTIVITY MODIFICATION + PHYSICAL THERAPY (hamstring stretching), NSAIDs
    • persistent→INTRAPLICAL CORTICOSTEROID INJECTION (TO)
  • Failed conservative→MRI (limited sensitivity)
  • Refractory / Sakakibara C–D→ARTHROSCOPIC PLICA EXCISION

Diagnosis & initial management

Most casesnonop: activity restriction, NSAIDs, PT · avoid repetitive jumping, squatting, lunging · usually successful

PT contentmoist heat, hamstring stretching · resistive strengthening avoided early (Orthobullets) · quadriceps strengthening part of rehab (OB) — read the options

Weightlifter, palpable painful anteromedial fold, McMurray −activity modification & physical therapy
✗ Wrong options: diagnostic arthroscopy · MRI · PRP · patellar stabilising brace

Arthroscopic resectionrare: plica band syndrome not responding to nonop · thickened Sakakibara C plica (TO) → arthroscopic excision

Knee & Sports · 44 / 61

1Basics

Definitionconstriction of the popliteal artery by adjacent muscles, tendons or fibrous tissue · usually an underlying anatomic abnormality

Demographicsmale 4:1 · age 25–40 years

Pathophysiology↓ flow distal to the popliteal fossa → symptoms mimic compartment syndrome

Classic pathoanatomy (OB)compression by the medial head of gastrocnemius · accessory slip of medial gastrocnemius head on MRI

Modified Whelan classification

Type Anatomy Image
I Normal medial gastrocnemius head, popliteal artery takes an aberrant course
II Medial gastrocnemius head located laterally, artery not deviated
III Abnormal muscle bundle from medial gastrocnemius head surrounds + constricts artery
IV Artery entrapped by popliteus
V Popliteal vein entrapped with the artery in any of the above

3Presentation

Symptomsintermittent claudication (OB) · limb swelling often the primary complaint · foot numbness, toe tingling after vigorous exercise · calf cramping even after light exercise as it worsens · may be asymptomatic

Examdiminished pulses with active plantarflexion or passive dorsiflexion · cool posterior calf, paraesthesias · easily confused with posterior compartment syndrome

Sensory pattern (OB)dysaesthesia in the sural distribution (posterolateral leg / foot)

Runner with pain, coolness, tingling (OB)pain with passive dorsiflexion + plantarflexion, compartment pressures normal → PAES
✗ Wrong options: exertional compartment syndrome · tibial stress fracture · lumbar radiculopathy · piriformis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
Radiographs Usually normal
Doppler US Less invasive; detects pulse change during active plantarflexion / passive dorsiflexion
Arteriogram Confirms diagnosis, ~100% sensitivity → stenosis, obliteration, post-stenotic dilation
MRA / CTA Usefulness still under study · MRA can show segmental popliteal occlusion (OB)

Differential of exertional leg pain (OB)

Exertional compartment syndromeneeds ↑ compartment pressures: rest > 15 · 1 min post > 30 · 5 min post > 20 · 15 min post > 15 mmHg (Orthobullets) → normal pressures exclude it

Lumbar radiculopathy / piriformisneuropathy does not explain a cool, crampy leg

Tibial stress fracturenot relieved by running, no claudication signs

Other differentialsCECS, medial tibial stress syndrome, tibial / fibular stress fracture, fascial defects, nerve entrapment, vascular claudication (atherosclerotic or PAES), lumbar disc herniation

5Management

Popliteal artery entrapment
  • Mild symptoms, rigorous exercise only→activity modification + observation
  • Refractory / artery or vein damage→vascular surgery
    • release the entrapping structure (depends on type)
    • damaged artery→saphenous vein bypass vs endarterectomy

Natural historymost patients eventually need surgery

Approachposterior → better exposure · medial → used when bypass needed

6Complications

Complication Rate
Surgical failure (entrapment returns) 30% → can need amputation
Wound infection < 5%
DVT ~10%
Asymptomatic after surgery 70–100%

X vs Y

PAES Exertional compartment syndrome
Compartment Posterior leg Anterior (± lateral) commonest
Mechanism Artery compressed (medial gastrocnemius) ↑ pressure in a closed compartment
Key sign ↓ pulses with active plantarflexion / passive dorsiflexion, cool leg Normal exam at rest
Nerve symptoms Sural distribution Dorsum of foot / 1st web
Confirm Arteriogram (Doppler US screen) Compartment pressures

LCL LFC, proximal + posterior to popliteus Most anterior on fibular head · anterolateral to PFL Runs superficial to popliteus · primary varus restraint
Popliteus tendon Distal + anterior to LCL (✗ Wrong options: proximal) · through LM hiatus Muscle → posteromedial tibia Dynamic internal rotator of tibia

Biceps femoris — Posterior to LCL on fibular head Long head: direct arm posterolateral, anterior arm lateral to LCL · short head: superior fibular head, medial + posterior to LCL

Lateral layer Structures
I Iliotibial tract, biceps
— Common peroneal nerve between layers I and II

III superficial LCL, fabellofibular ligament
— Lateral geniculate artery between superficial + deep III

Popliteus primary actioninternal tibial rotation · popliteus complex reinforces posterior third of lateral capsule; restrains ER, posterior translation, varus
✗ Wrong options: ER · posterior / anterior translation

Popliteus + PFLmaximal in flexion → resist ER

Mechanismsblow to anteromedial knee · varus blow to flexed knee · contact / non-contact hyperextension · ER twisting · knee dislocation · varus force + ER component (OB)

Symptomsinstability in full extension · difficulty reciprocating stairs, pivoting, cutting · lateral + posterior pain

Gaitstanding varus, varus thrust or hyperextension thrust

PLRIlateral tibial plateau moves posterior to femoral condyle on rotational stress → posterolateral rotatory instability · instability named by tibial position relative to femur
✗ Wrong options: AMRI · ALRI · PMRI

Diagnosis – dial test, reverse pivot shift & PLRI

Test Technique Positive means
Varus stress 30° — LCL
Varus stress 0° — LCL + cruciate (ACL or PCL)
Dial test Prone or supine; 30° + 90° > 10° ER at 30° only → isolated PLC · 30° + 90° → PLC + PCL
ER recurvatum Supine, suspend legs by great toes ↑ recurvatum + varus + anterior tibial translation → ACL + PLC
Posterolateral drawer Hip 45°, knee 80°, foot ER 15° · posterior drawer + ER ↑ posterolateral translation (lateral tibia ER on LFC)
Reverse pivot shift Tibia ER + valgus Clunk of reduction → PLC (PLRI)
Posterior drawer 90° PCL (negative in isolated PLC)

Dial threshold> 10° (Orthobullets) · 10–15° (OB) · 15° (TO supine description) — read the options

Supine dial (TO)leg over bed edge, stabilise distal femur, hold heel, max ER at 30° → tibial tuberosity position vs other side → repeat at 90°

Prone dial (TO)both feet rotated at 30° then 90° · angle between sagittal plane of sole and body (thigh–foot angle)

Prone preferred (Jung)dial more clearly positive when posterior sag is reduced

Other PLC tests (TO)ER recurvatum · posterolateral drawer · reverse pivot shift

Dial ↑ at 30° + 90° — least likely torn?posterior oblique ligament (medial)
✗ Wrong options: FCL · popliteus · PCL · arcuate

+ Reverse pivot, negative posterior drawerPLC without PCL → expect 10° ↑ ER at 30°
✗ Wrong options: at 90° · valgus opening · anterior drawer

Pivot tests (TO) Movement Instability
Pivot shift (Macintosh) Extension → flexion, tibia IR + valgus · tibia relocates posteriorly Anterolateral (ACL + lateral capsule / ALL)
Jerk test (Hughston & Losse) Flexion → extension (reverse of pivot shift) Anterolateral
Reverse pivot shift Tibia ER + valgus; clunk Posterolateral (PLC, ± PCL)

Reverse pivot directionstart at 90°, ER + valgus, extend → tibia reduces from posterior subluxation at ~20° (ITB flexor → extensor) (Orthobullets) · knee moved extension → flexion to feel clunk (TO) — read the options

ER recurvatum (TO)historically relative hyperextension + ER of tibial tubercle + varus · LaPrade: sensitivity 7.5% in 134 PLC patients · X-ray showed anterior tibial translation · all positives = ACL + PLC · doesn't identify which PL structures (multiple inferred)
✗ Wrong options: posterior

ER recurvatum yieldidentifies ~10% of PLC injuries (Orthobullets) · 7.5% sensitivity (TO) — read the options

Primary Tibiofemoral malalignment

Grade Examination Findings

PLC injury
  • Grade I or isolated midsubstance grade II → brace locked in extension 4 wk→rehab
  • Isolated acute grade II avulsion, reducible→repair (augment with graft if tenuous)

Option Indication
Nonop (brace in extension 4 wk, quad rehab, RTS 8 wk) Grade I · isolated midsubstance grade II
Repair Isolated acute grade II avulsion · structures anatomically reducible to attachment
Fibular head avulsion Screws or suture anchors
Reconstruction (hybrid) Grade III midsubstance · avulsion not repairable / poor tissue
PLC + ACL / PCL reconstruction Acute + chronic combined injuries
Valgus HTO Varus mechanical alignment (else ACL + PLC reconstruction fail)

Repair → higher failure (OB)midsubstance repair 40% failure (Orthobullets) · Levy: 40% repair vs 6% (1 pt) reconstruction · Stannard: 37% vs 9% (57 PLC injuries; both "near-normal" IKDC)
✗ Wrong options: quicker ROM · better stability · higher short-term scores · worse kinematics

After revision of failed repairoutcome scores ≈ primary reconstruction

Reconstruction Graft / technique Rebuilds
Fibular-based (Larson) Soft-tissue graft (semitendinosus / Achilles) through fibular head tunnel → figure-of-eight → single femoral tunnel LCL + PFL
Transtibial double-bundle Split Achilles to femoral epicondyle isometric point · fibular limb + tibial limb Fibular limb LCL · tibial limb (posterior tibia) PFL
LaPrade anatomic Two grafts · graft 1 femoral LCL site → fibular head (lateral → medial) · graft 2 popliteus site · both dock in tibial tunnel posterior → anterior LCL + PFL + popliteus

Classification Site
Intraneural Within epineurium
Extraneural Outside epineurium

Symptomsusually asymptomatic · pain, mobile palpable mass distal to lateral joint line, fullness, paraesthesias dorsum of foot

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
X-ray (AP + lateral knee / tibia) Usually normal · ± sclerosis lateral proximal tibia

Treatment Recurrence
Aspiration alone 80% (Orthobullets) · 25–80% (OB)
Decompression + excision (hockey-stick lateral approach, neurolysis, excise stalk) 8–25% · 1st excision success 7 / 8; repeat excision 3 / 3 recurred (Miskovsky)
PTFJ arthrodesis (6.5 mm partially threaded cancellous screw) < 5% — lowest

✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs / activity change · aspiration · arthrodesis / fibular head resection (reserved for recurrence)

Recurrent cystGulati: proximal fibular excision, good results in 9 · arthrodesis (Miskovsky: 2 fused, no recurrence)

Airway disorders

✗ Wrong options: warm weather

Chest wall & vascular conditions

Pneumothorax causesspontaneous (smoking, male, FHx, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos) · traumatic (contact athletes — ice hockey highest risk) · iatrogenic (interscalene block)

Haemothoraxmost common result of major chest-wall trauma · 30% of rib fractures → pneumohaemothorax

PE in athletes↑ risk: musculoskeletal injury ± immobilisation, repetitive motion (pitchers, tennis), long-distance travel

Asthmawheeze, SOB, chest tightness; expiratory wheeze, accessory muscles

Pseudo-asthma syndromeexercise-induced hyperventilation; no bronchoconstriction

EILOrapid onset, throat tightness / choking, "breathing through a straw" · inspiratory stridor · fails bronchodilators (often misdiagnosed as EIA / EIB)

Exercise-induced anaphylaxisonset within 30 min of exercise · pruritus, urticaria, GI cramps, SOB, throat tightness

Pneumothoraxsudden unilateral pleuritic pain, SOB · ↓ / absent breath sounds, hyperresonant · tension adds tracheal deviation + JVD, cardiopulmonary compromise

Tension pneumothorax on the fielddyspnoea, anxiety, deviated trachea, hypertympanic chest, ↓ breath sounds
✗ Wrong options: spontaneous (closed, no deviation) · haemothorax (dull) · EIB · HCM

Haemothoraxless pleuritic pain · hypotension if large · dull to percussion

PEsudden pleuritic pain, SOB, syncope · tachycardia, hypoxia, hypotension if large

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Condition Test Finding
Asthma PFT ± methacholine challenge ↓ FEV1, ↓ FEV1/FVC, reverses with bronchodilator
EIB Eucapnic voluntary hyperventilation (EVH) = gold standard > 10% ↓ FEV1; baseline PFT may be normal
EILO Continuous exercise laryngoscopy (CEL) = gold standard PFT: blunted inspiratory loop
Pneumothorax Ultrasound Absent lung sliding
Pneumothorax CXR Pleural line, absent lung markings · tension: mediastinal shift + depressed hemidiaphragm
Haemothorax CXR Opacified hemithorax
PE Helical CT first line · pulmonary angiography gold standard V/Q scan alternative
HAPE (TO) CXR Patchy opacities, often right middle lobe

Pneumothorax types

Type Communication Pleural pressure
Closed (e.g. bleb rupture) None < atmospheric → no tracheal deviation
Open Air in on inspiration, out on expiration = atmospheric, no tension
Tension One-way: in, cannot exit ↑ > atmospheric → lung + mediastinal compression — emergency

5Management

Return-to-play criteria

Condition Return to play
Asthma / EIB As tolerated · active wheezing = contraindication
Exercise-induced anaphylaxis After allergist review + comprehensive action plan · always carry EpiPen, exercise with a partner
Pneumothorax Radiographic resolution, ~4 weeks · pain limits RTP · no flying 2–4 weeks
PE ~6 months · on anticoagulation controversial · contact athletes withheld during anticoagulation

Exercise-induced bronchospasm

Acuterest, controlled breathing, inhaled β2-agonist (albuterol q15 min PRN) · severe / refractory → epinephrine + ER · moderate–severe asthma maintenance → inhaled glucocorticoids

Preventionwarm-up, environmental control · "refractory period" (deliberate induction) works in ~50% · albuterol 2 puffs 15–20 min before activity

EILO & anaphylaxis

EILOnonoperative mainstay: laryngeal control therapy (lower-abdominal breathing, controlled exhalation through mouth), speech therapy, SSRIs, botulinum toxin · surgery (debulking) rare

Anaphylaxis preventionno exercise 4–6 h after eating, avoid temperature extremes, avoid aspirin / NSAIDs before exercise · acute: epinephrine, antihistamines, steroids

Children2nd ICS mid-clavicular line still recommended

Why changed5 cm needle at 2nd ICS fails in 22–50% (chest-wall thickness) · risk to internal thoracic, subclavian, heart · no original evidence

Site wording"2nd or 5th ICS" acceptable (Orthobullets, OB)

Failed decompressioncheck catheter patency → longer 8.25 cm needle → finger thoracostomy
✗ Wrong options: any of these first

Traps✗ Wrong options: chest tube first (hospital; supplies rarely on hand) · digital thoracostomy first · long needle first (visceral injury)

Pneumothorax
  • Tension → needle decompression 5th ICS MAL→chest tube in ED
  • > 20% (lung edge > 2 cm)→chest tube + admit
  • < 20% (< 2 cm), stable→O2, observe 4–6 h, repeat CXR

Observation armO2 ↑ pleural air absorption · repeat CXR before discharge + at 12–48 h

Haemothorax & pulmonary embolism

Haemothoraxchest tube first · repeat CXR at 4–6 h and 24 h

VATS / thoracotomy criterion Threshold
Initial chest-tube output > 1500 cc
Ongoing output > 200 cc/h for 3+ h
Haemothorax size Increasing
Despite 2 chest tubes Incomplete resolution

PEanticoagulation 3–6 months (minimum 3) · IV heparin / Lovenox → oral

High-altitude pulmonary oedema (TO)

High-altitude illness (TO)AMS, HACE, HAPE · usual threshold 8000 ft (2500 m) with rapid ascent

HAPE (TO)noncardiogenic oedema; lowlanders ascending rapidly to > 2500–3000 m · exaggerated hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, ↑ PA pressure → capillary "stress failure" leak

Onset (TO)2–5 days after arrival · rare below 2500–3000 m or after 1 week of acclimatisation

Symptoms (TO)dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, ↓ performance → rest dyspnoea, orthopnoea · gurgling + pink frothy sputum = advanced · cyanosis, tachycardia, temp ≤ 38.5 °C · rales over middle lung fields

Treatment (TO)supplemental oxygen = first line / first step ✓ · immediate descent = definitive · portable hyperbaric chamber · nifedipine 30 mg SR 12-hourly
✗ Wrong options: descent by 1000 ft · hypoxia chamber · oral nifedipine first

Remote, no medical care (TO)descent has first priority — read the stem's setting

Quadriceps Contusion

Knee & Sports · 50 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

WhoM:F 2:1 · football, soccer, rugby · competition > practice

Pathophysiology

Mechanismdirect blow compresses anterior thigh muscles against the femur

Sequencesmall fibre tears → haemorrhage + swelling in anterior compartment → myonecrosis + haematoma → scar → muscle regeneration

Thigh compartment Muscles
Anterior Sartorius, rectus femoris, vastus lateralis / medialis / intermedius
Medial Gracilis, adductor magnus / longus / brevis
Posterior Biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus

Muscle healing biology (immobilisation, losartan)

Prolonged immobilisation↑ granulation tissue (→ myositis ossificans) · scar contraction · poor organisation · ↓ tensile strength + ↓ tensile stiffness
✗ Wrong options: ↑ stiffness · better tensile strength · ↓ MO

Brief immobilisation → mobilisationparallel penetration of muscle fibres through (limited) scar, in line with native muscle · ↑ myotubules, early nerve regeneration, ↓ inflammation
✗ Wrong options: lymphocyte / macrophage infiltrate · ↓ nerve fibrils · narrowed myotubes

Immobilisation alonedisorganised fibre penetration through dense scar

Losartan (angiotensin II receptor blocker)↑ muscle regeneration, ↓ fibrosis (animal model) · ↓ apoptotic cascade · thought to act via insulin-like growth factor blockade (OB)
✗ Wrong options: aspirin · allopurinol · acetaminophen · bupropion

PRP + losartan↑ angiogenesis + follistatin, ↓ phosphorylated Smad2/3, ↓ fibrosis

3Presentation

Historycollision / direct blow in competition

Painworsens over first 24–48 h · worse with dynamic movement + knee flexion

Examswelling, ecchymosis, point tenderness · compare firmness + circumference · palpable defect = partial / complete tear · ± knee effusion · ↓ knee flexion · antalgic gait

Straight leg raisetests extensor mechanism · able (even with pain) → extensor mechanism intact

Distal NV examscreen for thigh compartment syndrome

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
X-ray Only for severe injury with suspected fracture · chronic → myositis ossificans ("egg-shell" calcification)
MRI Concern for extensor mechanism disruption · best for soft tissue · oedema / haematoma in anterior compartment
CT for arterial extravasation not part of initial work-up (no signs of active bleeding)

Grade (knee ROM at 24 h) Knee flexion
Mild > 90°
Moderate 45–90°
Severe < 45°

Quadriceps contusion
  • All acute → 120° FLEXION 24–48 h + ICE + NSAIDs→PT
  • Compartment syndrome→THIGH FASCIOTOMY

    • painful, ↓ ROM / strength, MATURE (6–12 mo)→RESECT

Immobiliseknee in 120° flexion (ace wrap / hinged brace) immediately, 24–48 h · cryotherapy, NSAIDs · start at once to limit haematoma

Thenstretching + active ROM, protected WB with crutches → sport-specific rehab once full pain-free ROM

✗ Wrong options: CT for extravasation · emergent fasciotomy · splint in extension · MRI for extensor rupture

Knee immobilised in 120° flexion → injury?quadriceps contusion
✗ Wrong options: iliac crest contusion (hip pointer leg in extension) · lesser trochanter avulsion · hamstring rupture · sports hernia

MRI next dayhaematoma in anterior compartment of thigh
✗ Wrong options: meniscal, MCL, ACL, hamstring tears

Study Cohort Result
Jackson Midshipmen, 24 h hyperflexion RTP 3.5 days · MO 1 / 23
Aronen 47 military, 120° for 24 h RTP 3.5 days
Ryan 117 West Point cadets Disability mild 13 d, severe 21 d · MO 9%

Indicationcompartment syndrome (from rupture of deep perforating branches of deep femoral vessels)

Myositis ossificans

> 1.2 Patella alta Inferior pole patellar sleeve avulsion, patellar tendon rupture

Type Extensor mechanism Treatment

Indication Procedure

Suturesnonabsorbable, running locking in tendon, free ends through transpatellar drill holes or tied to suture anchors · retinaculum → heavy absorbable sutures

Site Where Who

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
AP chest X-ray Negative in up to 60% of rib fractures (any cause) · may show line or callus
