1Basics

Epidemiology

Aka (TO)coxa saltans = dancer's hip · a rare disease (TO)

Whoathletes + dancers in teens / twenties · ballet dancers + athletes needing repetitive extreme hip flexion + abduction (TO)

Common in (TO)dancers · applies to snapping hip generally and internal snapping
✗ Wrong options: gymnasts · long-distance runners · cyclists

Painless snappingup to 10% of general population → normal (OB)

Types & causes

Type Cause Snap / pain
External — most common (Orthobullets, OB, TO) ITB over greater trochanter · also TFL or gluteus medius over GT (OB) Lateral · visible
Internal Iliopsoas over femoral head, iliopectineal ridge / eminence, lesser trochanter exostoses, iliopsoas bursa · iliofemoral ligament (OB) Anterior · audible click
Intra-articular Loose bodies (traumatic, synovial chondromatosis), labral tears, osteochondral fragments (TO) Catching, locking, clicking

Extra- vs intra-articular (TO)extra-articular more common · divided into internal + external · external more common than internal

See vs hearexternal snapping seen from across the room · internal snapping heard from across the room

Internal snapping cause (TO)thickened iliopsoas tendon snapping over iliopectineal eminence
✗ Wrong options: labral tear · ITB over GT · FAI

Iliacus (OB)may contribute as it overlies anterior capsule + superior pubic rami

Internal snapping (iliopsoas) – anatomy

Iliopsoas origin + insertionanterior surfaces + lower borders of L1–L5 transverse processes + iliac fossa → lesser trochanter
✗ Wrong options: greater trochanter

Distractor structures (OB)anterior → posterior acetabulum = labrum (tear → pain on FADIR) · external lip of iliac crest → lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy's tubercle) = ITB
✗ Wrong options: medial condyle

Snap mechanicsiliopsoas tendon lateral to iliopectineal eminence in full flexion → snaps medially as hip returns to neutral

Tendon bands (Philippon, OB)single 28.3%, double 64.2%, triple 7.5% · psoas major most medial, primary iliacus tendon lateral → more than one tendon may need release

3Presentation

Symptomssnapping in / around hip · painful or painless · patient can reproduce it · worse with activity

Clicking / lockingsuggests intra-articular pathology

Pain (TO)tendon inflamed → snapping becomes painful · internal → anterior pain + audible click · external → lateral pain + click

External snapping (iliotibial band) – Ober test

Exampalpate greater trochanter as hip actively flexed · pressure stops the snapping → confirms

Ober testlimited hip adduction with hip extended ✓ · lateral decubitus, can't adduct across midline
✗ Wrong options: adduction in flexion · abduction flexed / extended · bow-legged gait

WhyTFL flexes + abducts hip → contracture limits extension + adduction

Prone Ober (Gautam)stabilises pelvis, holds extension → quantifies contracture

Internal snapping – provocative manoeuvres

Source Manoeuvre reproducing internal snap
Orthobullets Passive flexed + ER → extended + IR
OB (Yen) Flexion-abduction-ER (FABER) → extension, adduction, IR
OB (Frank, JAAOS 2013) Flexed + IR → extended + ER
OB Supine, flex > 90° → extend to neutral; accentuate with FABER in flexion, adduction + IR while extending
OB Flexion + extension, or flexion + ER + abduction
TO Rotate the extended + adducted hip IR / ER · flex the extended hip · extend the flexed hip

Manoeuvre conflictOrthobullets / Yen (ER → IR on extending) vs Frank (IR → ER on extending) — read the options; FABER → neutral is the commonest stem

Dancer, popping on FABER → neutralinternal snapping · no pain on IR of flexed hip → labral tear unlikely

Released psoas tendon — pre-op findingsnapping with active hip flexion ✓ · FABER → neutral triggers popping ✓

Finding (OB distractor) Diagnosis
Positive Ober External snapping (ITB / TFL)
Pain on IR + ER with hip + knee extended · IR only to neutral at 90° flexion, full ER Pincer FAI
↓ IR, limited FABER → FADIR, positive impingement (flexion, adduction, IR) Cam FAI
↓ active ROM, catching, locking, grinding on passive motion Intra-articular loose bodies
Loose bodies on X-ray Synovial chondromatosis → loose body removal
Labral tear on MRI Secondary to FAI → repair vs debridement
Pain on half sit-up + tender pubic ramus Athletic pubalgia

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical for external + internal (TO: mainly clinical in extra-articular) · advanced imaging usually needed for intra-articular

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
X-ray — AP pelvis / hip Usually normal · rule out synovial chondromatosis · occasional calcification near lesser trochanter (OB)
Dynamic ultrasound Best to confirm internal snapping (shows tendon in motion) · shows snapping band (internal or external) · guides diagnostic injection (trochanteric bursa / iliopsoas sheath / joint)
MRI (often arthrogram) Rule out intra-articular pathology + mimics · inflamed bursa · dynamic USG / MRI help intra-articular diagnosis (TO)
Iliopsoas bursography Contrast into bursa under fluoroscopy → tendon seen · ± therapeutic injection · radiation to pelvis

Confirm internal snapping (OB ×2)ultrasound
✗ Wrong options: conventional MRI · CT arthrogram · weight-bearing X-ray · fluoroscopy without contrast · bone scan · CT · plain radiographs

US anatomy (OB)hyperechoic oval iliopsoas tendon anterior to superior pubic ramus, posterior to hypoechoic iliacus

5Management

Snapping hip
  • Painless→no treatment
  • Painful, acute (< 6 months)→activity modification
  • Persistent, painful, limits ADLs→PT stretching + corticosteroid injection
  • Failed nonop→surgery by type
    • External→GT bursa excision + ITB Z-plasty
    • Internal→iliopsoas tendon release / lengthening
    • Intra-articular (MRI loose body / labral tear)→hip arthroscopy

Nonop (TO)NSAIDs, ice, rest, ultrasonic + interferential therapy, stretching of iliopsoas + ITB → effective in majority · local anaesthetic + corticosteroid into bursa / tendon sheath

Resistant (TO)surgical release + lengthening of iliopsoas tendon and ITB

Intra-articular (TO)arthroscopic loose body removal + labral repair = treatment of choice

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Painful external snapping, failed nonop GT bursa excision + ITB Z-plasty
Snapping after THR GT bursa excision + ITB Z-plasty
Painful internal snapping, failed nonop Iliopsoas tendon release
Intra-articular, failed nonop + MRI loose bodies / labral tear Hip arthroscopy — loose body removal, labral debridement / repair

External snapping (iliotibial band) – Z-plasty

Mainstaystretching (positive Ober = tight ITB) · often PT alone · occasional steroid injection for profound GT bursitis

Runner pattern (OB)long symptom duration · downward leg (left leg running on left side of road)

Most reliable surgeryZ-plasty of ITB near proximal origin · may be endoscopic
✗ Wrong options: release at Gerdy's tubercle — not described · iliopsoas release · labral debridement · FAI debridement

Results (OB)Z-plasty good in 10 patients (Faraj) · release good in 16 patients / 17 hips (White)

Internal snapping (iliopsoas) – release

Nonop success (Gruen, OB)63% of 30 improve nonop · rest do well with open lengthening

Open approachesanterior, medial, ilioinguinal, iliofemoral · partial or complete release · traditionally open → now arthroscopic

Arthroscopic routesendoscopic at lesser trochanter · transcapsular at the hip joint: from central compartment (Orthobullets) · from peripheral compartment (OB) — read the options

Ilizaliturri RCT (OB)lesser trochanter (10) vs transcapsular (9) → both ↑ WOMAC, no difference · both effective + reproducible

Regeneration (Marquez Arabia, OB)27 patients · tendon regenerates in all by 23 months (84% of original circumference) · all 5/5 hip flexion · muscle fibres attach directly to proximal femoral shaft → no retraction

Post-opno hip flexion strengthening for 6 wk

Frequency Most common Less Least (extra > intra)
Site Lateral, visible Anterior / groin, audible Deep, catching / locking

Spontaneous Osteonecrosis of the Knee (SONK)

Knee & Sports · 56 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology

Whomiddle-aged + elderly females · women > 55 yr (Orthobullets, OB) · women > 60 yr (OB5977) — read the options

Joints99% only one joint

Siteepiphysis of medial femoral condyle (weight-bearing MFC) · also lateral femoral condyle, patella (OB) · tibial plateau (OB)

Pareek (OB)223 patients with subchondral insufficiency fracture: femur 69%, tibia 55%, medial compartment 89% · > 5 yr: 47% surgery, 37% arthroplasty (~⅓ → TKA)

Ecker + Lotke (OB)15 patients (16 knees), medial tibial plateau tenderness · first X-ray lucent in 9 / 16, all 16 eventually · TKA 9, UKA 3, 2 refused, 2 resolved

Types of knee osteonecrosis

Type Fact
Spontaneous (SONK) Most common · idiopathic · MFC · elderly women
Secondary Risk factors (lupus, alcohol, sickle cell) · more diffuse · see osteonecrosis chapter
Post-arthroscopic Rarest · after meniscectomy, age > 55 yr (Di Caprio)

Pathophysiology

Core lesionsubchondral insufficiency fracture in poor-quality bone → crescent-shaped osteonecrosis

Cascade (OB)SIF of MFC → osteonecrosis + flattening → degenerative posterior horn medial meniscus tear

Meniscusposterior horn medial meniscal tears, may involve the root · root injuries in up to 80% of SONK (OB)

Root tear (Bhatia)loss of hoop stresses → extrusion → ↑ tibiofemoral contact pressure ≈ total meniscectomy

Post-arthroscopicmostly after partial meniscectomy → altered biomechanics + loss of shock absorption → insufficiency fracture → crescent osteonecrosis

Weight bearingexacerbates · treatment based on size + signal (Zaremski)

3Presentation

Onsetsudden severe knee pain · worse at night + with weight bearing

Exameffusion · ROM limited by pain · tenderness over MFC / medial joint line · slight synovitis

Tibial plateau lesion (OB)medial pain + tenderness, ROM normal, no deformity · misdiagnosed as degenerative meniscus or OA

Post-arthroscopic patternwell at 2 wk after partial medial meniscectomy → ↑ medial pain at 6 wk → MRI: osteonecrosis
✗ Wrong options: osteomyelitis (no infection signs) · advanced OA · inflammatory arthritis · osteochondral lesion

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
X-ray — standing AP + lateral of hip, knee + ankle Diagnostic in advanced disease · radiolucent subchondral lesion · flattened MFC · osteopenic area in medial tibial plateau on lateral · early films may be normal
MRI Most useful study · confirms + sizes lesion → guides treatment
MRI — lesion Crescent-shaped · subchondral hypointense crescent line, cortical irregularity
MRI — signal T1 marrow hypointensity + T2 hyperintensity (oedema) · serpiginous border · localised low-signal area + surrounding oedema

Diagnosis – MRI (osteonecrosis vs bone bruise / insufficiency fracture)

74-yr-old woman, acute medial pain, no traumaosteonecrosis
✗ Wrong options: OA · RA · medial meniscal tear · transient osteoporosis

52-yr-old man, sudden atraumatic pain, worse at night, tibial plateau lesionosteonecrosis
✗ Wrong options: CRPS (MRI normal) · OA (both MFC + MTP involved) · osteosarcoma (bone-forming) · inflammatory arthritis (whole knee)

28-yr-old skier, MRI after injurybone bruise · ↑ T2 = haemorrhage from trabecular microfractures · common after ACL + MCL injury
✗ Wrong options: osteosarcoma · bucket-handle tear · LCL tear · tibial spine avulsion

Concurrent injury with SONK (OB) Likely?
Horizontal tear of posterior horn medial meniscus ✓ Most likely
Complex lateral meniscus tear No (medial predilection)
PCL tear No
Patellofemoral arthritis No
LCL avulsion (lateral epicondyle) No

Differential diagnosis

Condition Who / key fact
SONK Elderly women, MFC (weight-bearing), 99% one joint
Osteochondritis dissecans Adolescent / young males, lateral aspect of MFC
Transient osteoporosis Young–middle-aged men
Bone bruise / occult fracture Trauma, bone fragility, overuse
Secondary osteonecrosis Risk factors, multifocal

5Management

SONK
  • Most / pre-collapse / small (< 3.5 cm)→NSAIDs, protected WB, quads PT, unloader brace
  • Failed nonop, unicompartmental→UKA
  • Failed nonop, large (> 5 cm) / collapse / diffuse→TKA
  • Younger with angular malalignment→HTO

Nonopmainstay (most resolve, self-limiting) · NSAIDs, narcotics, protected WB · PT for quadriceps strengthening · unloader brace, sometimes bisphosphonates (OB) · good results

Post-arthroscopicmost nonop · protected WB 4–8 wk (Di Caprio)

Timing (OB)most patients seen post-collapse → arthroplasty treatment of choice · pre-collapse treatment controversial

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Failed nonop, small lesion, one compartment UKA
Failed nonop, large lesion / bone collapse, diffuse / multicompartment TKA
Angular malalignment (younger) · offload an osteochondral allograft HTO
Younger / active (OB) Microfracture, osteochondral allograft, HTO
Lesion size (OB) < 3.5 cm → nonop · > 5 cm + failed nonop → arthroplasty

59-yr-old librarian, MFC lesion, failed nonopUKA
✗ Wrong options: open biopsy (no matrix / periosteal reaction) · chest CT + bone scan (subchondral condyle not a metastatic site) · OATS (defect size + age) · valgus HTO (59 yr, no varus)

58-yr-old, antiphospholipid, crescentic collapse, failed PT / NSAIDs / PRParthroplasty
✗ Wrong options: core decompression (can't treat full-thickness collapse) · HTO (younger + angular deformity) · medial root repair (doesn't fix cartilage loss) · stem cells (not FDA approved)

Treatment – unicompartmental / total arthroplasty & outcomes

UKA for SONK — truereliable long-term outcomes · treatment of choice for severe localised disease · TKA rarely needed as primary

UKA traps✗ Wrong options: only for spontaneous (works for secondary localised too) · higher failure than OA (comparable) · tibial stress fracture commonest failure · TKA needed because UKA fails

UKA series (OB) Result
Myers (systematic review) TKA / UKA for SONK ≈ for OA (correct indications)
Parratte Pain relief 96% (≥ 3 yr) · 12-yr survivorship 96.7% · spontaneous + secondary
Heyse (52) 97.3% satisfied · survival 93.1% at 10 yr, 90.6% at 15 yr
Bruni (84) 10-yr survival 89% · revisions: tibial subsidence 4, aseptic loosening 3 · no lateral progression
Kaneko (61) 10-yr implant survival 90%
Chalmers (46) Secondary ON less durable than SONK · failure from arthritis progression

Commonest reason for revision after UKAprogression of arthritis (OB213949) · aseptic loosening most often (OB213790) · loosening + progression both (OB213790 answers) · subsidence + loosening, no progression (Bruni) — read the options
✗ Wrong options: aseptic loosening · bearing dislocation · implant failure · periprosthetic fracture

UKA contraindications (OB)inflammatory arthropathy, fixed deformity > 5–10°, motion < 90°, previous meniscectomy, symptomatic other compartment

Bone marrow oedema adjuncts

Persistent BME (Akhavan)prognostic for pain, dysfunction, cartilage damage · surgery: core decompression, bone-graft injections, arthroplasty

Zoledronic acid (Flores-Robles)primary BMES (ankle > hip) · 75% complete response at 12 months

Subchondroplasty (Cohen)fluoroscopic calcium phosphate injection into bone marrow lesions · ↑ VAS + IKDC to 2 yr

Steroids & Stimulants

Knee & Sports · 57 / 61

1Basics

Anabolic steroids – mechanism & adverse effects (lipids, aggression, alopecia, surgical risk)

What they aresynthetic derivatives of testosterone (anabolic-androgenic steroids, AAS) · oral or injection · mimic testosterone + dihydrotestosterone → ↑ protein synthesis

Primary mechanism of ↑ muscle↑ production of messenger RNA
✗ Wrong options: ↑ cortisol production · VEGF · ↓ HDL (HDL falls but doesn't affect muscle)

Other actionsstimulate GH release · reverse / attenuate cortisol (catabolic hormones) → ↓ catabolism · more intense + sustained workouts · ↑ strength, ↓ recovery time · used to gain muscle + lose fat · ↑ erythropoiesis
✗ Wrong options: ↑ fat

Examplesmethandrostenolone (Dianabol): first made 1960, most used + abused steroid worldwide · stanozolol: Winstrol (oral) / Winstrol Depot (IM), derived from dihydrotestosterone · metandienone, DHMCT (TO doping cases)

AAS adverse effect (cardiometabolic) Fact
HDL ↓ HDL (20–70%) + ↓ apolipoprotein A1 (main HDL particle protein) ✓ (✗ Wrong options: ↑ HDL)
LDL ↑ LDL > 20% (OB) · ↑ or no effect on LDL (OB) · ↑ LDL, hypercholesterolaemia (Orthobullets)
Coronary risk Lipid changes → CAD risk 3–6× · premature CV events
MI in young athlete ↑ LDL (+ ↓ HDL) ✓ · ↑ O2 demand at peak exercise + accelerated atherosclerosis (✗ Wrong options: direct endothelial damage · ↓ BP · conduction change)
Blood pressure ↑ systolic + diastolic (hypertension) (✗ Wrong options: ↓ BP)
Heart LVH, impaired diastolic filling, thrombosis
Ventricular arrhythmia Cause of sudden death (✗ Wrong options: cause of CAD) · fatal cases in small case series
Coagulation ↑ factor VII, IX + thromboxane → hypercoagulable → ↓ bleeding time (✗ Wrong options: ↑ bleeding time)
Liver Liver tumours (Orthobullets) · ↑ liver enzymes (OB) · oral AAS induce hepatic enzymes → less sensitive to anaesthetics (✗ Wrong options: impaired liver function)
Fluid Mineralocorticoid effect + diuretics used to mask it → fluid + electrolyte imbalance ✓
Ventilation Large muscle mass + high calories → ↑ O2 use + CO2 → ↑ ventilatory requirement (✗ Wrong options: lowered O2 requirement)
Spleen No effect (✗ Wrong options: splenomegaly)
Immune Immunosuppression (OB)
AAS adverse effect (endocrine, skin, MSK, psych) Fact
Gonadal Testicular atrophy (40–51%) · ↓ gonadotropins + sex hormones (oestrogen, testosterone) → ↓ BMD, oligo- / azoospermia (↓ sperm count) · uterine atrophy
Gynaecomastia 10–34%
Skin Acne (40–54%) · cutaneous striae (34%) · injection-site pain (36%) · alopecia / male-pattern baldness
Female Irreversible deepening of voice (Orthobullets)
Child Growth retardation
MSK Tendon + muscle injury / rupture (e.g. pectoralis major) · osteonecrosis of hip (OB) · ↑ body weight
Behaviour Aggression, hostility, violence = most common ✓ · psychosis, depression, mania rare · suicidal behaviour · no drug dependence (✗ Wrong options: like narcotics)
Not linked Decreased vision ✓ (methandrostenolone EXCEPT question)

Reversibilityalopecia = only nonreversible effect (OB) · Orthobullets also lists irreversible female voice deepening — read the options · on stopping: hypertrophy + training gains lost quickly, acne + personality effects reversible

Lipids after stoppingHDL / LDL ratios return to pre-existing levels (OB) · changes persist after withdrawal (Hartgens, OB) — read the options

Surgery + anaesthesia in AAS userfluid and electrolyte imbalance ✓
✗ Wrong options: ↑ bleeding time (actually ↓) · impaired liver function · lowered O2 requirement · splenomegaly

Other hormones – HGH, androstenedione, DHEA, EPO, somatotropin

Agent Source / mechanism Effect Adverse
Human growth hormone (HGH) Most abundant pituitary product · direct anabolic (amino acids → protein) · popular AAS substitute · IGF-1 similar ↑ muscle size, not strength Myopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, insulin resistance (Orthobullets) · acromegaly, heart disease, cardiac failure, glucose intolerance (OB)
Androstenedione Androgen from adrenal glands + gonads Potent anabolic · liver → testosterone As testosterone
DHEA Natural, adrenal cortex → androstenedione → testosterone = testosterone effects
Erythropoietin (EPO) Stimulates Hb / RBC production · doping agent ↑ O2-carrying capacity ↑ blood viscosity → stroke / MI · ischaemic + thromboembolic events, HTN, flu-like symptoms, hyperkalaemia (OB)
Somatotropin Growth hormone Type 1 hypertrophy, type 2 atrophy —
Glucagon Fasting hormone Catabolic to skeletal muscle —

Glucagonmobilises + uses stored nutrients to maintain fasting glucose → catabolic ✓ · acts mainly on liver (insulin: liver, adipose, muscle)

Beta blockers – pharmacology (TO)

Actioncompetitive antagonists of adrenaline + noradrenaline at β-receptors · β1: heart, kidney · β2: lungs, GI tract, vascular smooth muscle, skeletal muscle · β3: fat cells

Haemodynamics↓ HR + ↓ cardiac output, no effect on stroke volume · ↓ myocardial O2 demand

In endurance sport↑ perceived exertion, ↓ cardiac output + VO2max, earlier fatigue + lactate threshold, may worsen EIB / asthma → avoid in asthmatics + endurance athletes

Why banned in precision sports↓ HR, ↓ hand tremor, anxiolysis → steadiness (archery, shooting, billiards)

Definitionnon-therapeutic gene therapy · DNA inserted via vector to enhance performance (✗ Wrong options: restore missing gene function) · banned by WADA in 2003 ✓ (✗ Wrong options: 2001, 2006, 2008)

Gene doping (TO) Detail
Viral vector Efficient · immune response may ↓ effect · = transduction
Non-viral (bacterial plasmid) No immune response · = transfection
Strength genes IGF-1, myostatin
Endurance genes EPO, PPARδ (fibre-type switch; TO text prints "fast type 1 → slow type 2"), PEP carboxylase, VEGF
Tissue repair genes BMPs, endorphins
Detection — direct Doping vector
Detection — indirect Consequences: transcriptomics (mRNA), proteomics (protein set), metabolomics (non-protein low-MW metabolites)
Risks Immune response to viral vector (SIRS), autoimmunity to recombinant protein, no expression, insertional mutagenesis

Orthokine vs PRPboth autologous blood · Orthokine cultured at higher temperature · ↑ growth factors per procedure · blocks IL-1 → anti-inflammatory · FDA: too much manipulation → unapproved drug

Jet lagcircadian desynchronisation after rapid travel across ≥ 3 time zones · poor sleep onset / maintenance, fatigue, ↓ motivation + concentration, ↓ appetite, altered bowel · phase markers: core body temperature, melatonin

Jet lag intervention (TO) Examples
Melatonin 0.5–5 mg · hypnotic + chronobiotic
Melatonin analogues Tasimelteon, ramelteon
Sedatives Benzodiazepines (temazepam)
Stimulants Amodafinil, caffeine — ✓ used, not depressants
Non-drug Timed exercise, sleep, light, meal timing / composition
Caveats Drugs only up to 4 days after arrival · consider DVT risk

Jet lag odd one outdepressants ✓ (other options: glucocorticoids, melatonin analogues, sedatives)

Melatonin timing1–2 h before sleep, up to 4 nights after arrival ✓ · dose 1–5 mg (child 1–2 mg) · after food, don't crush / chew · avoid with caffeine, alcohol · avoid in galactose intolerance, congenital lactase deficiency, glucose–galactose malabsorption · melatonin dose 0.5–5 mg (jet-lag table) vs 1–5 mg (dosing note) — read the options
✗ Wrong options: 30 min · 2–4 h · 3–6 h

Melatonin physiologyN-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine from serotonin, pineal · retina → SCN → pineal · rises after sundown, peaks 2–4 am · sleep = ↑ melatonin + ↓ body temperature · extrapineal: retina, marrow, platelets, skin, lymphocytes, cerebellum, GI enterochromaffin cells (follows tryptophan intake) · child side effects: agitation, bed-wetting, dizziness, drowsiness, headache · patches, tablets, liquids, gummies, spray

Melatonin timing effectafternoon / evening → phase advance · early morning → phase delay

↑ free tryptophanprotein with more Trp than LNAA · CHO (insulin drives BCAA into muscle → ↑ free Trp : BCAA) · high-fat meal (↑ FFA) · strenuous exercise

Mediateam doctor may give only own name + country / practice ✓
✗ Wrong options: player name + injury · drugs / treatment · photo with athlete

Team physician ethics (TO) Point
Conflict of interest Personal physician = athlete's health · team physician = team's health + fitness to compete
Confidentiality Contract may require sharing with management · never with media
Decision-making Explain all alternatives, risks, benefits
Autonomy Hierarchical team culture → players may not feel free to opt out
Informed consent Competent · risks + benefits explained · understood · voluntary
Return to play Main ethical conflict · sports medicine physician decides on athlete's short + long-term health, not result or coach
Advertising Once illegal in USA · still illegal in Italy, Germany
Medical bags (TO) Contents
Off-field (pre / post game) Physio supplies bag (strapping), doctor supplies bag (suture box, otoscope, HIA tablets in rugby), medications case (locked), recovery devices, medical folder (allergies, medications)
On-field Physio pitch bag (tape, blood management), doctor pitch bag (player-specific drugs, inhalers, contact lenses)
Pitch-side Splints bag, emergency bag (defibrillator, analgesia, O2), vacuum mattress, spinal board + blocks, collar
Odd one out "Athlete medical bag" ✓ — athletes only clear sports kits through customs

Bag ruleslist agreed at start of season · check governing-body standards · check customs rules for each country + carry documentation · consistent packing · checklist; post-game list of items to replace

Medications caseoral analgesics, anti-inflammatories, antihistamines, antiemetics, Fucidin, chloramphenicol ointment, loperamide, Buscopan, GTN, aspirin, OCP, tranexamic + mefenamic acid

On-field tipsgloves · gauze + nose plugs under glove on dorsal thenar of non-dominant hand · saline pods · labelled contact lenses + pocket mirror · energy gels, hair bands · pocket mask, methoxyflurane, oropharyngeal airways in outer pockets

The Female Athlete

Knee & Sports · 58 / 61

1Basics

Physiologic sex differences

Women have↑ body fat % · ↓ maximal O₂ consumption + haemoglobin · ↓ cardiac output · ↓ muscle mass + strength

↑ incidence in womenpatellofemoral disorders, stress fractures, ACL injuries

Triad definition & components (low energy availability, amenorrhoea, BMD; thyroid not included)

Component Detail
Low energy availability ± disordered eating (with or without an eating disorder) · insufficient caloric intake for demand
Menstrual dysfunction Amenorrhoea / oligomenorrhoea · energy imbalance, low body fat, hypothalamic–pituitary axis changes
↓ Bone mineral density Osteoporosis (often presents as a stress fracture)

NOT componentsstress fracture (TO) — a consequence, not a component · thyroid dysfunction (OB) · ligamentous laxity, ↑ ACL tears, hirsutism (OB)

Dysmenorrhoea in the options (TO)counted under menstrual dysfunction → not the answer; stress fracture is the odd one out

Eating disorderboth "LEA with an eating disorder" and "LEA without an eating disorder" = components (OB)

Namesfemale athlete triad, coined 1992 by ACSM (adolescent + young female athletes) · anorexia athletica = synonym (Orthobullets, OB) · RED-S (relative energy deficiency in sport) — IOC 2014, broader, includes males

Anorexia athletica criteria (OB)GI complaints, restriction of caloric intake, weight loss, menstrual dysfunction · requires ABSENCE of an affective disorder (e.g. depression) · true osteoporosis relatively uncommon in female athletes → traditional triad criteria rarely met
✗ Wrong options: presence of affective disorder

Thyroid (OB)not a core component; may occur secondarily to the metabolic + hormonal disruption
✗ Wrong options: core component · unrelated · primary cause · always present / needed for diagnosis

Associated (OB)amenorrhoea, osteoporosis, ↓ immune function, insufficient caloric intake · not low LDL → actually ↑ LDL (hypoestrogenism)

Cardiovascular (OB)endothelial dysfunction (nitric oxide imbalance between vasodilators + vasoconstrictors) → atherosclerosis, ↑ future CVD · RED-S: dyslipidaemia + ↑ visceral adiposity → precocious coronary atherosclerosis

Pathophysiology – energy deficit & hormones

Root causelow energy availability (LEA) = cornerstone of RED-S + triad · drives the hormonal + bone deficits

AxisLEA disrupts hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis (OB) · "hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis disruption" (OB, RED-S) → reproductive hormonal dysfunction

Bone↓ BMD from ↑ bone turnover · loss of oestrogen / progesterone protective effect → osteoporosis → stress fractures

Undernutrition (TO)↓ IGF-1 + ↓ leptin → ↓ appetite stimulation, menstrual problems, impaired bone remodelling → osteopenia + stress fractures

Marker Direction / value Why
Cortisol ↑ Maintains blood glucose (OB)
Free T3 ↓ Lowers basal metabolic rate (OB)
LH ↓ Diverts energy from reproduction (OB)
IGF-1, leptin ↓ Undernutrition (TO)
Oestrogen ↓ Hypoestrogenism from menstrual dysfunction
LDL ↑ Hypoestrogenism (OB) (✗ Wrong options: low LDL)
Serum calcium Normal Not a useful next test (OB)
25(OH)D Normal ≥ 30 ng/mL · < 75.8 nmol/L = stress fracture risk TO
Iron status Ferritin / transferrin ratio TO — see Calcium & iron
COL5A1 CC genotype under-represented in females with ACL rupture Orthobullets

Hormone trap (OB)↑ cortisol, ↓ free T3, ↓ LH
✗ Wrong options: ↑ T3 · ↑ LH · ↓ cortisol

Amenorrhoea prevalence Source

Sex differences in ACL injury

Risk2–10× males (Orthobullets, this topic), esp. pivoting sports · ACL Tear chapter: 4.5 : 1 (Orthobullets), 2–9× (OB), ~8× (TO) — read the options

Factor (Orthobullets) Detail
Landing biomechanics + neuromuscular control Conditioning + strength = biggest role · land with knee in more extension + valgus (from hip IR)
Notch Smaller notch
Ligament Smaller ACL
Cyclic hormones ↑ risk in first half (preovulatory phase) of cycle
Alignment Leg alignment
Genetics CC genotype of COL5A1 under-represented in females with ACL rupture

Menstrual phase conflictpreovulatory (Orthobullets, this topic) · no consensus (ACL Tear chapter) — read the options

✗ Wrong options: ACL size · oestrogen levels · notch size · valgus alignment

Preventionneuromuscular training (jump training), plyometric conditioning ↓ ACL rate · NM training ↑ medial hamstring EMG → ↓ dynamic valgus on sidecutting (Zebis)

3Presentation

Stress fracture as presentation – menstrual & nutritional work-up

First contactoften presents to the orthopaedic surgeon / team physician with a stress (osteoporotic) fracture

Stress fracture riskamenorrhoeic athletes 2–4× eumenorrhoeic (TO) · most frequent site = tibia (TO) · menstrual irregularity → more and multiple stress fractures (Warren)

Sites (OB)weight-bearing cortical bone: tibia, metatarsals, femur · not usually trabecular bone

NOT ↑ in amenorrhoeic athletes (OB)femoral head AVN, ACL rupture, labral tear, FAI → answer = stress fracture

Amenorrhoea + Beighton 4 (volleyball)at risk of tension-side femoral neck stress fracture (Figure A) · Beighton > 5/9 = hypermobility (OB)

Runner, tibial stress fracture, BMI 16, no menses 7 mopoor caloric intake = most common cause of amenorrhoea in female athletes
✗ Wrong options: NF1 (tibial bowing, MPNST) · osteofibrous dysplasia (anterior eccentric tibial lesion in child) · EWS-FLI1 (Ewing) · focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia (abrupt varus at metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction)

4th MT stress fracture + contralateral 1 yr agoamenorrhoea 12 months
✗ Wrong options: daily OCP (helps regulate menses) · multiple sports · T-score −0.5 (normal) · BMI 26 (normal)

Thresholds (OB)BMI < 21 predictive of stress fracture (some) · T-score < −1.0 osteopenia, < −2.5 osteoporosis

Marine recruits (OB)~5% of female recruits fracture in 13 wk basic training · ~40% femoral / pelvic (more severe) · biggest risk = no menses in the previous year (vs 10–12 menses) · lesser irregularity → trend only
✗ Wrong options: prior mileage · running frequency · self-rated fitness · race

Peak bone masshypoestrogenic athletes may never reach peak bone mass → possibly irreversible deficit · neither calcium nor ↑ activity compensates · lost BMD may never be regained

Runner's nipples (TO)

Cause (TO)irritation from rubbing against clothing · cold-weather sports (cold → hard, prominent nipples) · common in cyclists (cold + perspiration)
✗ Wrong options: warm weather precipitates

Treatment (TO)tape nipples to restrict movement · petroleum jelly, moisturisers, vitamin E soaks · sports bra

Sports bra (TO)firm but elastic (room for padding), non-abrasive, absorptive · crossed Y-shaped back, no hooks / fasteners · no seams over nipple · personally fitted

Diagnostic criteria

Term Definition Source

Secondary amenorrhoea Absence of bleeding 6 months or of 3–6 consecutive cycles after normal menses (no pregnancy) OB
Amenorrhoea (RED-S) No menses for ≥ 3 months OB

Hypermobility Beighton > 5/9 OB

✗ Wrong options: ↑ volume 3 mo · pain 2 mo · missed month after peak training · ↓ volume 2 mo

Pre-participation screening (TO)triad domains = eating patterns, menstrual cycles, stress fracture history · source gives no key; the item outside the triad = supplement / drug-abuse history (inferred)

Work-up of a female athlete with a stress fracture

Any female athlete with a stress fracturework up for triad: menstrual history + nutritional consultation + bone density (OB)

DEXAfemale athlete with amenorrhoea + stress fractures (Orthobullets)

Runner, femoral neck stress fracture on MRIevaluate osteoporosis + anorexia + secondary amenorrhoea (all of the above)

Prior 5th MT stress fracture, now tension-side femoral neckfix + obtain menstrual history

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
Radiographs May be normal or equivocal · screening films may miss stress reaction
X-ray femur Smooth cortical thickening, distal medial femoral diaphysis = femoral stress injury
X-ray tibia (lateral) Anterior cortical thickening = stress reaction · "dreaded black line" = poor prognosis → surgery
MRI Preferred · rule out fracture in high-risk areas (femur, femoral neck) · before return to sport · stress reaction vs impending / complete fracture · STIR oedema (periosteum, cortex, marrow)
Bone scan Fallen out of favour — radioisotope + relatively high ionising radiation
DEXA BMD — amenorrhoea + stress fractures

Hip flexor tightness – modified Thomas test (TO)

Technique (TO)supine, knees bent over table edge · hold one knee to chest · test knee should stay at 90°, hip + posterior thigh flat on table · pass = knee stays at 90° · fail = knee extends to < 90°

Finding (TO) Interpretation Muscles short
Thigh touches table, knee stays flexed Negative —
Thigh off table, knee extends Both one- + two-joint flexors short All below
Thigh touches table, knee extends Two-joint hip flexors short Rectus femoris, TFL, sartorius
Thigh off table, knee flexes > 80° One-joint hip flexors short Iliopsoas, pectineus, adductor longus / brevis / magnus
Thigh abducts as hip extends, lateral patellar deviation, thigh IR + leg ER TFL short TFL
Hip abduction + flexion + ER and knee flexion (≥ 3 = tight) Sartorius short Sartorius
Muscle (TO) Joints crossed Actions
Iliopsoas 1 (hip) Hip flexion, ER
Pectineus 1 Hip flexion · abduction (as listed)
Adductor longus / brevis 1 Adduction, flexion, ER
Adductor magnus 1 Adductor part: flexion, adduction, ER · hamstring part: extension, IR
Rectus femoris 2 (hip + knee) Hip flexion, knee extension
TFL 2 Hip abduction, flexion, IR · knee extension
Sartorius 2 Hip flexion, abduction, ER · knee flexion

5Management

Female athlete triad with stress fracture
  • First / most critical step→multidisciplinary nutrition + psychological counselling
  • Thigh pain at rest, equivocal X-ray→stop training + MRI
  • Tension-side femoral neck→fixation + menstrual history
  • Tibial stress reaction, no fracture line→nonop + review diet and training

Treatment – nutrition rather than bisphosphonates

Arm Content
Psychological counselling Core of treatment (Sabatini) · eating behaviours, self-esteem
Dietary management Establish energy balance · ↑ weight / food intake, ↓ exercise · ↑ calcium + vitamin D
Training ↓ intensity + cross-training (↓ stress fracture risk) · limit training until menses resume
Supplements Calcium + vitamin D for osteoporosis · consider cyclic oestrogens / progesterones for osteoporosis
OCPs May help amenorrhoea (Orthobullets, OB) · use OCPs to normalise menses (TO)
Team Physician, athletic trainer, sports dietician, mental-health provider, family, coaches

Least appropriate (OB)bisphosphonates
✗ Wrong options: calcium + vitamin D · ↑ food intake · ↓ training · counselling

Advice NOT suitable (TO)"avoid OCPs" · TO Rx = OCPs to normalise menstruation + ↑ body fat via diet + prompt stress fracture care
✗ Wrong options: improve nutrition · increase body fat

Hormone conflictOCPs beneficial (Orthobullets, OB, TO) · hormone replacement does not fix the energy deficit; no longer primary Rx for functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (OB) — read the options

Most critical initial step (OB)multidisciplinary nutritional + psychological counselling to correct energy deficit
✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs + crutches (NSAIDs impair bone healing) · oral oestrogen / progesterone · 6 wk complete rest (deficit persists → recurrence) · DEXA first

Tibial stress reaction, 3 mo amenorrhoea (15 yr)discuss eating habits + training regimen · stop the precipitating activity, protected WB rehab
✗ Wrong options: keep running · CAM walker / casting (stiffness) · IM nail (no clear fracture line → nonop first)

✗ Wrong options: ↓ intensity + PT · dietician only · bone scan + oncology · bone stimulator / US (evidence limited for femoral)

Natural courseappropriate diet + moderated exercise → natural return of menses

Recovery ratesenergy status: days–weeks (↑ IGF-1, reverses energy conservation) → menses: months (oestrogen anti-resorptive) → BMD: years

Return to sportwhen properly counselled, may return to high-endurance sport (OB)

✗ Wrong options: 500 · 1000 · 1500 mg

Tibial Shaft Stress Fractures

Knee & Sports · 59 / 61

1Basics

Epidemiology – tibia most common site

Most common stress fracture bonetibia in athletes + military training (OB)
✗ Wrong options: femur · fibula · navicular · 5th MT

Most common site (TO)posteromedial tibia, junction of middle + distal third → answer "distal third of tibia"
✗ Wrong options: 2nd MT · fibula · femoral neck

Series (Ohta-Fukushima, OB)370 athletes: tibia 49.1% > tarsals 25.3% > metatarsals 8.8% · evaluation > 3 wk after pain onset → prolonged recovery

2nd commonest2nd / 3rd MT shaft (March fracture) (TO) · tarsals (OB series) — read the options

Whorunners + military recruits · after a change in training routine · incidence in runners up to 20% (OB)

Risk factors (OB)sudden ↑ training intensity, low BMD, menstrual irregularities, low energy availability · always evaluate female athlete triad

Stress fracture sites (TO)

Site Detail (TO)
Tibia Posteromedial, middle–distal third junction — most common
2nd / 3rd MT shaft March fracture — 2nd most common
Other metatarsals —
Medial malleolus Jumpers + runners
Distal fibula Runner's fracture
Femoral neck Inferomedial (compression) commoner than superior (tension) · tension more dangerous → completes without fixation
Femoral shaft Posteromedial or medial cortex
Navicular Central third — runners / sprinters, ballet dancers, football players
Calcaneus Tuberosity — military recruits, runners
Ribs Middle ribs (4th–9th) — rowers, serratus anterior traction
Pubic ramus Female long-distance runners

Pathophysiology

Mechanismrepetitive submaximal loads → resorption > formation · abrupt ↑ duration / intensity / frequency without rest → ↑ osteoclast activity (OB)

Bone type conflictlinear microfractures in trabecular bone (Orthobullets) · weight-bearing cortical bone, not usually trabecular (OB, Female Athlete chapter) — read the options

Healingcallus → woven bone → endochondral bone formation

Why the anterior cortex failstension side from posterior muscle force (Orthobullets) · tensile forces + relative paucity of blood supply in anterior midshaft (OB)

High- vs low-risk sites – tension vs compression

Anterior cortex (tension) Posteromedial cortex (compression)
Frequency Uncommon Typical / most common
Risk High — delayed union, nonunion, propagation to complete fracture Low — usually heals
X-ray "Dreaded black line" (transverse anterior lucency) Periosteal reaction, cortical thickening
Rx Often IM nail Protected WB

Greatest risk of delayed healing / nonunion (OB)anterior cortex of tibia · 2nd + 5th MT can delay / nonunite (OB)
✗ Wrong options: posteromedial tibia · distal fibula · inferior femoral neck (compression side) · 3rd MT — heals well

High-risk sites (TO, Femoral Neck Stress Fractures chapter)tension femoral neck, tension patella, anterior tibial cortex, medial malleolus, talar neck, dorsal navicular cortex, 5th MT proximal metaphysis, great-toe sesamoids

Low-risk sites (TO, same chapter)femoral shaft, medial tibia, ribs, ulnar shaft, 1st–4th MT · 2nd MT low risk (TO) vs can delay / nonunite (OB) — read the options

Historychange in exercise routine · insidious onset · pain with running first → then daily activities / walking

✗ Wrong options: posteromedial tibial stress syndrome · gastrocnemius strain · bone contusion

Key radiology findings

Study Findings Facts
Radiographs (AP + lateral) Lateral: "dreaded black line" anteriorly (tension) · endosteal thickening · periosteal reaction + cortical thickening Often diagnostic (Orthobullets) · usually normal early → later periosteal reaction, new bone, fracture line (OB)
MRI Earliest: T2 periosteal high signal · marrow oedema · T1 linear low-signal zone Most sensitive · replacing bone scan · normal X-ray + high suspicion → MRI
Tc-99m bone scan Focal uptake in cortical and / or trabecular region Highly sensitive, low specificity (OB)

Investigation of choice (TO)MRI — best combined sensitivity + specificity even early; recommended for the whole bone-stress spectrum
✗ Wrong options: CT · clinical exam · bone scan

X-ray-negative suspected tibial stress fracture (TO)MRI — most sensitive + specific · beats bone scan + CT for soft-tissue / oedema, earlier than bone scan · sensitivity ≈ bone scan but far more precise for location + extent

MRI vs bone scan (OB)MRI better (Ishibashi)

Normal films, high suspicion (OB)trial of rest + serial radiographs also appropriate

MRI grading of bone stress injury (TO)

Grade (TO) MRI signs
1 Mild–moderate periosteal oedema on STIR, no marrow change
2 Moderate–severe periosteal oedema on STIR + marrow change on T2WI
3 Grade 2 + marrow change on T1WI
4 Fracture line visible

5Management

Tibial shaft stress fracture
  • Posteromedial / X-ray normal, MRI oedema→protected WB 4–6 wk, stop running
  • Anterior cortex, dreaded black line→reamed IM nail
    (esp. if the line violates the anterior cortex)
  • Failed nonop, complete, or fixed deadline→IM nail

Operative criteria

Indication for IM nail (OB, Orthobullets)
High-risk fracture — anterior tibial cortex ("dreaded black line", esp. violating the cortex)
Failure of nonoperative management (no improvement with rest — Boden)
Complete fracture
Need to return on a specific timeline (athletes, military)

Posteromedial compression-side fractures – protected weight bearing

Standard (most cases)activity restriction + protected weight-bearing · avoid NSAIDs (slow bone healing) · consider bone stimulator · correct nutritional deficiencies

Duration (OB)4–6 wk limited WB → progress to full WB

Runner, normal X-ray, MRI oedema, positive bone scanprotected WB 4–6 wk
✗ Wrong options: immediate return · IM nail without nonop trial · long-leg cast · biopsy

Distance runner, proximal tibial pain now with walking, normal X-ray, MRI +protected WB with crutches
✗ Wrong options: switch to elliptical · prescription NSAIDs · arthroscopy · ORIF

Pneumatic bracing + modified rest (OB, Batt)effective, but return to full activity ~12 months

Pulsed ultrasound (OB, Rue)no effect on healing or return to duty (26 servicemen, 43 fractures)

Most important factor in an athlete with a stress fracture (TO)source gives no key; best fit = correction of biomechanical + training errors (inferred) (vs immobilisation 8 wk, gradual return, analgesics)

Anterior cortex tension-side fractures – nonunion risk & intramedullary nailing

Footballer, 6 mo pain, failed nonop, anterior linear lucencytibial IM nailing — fastest WB + return
✗ Wrong options: posterior plate + graft · graft alone · cast · protected WB

Special-forces soldier, dreaded black line, deploys in 4 motibial IM nail
✗ Wrong options: activity modification + vitamin D (high-risk site, no deficiency stated) · pulsed US · pneumatic brace NWB (up to 12 mo) · observe + repeat imaging (risk of completion)

Outcome (Varner, OB)11 athletes, reamed IM nail for chronic anterior stress fracture → return to sport ~4 months

Platinganterior tension-band plating described · not posterior

IM nail caveat (OB)allows return to sport but does not guarantee healing

6Complications

Anterior cortexdelayed union, nonunion, propagation to complete fracture · highest risk of all tibial sites

Delayed diagnosisevaluation > 3 wk after pain onset → longer recovery

Tenderness Point / focal Diffuse posteromedial border Normal exam at rest

X-ray Dreaded black line (anterior) Normal · periosteal exostoses (late) Normal
Bone scan Focal, intense, all 3 phases Diffuse, longitudinal, delayed phase only —
Test MRI (oedema / line) Clinical · bone scan / MRI Compartment pressures
NSAIDs Avoid (slow healing) Used Used

Tibial Stress Syndrome (Shin Splints)

Knee & Sports · 60 / 61

1Basics

Definitionoveruse / repetitive-load injury of the shin → persistent dull anterior leg pain

Incidence10–15% of running injuries · 60% of leg pain syndromes

Locationmedial (posteromedial) tibial stress syndrome = most common · anterior (anterolateral) tibial stress syndrome · distal + posteromedial tibia

Risk factorspoor shock absorption (cement / uneven surfaces, improper shoes) · training errors (sudden ↑ intensity + duration) · > 20 miles / week · early-season hill training · previous lower-limb injury · over-pronation / ↑ internal tibial rotation

Pathophysiologytraction periostitis · anterolateral → tibialis anterior on tibia + interosseous membrane · posteromedial → tibialis posterior + soleus

Associatedfemale athlete triad (critical to diagnose + treat) · tibial stress fracture — females 1.5–3.5× risk of progression

3Presentation

Symptomsvague, diffuse pain along middle–distal tibia that ↓ with running (early) · later: pain earlier with more frequent training

Examtenderness along posteromedial tibial border, from 4 cm above medial malleolus extending up to 12 cm proximally · pes planus, tight Achilles, weak core

Provocative testpain on resisted plantarflexion

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Shin splints vs stress fracture
Radiographs Normal first 2–3 wk · late periosteal exostoses "Dreaded black line"
3-phase bone scan Diffuse, longitudinal uptake along posteromedial (posterior) tibial cortex, delayed phase (3) only · phases 1 (flow) + 2 (blood pool) normal Focal, intense hyperperfusion + hyperaemia in phases 1 + 2 · focal, fusiform uptake in phase 3
MRI Periosteal oedema → progressive marrow involvement · shows other soft-tissue injury Marrow oedema ± line

Distinguishing finding (OB)bone scan: diffuse, longitudinal uptake of posterior tibial cortex = shin splints
✗ Wrong options: shin splints scan more intense · more diffuse tenderness in stress fracture · all 3 phases positive in shin splints · pain persists longer after activity in stress fracture

Differential diagnosis – exertional leg pain

Condition Characteristics Tissue
Anterior tibial stress syndrome Diffuse anterolateral pain, worse at start, ↓ during training Periosteum
Medial tibial stress syndrome Diffuse middle–distal pain, worse at start, ↓ during training Periosteum
Tibial / fibular stress fracture Pain with running, point tenderness, dreaded black line Bone
Exertional compartment syndrome Starts 10 min into exercise, resolves 30 min after · sensory / motor loss · ↑ anterior compartment pressure Muscle + fascia
Leg tendinopathy Achilles, peroneal, tibialis posterior Tendon
Sural / SPN entrapment Dermatomal symptoms Nerve
Lumbar radiculopathy Worse sitting (lumbar tension position) Nerve
Popliteal artery entrapment Vascular studies Vessel

5Management

Nonop — first line, works in vast majorityNSAIDs, rest, activity modification

Activity modification↓ running distance, frequency + intensity by 50% · low-impact cross-training · stretching + strengthening · synthetic track · avoid hills, uneven / hard surfaces

Shoeschange every 250–500 miles (lose shock absorption) · orthotics for pes planus

Therapystrengthen invertors + evertors of the calf · local phonophoresis with corticosteroids may help

Operative (failed nonop)deep posterior compartment fasciotomy + release of painful periosteum · variable results, complete relief unlikely

6Complications

Recurrencecommon after resuming heavy activity

X vs Y

Shin splints (MTSS) Tibial stress fracture CECS
Pain with running ↓ during training (early) ↑ → walking ↑, starts ~10 min in
Tenderness Diffuse posteromedial Point Normal at rest
Bone scan Diffuse longitudinal, phase 3 only Focal, all phases —
Cause Traction periostitis Bone fatigue ↑ compartment pressure

How it's asked

"Bone scan finding separating shin splints from stress fracture?"diffuse, longitudinal uptake of posterior tibial cortex in shin splints

Visceral Blunt Trauma

Knee & Sports · 61 / 61

1Basics

Overview

Injuriesabdominal wall, spleen, liver, kidney, testicular + penile

Risk factorscontact sports, direct blows · deceleration → spleen, liver, kidney

Commonest sport injuries (Rifat, OB)abdominal wall muscle, liver, spleen · spleen = most frequent intra-abdominal organ in sport

Organ Rank / fact Clue
Spleen Most common abdominal organ in blunt trauma · most common cause of death from abdominal / visceral injury LUQ pain, Kehr's sign (left shoulder), N/V · mononucleosis
Liver 2nd most common RUQ pain → right shoulder
Kidney Contact athletes, blow to flank Haematuria (may be absent), flank ecchymosis
Abdominal wall Commonest sport injury Localised pain, pain on trunk flexion / rotation

3Presentation

Warning patternlocalised pain → diffuse pain = visceral injury

Spleennausea + vomiting · sharp LUQ pain → dull + diffuse · shoulder pain (Kehr's sign) before hypotension + collapse

Signs (Juyia, OB)referred shoulder pain, umbilical or flank ecchymosis, guarding / rebound · high index of suspicion with any abdominal pain

Diaphragmatic spasm

"Wind knocked out"direct blow to epigastrium → diaphragmatic spasm → observe, resolves, may continue play

Abdominal wall injury / rectus sheath haematoma

Causeepigastric or intramuscular vessel injury

Clinicalacute localised pain · mimics surgical abdomen (N/V) · pain on active trunk flexion or rotation

Treatmentice + rest (most) · surgical decompression if progressive + persistent pain

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
CT abdomen (± pelvis) Diagnosis for all organs — wall haematoma, spleen, liver, kidney, bowel · grades severity, guides treatment
Scrotal ultrasound (urology) Testicular rupture / haematocoele
Pelvic X-ray Fracture → posterior urethral injury

5Management

Hypotension after abdominal trauma – work-up

Athlete with abdominal blow
  • Haemodynamically unstable → fluid resuscitation + transfer to ER→abdominal CT
  • Stable, abdominal pain / haematuria→ER + CT abdomen / pelvis
  • Epigastric blow, transient breathlessness→observe, may play

Footballer, BP 70/48, vomiting ×2, resolving arm numbnessfluid resuscitation + transfer to ER for abdominal CT
✗ Wrong options: antiemetics + sideline rest · non-emergent C-spine MRI (stinger resolved) · RTP when arm settles · head CT (no concussion signs)

RTP (Juyia, OB)varies with organ + grade · up to 6 months after severe spleen / liver injury

Splenic rupture – mononucleosis risk

Monoacute splenomegaly → ↑ rupture risk with trauma

Spreadoral mucosa: sharing water bottles, kissing ✓
✗ Wrong options: creatine · spider bite (skin necrosis) · alcohol · NSAIDs on empty stomach (gastric irritation)

Timing4–21 days after infection (OB, this topic) · first 3 weeks / within a month (infectious diseases chapter)

Farley (OB)> 8,000 IM patients → 9 splenic ruptures (~0.1%; 0.1–0.5% in infectious diseases chapter)

17-yr-old, mono 1 month ago, tackled, LUQ pain, tachycardiasplenic rupture
✗ Wrong options: fractured kidney · ruptured appendix · ruptured gallbladder · pneumothorax

RTP after monono contact sport until splenomegaly resolved · radiographic surveillance debated

Spleen treatmentobservation in most · splenectomy only for severe injury · range: observation → laparotomy + packing ± splenectomy

Liver injury

Treatmentconservative: monitoring + rest

Renal contusion – haematuria

Patternmales, single blow to the flank · flank / abdominal pain, ecchymosis, haematuria

Lacrosse, right flank blow, pink urine > 5 RBC/hpf, stablerenal laceration
✗ Wrong options: splenic laceration (left side, intra-abdominal bleed not haematuria) · haemothorax (chest pain + dyspnoea) · liver laceration (no haematuria) · posterior urethral injury (displaced pelvic fracture)

Work-upCT abdomen + pelvis ASAP (risk of instability with continued bleeding)

Treatmentstable → nonop · small subset → exploration, partial / complete nephrectomy · urgent surgery: extensive bleeding with renal fracture or vascular pedicle injury

Patel (OB)grade III / IV: contact sports + skiing / snowboarding commonest · sports injuries more isolated, ↓ instability + mortality

Dangle (OB)paediatric: low-grade injuries in males commonest · few need surgery

McAleer (OB)< 5% of testicular / renal injuries from team sports, no organ loss → solitary kidney / testis may not need restriction

Penile & testicular injuries

Pudendal nerve neuropraxiacyclists · penile shaft numbness · seat modification

Testicular ruptureusually a kick → tunica albuginea rupture → haematocoele · painful firm scrotal mass, doesn't transilluminate · urology ultrasound · observation
